title: I Hold onto Myself.
author: Sobu
imageAlt: Cover image for I Hold onto Myself.

runs.text: There's a saying in Japanese -
'Ichigo Ichie'
This profound term articulates a sense of longing within me.
Ichigo Ichie
translates to the philosophy 'one time, one meeting'. It embodies the idea
that every encounter is a once-in-a-lifetime experience; that no matter how
familiar a person, place or circumstance may seem, no two moments can
ever be exactly alike.
I have a personal grudge over this term. I realise how difficult it is to
comprehend when it comes to love. Because if the kindness of my beloved, if
the lightness of our laughter, and that version of love stays in that
moment... Am I being foolish to ask for it again?
Am I longing for something that no longer exists, except the familiarity of my
own memories?
Those memories feel like a fever dream now. I am stuck by how I no longer
recognise the same face, how I cannot fathom the absence of warmth in his
voice, and how the conversations that once flowed effortlessly now seem to
stumble over an unfamiliar silence.
Then I look at myself in the mirror. Now I am suddenly consumed by the
very question I was avoiding ...
'If I lose you, do I lose myself too?'
You no longer seem like you. And if I can no longer find you in yourself,
where am I supposed to find the person, I used to be?
Perhaps, in an attempt to honour this philosophy, I must take the sharp
sword of acceptance and let it pierce my heart, allowing sorrow to wrap me
like a warm blanket, familiar in its agony- the final tribute to everything I
have yet to grieve, till my body runs cold.
But I shall murmur under my breath and say
'Don't take me with you'.
Leave me here, for I am beginning to understand the philosophy. Perhaps,
Ichigo Ichie
is not asking me to forget, but to acknowledge that some
encounters are meant to remain exactly where time left them.
I bid that time a sweet goodbye, I let what you meant to me remain frozen
there- in the days when your hands held me with a tenderness that no longer
exists. I may miss you, but I can't spend forever missing myself.
So, I shall leave you in that little pocket of time, but I shall take that version
of
me
with me. Maybe
Ichigo Ichie
will grant us another encounter; a timeline
where we share a moment again as two people who have lived entirely different
lives ever since.
But if that day ever comes, I may not recognise you, but I hope to recognise
myself. I hope the girl who once looked at you with stars in her eyes will be
there, too.
I will hold onto her not only because she loved you, but because she loved
herself too.
Yet again,
'I shall keep her and let you go'.

content: Fallen women

Only a fallen woman
Understands another fallen woman.

She will kneel, she will cry;
Will not bend at disregard.

She can feed, nurse, and care
Also bear an invisible spear;
A proud daughter and wife they ask,
A warrior hiding under the mask.

She is not a coward, nor a kind;
She carries poison in her vein.
She will stand afar in the most glorious light,
Surrounded by mockery and disgusted eyes.

The honor they cry so much for
Never could understand the meaning at all.
They call the earth mother, crave for love;
Her soul they shatter at every chance.

The beauty, the judgment, the rules
Only were made for women they fear.

They say weak, pitiful, fragile;
Not as much as the male ego they bear.

Her struggles they see as daily work,
A responsibility inherited from the birth;
Her dreams are taken, wings are crushed,
Her duties are written in her palms.

Chains are dug in her heart;
Now she can never hide or run.
Accepted bravely the brutal fate
With a silent smile and boiling tears.

The one she raises burning in the pit,
Kill her with the coldest heart?

They fear her, the fire of her eyes;
They could never achieve, nor could fight.
Her sword she held, cut the heads,
One of them become hers.

Not only the enemy she fights,
But also her dear ones;
She has fallen, in the battlefield of war.
They drag her bare body, curse and jest at her.
But I see a warrior, protected the people she cares.

title: Borrowed Feelings
author: Aparna Banik
imageAlt: Cover image for Borrowed Feelings

runs.text: Borrowed Feelings
The kittens were all bundled up together, cuddling with the mama cat to stay warm. They looked
cozy in the late autumn afternoon. The sun was almost about to set. All the birds were coming
back to their nests. She was watching them from a small oak tree. She was used to seeing them
every day - the cats, birds, people. All these wholesome scenarios created an emptiness inside
her. Always.
“Still watching the kittens?” Maya asked her with a warm smile.
“Uh-huh,” she replied with the least amount of effort she could manage.
“You should come with me sometimes to see other things,” she said exhaustedly.
“I don’t have any memory, unlike you. And no, I’m not interested in seeing your family,” she
replied in a flat tone.
“Why not? You don’t have anywhere to be.”
“Move on, woman,” she said dismissively.
Maya had been pestering her for years to accompany her while she floated to visit her family.
They were souls, so they didn’t need vehicles. Maya was 47 years old when she died. She
couldn’t move on from the grief of leaving her family so early. Many souls had difficulties moving
on. Some did eventually; some didn’t. But they all have memories of who they were, how they
died, and their families. She did not have any– including her name. She didn’t feel anything
either. Just a deep hollow inside her. Numbness was something she had gotten used to during
her eighteen years of death. While other souls grieved, laughed, and shared memories, she
simply sat in her oak tree and watched life go by.
Recently, she noticed she had begun to fade. Maya told her that she was being forgotten in the
living world. She was so tired of living like that.
Living.
What was it like being alive? She wondered sometimes.
She was tired of being the way she was and not feeling anything, not remembering anything.
Now that she had a sign that she was going to fade away like withered leaves soon, she wanted
to feel something, anything. Once, she heard from Ayan that there was a shop in the
underworld. She didn’t want to go before, but now times were changing. Ayan lived all the way
across the city in an abandoned building and only came out during full moons. By luck, today
was a full moon.
“Hey there, sunshine,” a husky voice called her out from behind, breaking her thoughts.
“What ghost creeps on another ghost?” she asked in an exasperated tone.
“It’s rare to get you worked up like that,” he laughed.
“Haha, very funny. So, how’s the wife?”
“I stopped keeping tabs on her.”
“Then why is there a hair clip in your pocket?” she asked, her eyes narrowing with a smile.
“Why are you jealous?”
“Hah! You wish,” she scoffed.
“You’re the only soul I care about, babygirl,” he cooed.
“Liar.”
“Let me take you out, and I'll prove it to you.”
“Okay,” she agreed, surprising herself.
“When will you ever–wait, what did you say?”
“I said okay”
“As in you’ll go out, okay?”
“Do you want me to say no?”
“No! Yes. No. Let’s go,” he said excitedly.
“I regret saying yes,” she replied while rolling her eyes as they took off.
They floated through the city, passing through walls, objects, sometimes people. The wind was
cold but soothing, gentle. The sky was clear with the moon shining brightly over them. She was
looking at the city from above, absorbing everything.
“You look…” he said, observing her.
“Transparent?”
“How do you like the city?” he asked, changing the topic
“It’s nice. Where’s your building?”
“We passed it a while back. Why?”
“You mentioned before there was a shop”
“You’re very outgoing today. I like it,” he said approvingly.
“Well, as you can see, I’m kinda getting transparent. So figured, why not,” she shrugged.
Ayan looked at her for a moment. Then, pointed down towards a small shop at the intersection
of a road. The shop looked really old. The whole place was dark, as if everyone had abandoned
it. Only one light was on. He pushed the door open, and a bell rang. She entered behind him.
The shop wasn’t that big. It looked cozy, well kept. There were several things in the shop.
Clothes, books, candies, lights, small vials of mystery liquids. She was walking past an aisle
when a set of bottles caught her attention. She picked one to take a look. Grief. It was blue. She
picked another one, envy. It was green. She put it down to move forward when one bottle in the
back caught her attention. It was soft yellow. Almost glowing, like liquid gold. The label read joy.
She was about to open the bottle when someone caught her wrist. She looked up to see a man
in his forties looking down at her.
“It is a bottle of emotions,” he said in a boring tone.
She looked at him pointedly. He explained, “If you drink it, you’ll be able to feel this emotion.”
“How much is it?”
He looked at her for a moment, then laughed, “Do you have money?” He walked toward the
counter with the bottle in hand, with her following behind.
Right.
She thought with her eyes closed.
“Emotions can only be borrowed,” the man said.
She nodded when he handed her the bottle back. She screwed the cap off and took a small sip.
Nothing. She shot the shopkeeper a skeptical look, but he merely shrugged. With an impatient
sigh, she took a heavy gulp, draining nearly half the golden liquid. Still nothing—just a faint,
warm buzz at the base of her skull. She raised the bottle to her lips again when Ayan seized her
wrist, exclaiming with panic. “Give it time!”
She scoffed, ready to shoot back a reply, but the words died in her throat when a tight knot
twisted in her chest. The golden numbness shattered, and with the rush of warmth came
jagged, sudden fragments of a life once lived. A woman's laughter. A little girl's hand in hers.
The images disappeared before she could understand them. She blinked, confused.
Ayan looked at her, “What?”
“I saw something.”
Before he could answer, another knot formed inside her chest. This time, the memories came
faster.
A little girl running through a garden. A woman chasing after her. A plate of mangoes. A birthday
cake. A rainy afternoon. A hand brushing her hair. A voice saying,
“Come here, you're going to
catch a cold.”
She laughed. She didn't know why. Then another memory came. A hospital room. The same
woman, older now, sitting beside a bed. The girl was lying there. The woman was crying.
She stared at the bottle in her hand. For the first time in eighteen years, something inside her
felt full. Warm.
She smiled. “Who was she?”
The shopkeeper replied, “Your mother.”
“I want to remember more.”
The shopkeeper immediately shook his head. “You shouldn't.”
He looked at her hand. She followed his gaze. Her fingers had become more transparent.
“Why am I fading faster?”
“Emotions carry memories with them. You borrowed the feeling, and with it, you borrowed what
belonged to her.”
“Why didn’t you say anything earlier?”
“You didn’t ask.”
She stared at him. Every memory suddenly felt different. She thought about the woman
laughing. The woman waiting. The woman crying.
“She remembers less than yesterday,” he added.
Her smile disappeared. “Can I give it back?”
The shopkeeper shook his head. “Too late.”
She wanted to stop. Then she remembered her mother's hands. She remembered the sound of
her laughter. She remembered being loved. And she took another sip.
The memories came again. Her mother packing her lunch. Her mother scolding her. Her mother
waiting at the door. Her mother hugging her after a bad day.
She cried. She laughed. She cried again. She didn't care that her body was fading. For eighteen
years, she had felt nothing. Now she finally had something. So she kept drinking. One memory
after another, until she couldn't remember where one ended, and another began. Then she
suddenly couldn't remember the girl's name. She froze. She tried again. Nothing. She looked at
the shopkeeper.
“My memories are disappearing.”
He nodded. She looked down. Her body was almost completely transparent. Ayan reached for
her hand. His fingers passed right through hers. She stared at him. “I'm really disappearing.”
She laughed weakly.
She went back to her oak tree. The kittens were still there. The same mama cat. The same little
bodies curled against her. Something about them felt familiar, but she couldn't remember why.
Maya floated toward her. Her expression changed. “What happened to you?”
“I wanted to feel something.”
Maya looked at her sadly. “Did you?”
She nodded. “Everything.” She looked at the kittens again. “I think I regret it.”
Maya sat beside her. “Why?”
She thought for a moment. “Because now I know what I was missing.”
The sun began to rise. The kittens curled closer to their mother. She watched them. She still
remembered one thing. She had been loved. And somehow, that hurt more than not knowing
anything at all. The wind passed right through her as she melted into the air. For the first time in
eighteen years, she knew what it meant to feel. And for the first time, she wished she didn't.

title: My Dearest Friend
author: Manthan Chakraborty
imageAlt: Cover image for My Dearest Friend

runs.text: Name: Manthan Chakraborty
Category: Poetry.
Submitted to: TAMED
My Dearest Friend
The world is black and white
For a boy with narrow sight
Laughter and melody, all shall collapse
Into but futile oblivion, leaving nothing to withstand
Hence the cycle completes its unnumbered relapse
Leaving behind a question
That he didn’t know how to countermand
But then on a day just as the hundreds past
A gentle breeze is caressed through his heart
He didn’t know what the words would mean to him back then
He assumed it was just another cycle in its wake
He did not know, that this olive branch would
Become the transcendence and reignition of his heart
He just played along, but soon he poured his innermost lows
Hoping that the other wouldn’t brush his echoes forth
And alas this marked the start of an undying flame
A flame of trust, reliance and utter faith
Days into fortnights, fortnights into seemingly millennia
Their bond never retreated to the fears of lasting embers
For the echoes remained within their safest chambers
Now the boy stands on a field of daisies
His world no longer just two dull colors
He is seen sitting on the field, penning a poem
For none but his utmost, beloved, friend
‘Friend’ he smiles into the air, once rusted but now full of layers
What does a friend mean to you, my lad?
He pauses, looking at the unknown raft
‘Colors to a lifeless world’ he said with a smile
With that he went ahead, stepping into the defile
Where shall I take you then, my lad?
‘Take me to her, my friend’ he murmured as he glanced through
Who is she?
The raft had asked
She is nothing less than the hue carving through my canvas
She is but a soul named after wisdom, a heart with a fierce benevolence
A protector, savior and keeper of her own light
A lullaby to my aching might
Her embrace my only sanctuary, her words my only strength
She is the anchor to my wings and yet, also just my dearest friend

Days into fortnights, fortnights into seemingly millennia
Their bond never retreated to the fears of lasting embers
For the echoes remained within their safest chambers
Now the boy stands on a field of daisies
His world no longer just two dull colors
He is seen sitting on the field, penning a poem
For none but his utmost, beloved, friend
‘Friend’ he smiles into the air, once rusted but now full of layers
What does a friend mean to you, my lad?
He pauses, looking at the unknown raft
‘Colors to a lifeless world’ he said with a smile
With that he went ahead, stepping into the defile
Where shall I take you then, my lad?
‘Take me to her, my friend’ he murmured as he glanced through
Who is she? The raft had asked
She is nothing less than the hue carving through my canvas
She is but a soul named after wisdom, a heart with a fierce benevolence
A protector, savior and keeper of her own light
A lullaby to my aching might
Her embrace my only sanctuary, her words my only strength
She is the anchor to my wings and yet, also just my dearest friend

title: The architecture of an unpainted block
author: Maliha Tabassum
imageAlt: Cover image for The architecture of an unpainted block

runs.text: October 19th. 3 p.m., sunny afternoon.
With the sun glazing half
of

my face from the window, I was lying down on my bed contemplating life while being treated for severe anemia. That was the first time I had a cannula injected into my veins. My vein hadn't fully recovered from the insertion yet
. E

ven holding a phone felt heavy. With my metabolism running high to process the injected iron, the exhaustion completely wore me down. But in that physical weight, it was as if all the problems in my life suddenly disappeared.
So, that’s why they say:
“You have a hundred problems until it’s your health, then you only have one problem,”
my brain whispered.

A tissue box and the mug my best friend had gifted me were staring right back at me from my study table. With no energy to turn my face toward something else or the willingness to get out of bed, I was left staring at
or being stared at by

these inanimate objects. I realized they had something quiet in common: daisies printed on both of them. Soon enough, I noticed there were daisies printed on my clothes, too. Bored out of my mind with nothing better to do, I searched what they represent.
Renewal and healing.
Sigh. Classic, I said to myself. A neat, predictable little definition
I looked out my bedside window and caught something interesting

or perhaps boredom is simply the greatest drug to start finding meaning in everything. The neighboring building had an unpainted block with sunlight shining directly on the raw cement. Yet it stood out far more than standard white paint ever could. The interesting part
or should I say, the interesting part to a bored teenager

was that it was sparkling, as if someone had intentionally thrown glitter over it. It looked more authentic as an unpolished block. More unique. I didn't think it was inferior or imperfect for a second.
So why do we look at a human being and try to demolish their unique features just to look the same as an AI model?

It feels like everybody around is constantly trying to be a smooth, white-painted block. Like a white daisy printed on everything. And it’s an injustice to our unique existence. A building with different paint on different blocks would look so much cooler, I thought to myself.
Then my eyes fell on my dressing table.
The callously opened pack of skincare on the counter, the bottle of lotion that isn't standing straight

they reflected the last time I used them, the exact mental state I was occupying in that moment. I may have been in a rush, but looking at them now, I realized that the messiest things were actually the most real.
The unopened books, the tilted bottles, the unwashed mugs
. T
hey aren't just clutter. They have a story engraved in them. A moment. An emotion. Life.

We spend so much time trying to paint over our raw cement, terrified of being seen as unpolished or incomplete, scrambling to look as sterile as a printed daisy. But lying here in the quiet hum of my own recovery, surrounded by the physical evidence of my un
curated days, I see the truth.
Some are here for life to pass them by, and some are just passing by life. But the ones who truly live are the ones brave enough to stay unpainted.

title: The Raindrop
author: NAFIZ-BIN-HAFIZ
imageAlt: Cover image for The Raindrop

runs.text: The Raindrop
By
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
First Edition
Published independently
Cover design by Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
This book aims to explore
philosophical concepts, encourage critical
thinking and express social commentary
using fiction as a narrative vessel.
The ideas presented here are meant to
be taken as the author’s personal views
rather than legal/medical/professional
advice or personal attacks targeted
towards any individual.
All characters, events and places
mentioned in the book are entirely
products of imagination, thus any
resemblance to actual places or people,
whether living or dead, is coincidental.
Copyright © 2026 Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
All rights reserved
“Those who aren’t eligible for the 2nd professional
exam have been advised to report at the community
medicine department at 11 AM.”
Waking up and seeing this message in the class
group chat is probably the worst way to start a rainy
morning.
It’s bad enough that the prof is hitting me twice
– once in the form of the supplementary exams that
I’ll have to retake, and then there’s the actual prof
two months later – and now it seems I’ll also have to
roam around the department a dozen times
throughout the next few days.
But to be brutally honest, I have no one else but
myself to blame for this. I treated the last one year
of med school like a merry-go-round for toddlers. I
failed one half of the exams and didn’t even bother
to show up for the other half. So I rightfully deserve
a good spanking from the college right about now.
The clock on my phone shows 10:11 AM, which
theoretically should be enough to make it to college
in time.
The Raindrop
But the college is fairly far away from my home, and
on top of that, it’ll likely take a while to find a ride
there thanks to the rain. Which means I’ll have to
sacrifice my breakfast as well as my comfy morning
nap.
I got up from my bed, more pissed off than usual
and went to the bathroom for the first step of my
daily routine – which is sitting in the toilet for 10
minutes while scrolling through brainrot memes and
pictures of raccoons. But my phone battery was at
1%, so I decided to plug it to the charger and then
do the unthinkable – peeing without a phone in
hand.
Washing my face and brushing my teeth after
waking up is one of my least favourite parts of the
day. That’s because I end up watching my ugly face
every time I’m doing that. I’ve thought about
removing the mirror from the bathroom wall a few
times, but I’m not exactly the boss around here.
When you’re a freeloader leeching off your parents,
you must make a few compromises.
I was halfway out the door before mom even
realized I’m up.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
“Where are you going?” She asked with visible
confusion in her eyes. “I thought you didn’t have any
classes for the next few days.”
“The nation’s brightest have been summoned to
college, ma. Gotta go.” went my monotone tin can
voice.
Mom totally ignored my low quality sarcasm and
asked, “Aren’t you going to eat something before you
go?”
“Nah. The world needs your son more than your
son needs his breakfast.
I’ll be back in an hour by the way. Don’t worry”
“Okay then. Remember to take the umbrella.”
“Yeah it’s in my bag”.
Though the last couple of days including the
previous night up to this morning were quite rainy,
it thankfully wasn’t raining when I reached the street.
But that didn’t stop me from getting drenched
anyway. The water-clogged street was playing its role
pretty well. I thought of rolling up the sleeves of
my pants, but they were too tight for that. It seems
Being a stupid brick-brain is really taking a toll on
me today.
The Raindrop
Just when I thought I couldn’t be fucked up any
more, the rain started again. No light drizzle, no
warnings – just a straight up full throttle shower out
of nowhere.
A shallow “Fuck my life” came out of my mouth
like it was on autopilot. It’s been less than an hour
since my day began and it already feels like a hidden
camera prank, conducted by God himself.
I rushed into a departmental store and opened
my backpack to take out the umbrella, only to
discover I’m carrying a perfectly empty bag.
Perfect. Just perfect. After all, why would you
even check your bag before getting out, right?
It’s a fortunate tragedy that I can’t choke myself
to death with my own hands. Otherwise this circus
would have been long over by now.
As standing here and giving myself a silent hate
speech won’t magically teleport me anywhere, so I
started walking. I could have went back home to
fetch the umbrella though, but I was already getting
late for college, plus there would be a guaranteed
case of mom lecturing me about what a clumsy
moron I am.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
Since there’s no need to hear something I already
know, so I started walking towards the college
instead.
I looked down at my wrist watch. Through the
wet, clouded crystal, the analog dial showed it was
10:50. Today’s the 2
nd
or 3
rd
day I’m wearing this
watch, and it might be the last day too based on how
much rainwater the poor thing is drinking. It was
advertised to be water resistant though, but I highly
doubt a 400 taka quartz watch with “Rollex” written
on it would be a testament to business integrity.
The street’s pretty much empty aside from the
occasional one or two rickshaws passing by, all with
passengers on them.
There aren’t any pedestrians anywhere in sight. I
guess no one’s in the mood for swimming today.
I wasn’t either. But since when does life give a
shit about our what we want anyway?
Life isn’t some sandal shop on the footpath that
you can bargain your way through.
Rather it feels like a giant machine to me. We
humans are like the nuts and bolts on it.
The Raindrop
Our only purpose – is getting screwed. Both
literally and figuratively.
Why do students still have to manually attend
exams, I wondered while cruising through the knee -
level water. How much longer do we have to wait
until someone invents a machine that can scan our
brain and instantly reveal what we know, without
making us take any written or oral tests? Just imagine
how many hours that would save in everyone’s life.
A device like that sounds impossible now, but it may
exist somewhere in the distant future. After all, if I
were alive a hundred years ago and my friend told
me about a small rectangular piece of metal and
plastic that can let me talk to and see someone
standing on the other side of the planet, I’d probably
say, “Dude, have you been smoking those purple
mushrooms again?”
Yet that little machine is pretty much everywhere
right now.
It’s crazy how drastic the change of time can be.
Every 10 year old child today knows that the
earth moves round the sun. But Aristarchus got
cancelled by everyone, just for saying that same thing
two thousand years back.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
In today’s world, a guy who doesn’t believe in
germs will be unanimously labelled as crazy, and a
doctor will probably be put in jail for not taking
proper antiseptic precautions.
But when Dr Semmelweise, in the 19
th
century,
told us about germs and suggested that doctors
should wash their hands before medical procedures,
he received quite an unwelcoming reception.
And as a reward for his courage to stand up and
the ingenuity of his discovery, he had his medical
degree nullified and died in a mental asylum. I’ve
even read that he was beaten up by some guard who
used to work there.
I wonder if the phrase “fortune favours the
brave” was invented before or after the death of
Semmelweise. If it’s the latter, then the guy who
came up with this proverb could have used some
serious re-education.
The remorseless rain and the splashing noise that
arose with every step I took provided a good
background music for my train of thought. The
water was flowing in from the opposite direction,
caressing my legs with all the filth it’s carrying, and
just passing me by without showing any kind of
regret or sympathy.
The Raindrop
As I kept cutting through the opposing waves, I
imagined if Aristarchus or Semmelweise also felt the
exact same way. Except in their case, the oncoming
waves were made of humans, bigger and scarier; and
the dryness of their clothes wasn’t the only thing at
stake.
It baffles me that people still use the logic ‘If
everyone has been doing something, then it must be
right’. I mean, it’s pretty obvious that what the
society thinks to be true is a relative and dynamic
thing. It changes with time. What was right to them
in the last millennia, would be considered a lunatic
delusion or a crime today. So I don’t see why people
would take the society’s approval as a standard to
justify their acts. In a world where insanity is the
norm – rationality would be seen as a sickness.
But again, what do I know? I am just a fool who
goes out on a rainy day with an empty bag on his
shoulders. Who am I to question the humanity’s
collective intelligence?
An auto-rickshaw passed me by from behind
suddenly. It was going towards my medical college.
But as it was already filled with passengers, it didn’t
serve me any purpose – other than splashing some
dirty water on me of course.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
By the way, even if we do have a machine that
can figure out our knowledge by scanning our brains,
what would that be called?
Brain Scanner? Neh. Sounds way too lazy.
Neural Network Navigator?
This one’s clearly cooler. But the abbreviation
would be NNN and that might create some very
awkward confusions.
Cerebral Circuit Reader? Good, but the sci -fi
vibe of this one is too on the nose.
How about, Student Hospitable Automated
Machine for Examination?
Sounds like something a second grader would
come up with.
But on the flip side, it abbreviates to S.H.A.M.E,
which perfectly sums up the viva experience of most
med students. So my vote would definitely be on this
one.
A few steps ahead, there was a bench at the side
of the road with a shade on top. I was already getting
late for class. But since walking at this rate would
The Raindrop
never take me to class on time anyway so I figured
the best move would probably be sitting here and
waiting for a local auto.
There was a girl sitting there all by herself near
the far end of the bench. She was a bit older than
me, probably 25–27 years old, with a small purse on
her lap, a shopping bag and a bouquet of flowers
laying next to her on the bench.
She looked pretty beautiful too. If someone with
actual literary talent was here, he’d probably drop a
two and a half page long hymn about the
mesmerising beauty of this young lady.
Like how she had the eyes of a deer, roaming the
gardens of paradise; with a glance sharp as razors
and yet as soft as the fabric of dreams, and the lips
like the petals of a divine flower, and a smile that
shines, and glows and gleams; and how she had the
heart like the sky, so full of love and kind; and a
voice like a harp, raining bliss upon my mind —
that kind of corny stuff.
But since I’m a good for nothing brat with a PhD
in being talentless, I’ll just spare the details here.
But one thing that struck me the most was a dark,
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
shiny and irregular scar, most likely from a burn,
extending from the right side of her face all the way
down to her neck before disappearing underneath
her dress. It’s like someone drew a rough map of hell
on a portrait of heaven, almost as to intentional ly
mar the beauty of it – only to fail miserably. That
mark could not even put a dent on how stunning she
looked, rather it strangely complemented her
majesty. It was as if she was wearing it as a piece of
jewellery, and it didn’t feel out of place at the
slightest. She looked just as pure and elegant as the
flowers put next to her.
When I, a quite visually repulsive man, with his
villainous look further intensified with the
‘Drenched Crow’ appearance, went under the shade
and sat a few feet away from the girl, with no other
people anywhere nearby; that must have felt a bit
uncomfortable to her. And considering the things
that happen in this world I can’t even blame her for
being scared. Although she did seem very composed
and unaffected by my arrival. Brave girl. Or maybe
she just sensed that a scrawny twig like me couldn’t
be a threat to anyone even if it wanted to. I don’t
know.
Sitting on the bench instead of walking through
a pool of noxious water may be more comfortable,
but it sure was more boring too.
The Raindrop
I have a beautiful companion here to chat with.
But that’s of no good to me because I have the social
skills of a comatose rock. Naturally I just awkwardly
sat there staring at the clogged up street and
rethinking all my life choices.
“What time is it?”
My mind went temporarily blank and my heart
decided to punch me in the chest really hard. I wasn’t
expecting this girl to talk to me, because almost no
girl ever has spoken to me on her own.
Also I wasn’t expecting her voice to be this
beautiful as well.
With my brain going haywire inside my skull, I
hastily reached into my pocket to take my phone out.
My heart plunged down 3 feet into some physics-
defying abyss inside my chest when I noticed my
phone is not inside my pocket.
Shit! Did I drop it on the street? How am i going
to find it with the whole road bathing under 6 inches
of water? Is it – oh wait. I remembered. I had left
my phone charging back home because it was low
on battery. The sigh of relief accompanied another
epiphany – I had my wrist watch on. When I looked
at my watch, I learned that it was still telling the same
time as it had shown a while ago – 10:50.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
It seems the 400 taka quartz watch with “Rollex”
written on it wasn’t a testament to business integrity
after all.
I thought I’d lie to her and tell her an
approximated time based on what I saw the last time
I checked and roughly how long had passed since
then, because I didn’t want to look like a fool who
didn’t bring his phone with him and was also wearing
a cheap watch that drowned to death.
But then I thought, maybe the exact time might
be very important to her and an inaccurate answer
might end up messing with her schedule. I chose
honesty instead.
“Sorry, I don’t have my phone with me and my
watch got broken.“I tried to hide my insecurity with
an awkward smile. “But if it helps, the last time I
saw it working was 20–30 minutes ago and it was
10:50 AM back then.“
“Oh. Okay. Thank you “.
Speaking 2 sentences like a normal human being
may not sound like a lot, but for me – it was
exhilarating. Most of the conversations I’ve had
were online, and the contents of my conversation
never failed to get myself tagged as a raging
psychopath. Therefore giving a normal reply to a
The Raindrop
pretty girl asking the time was quite a great milestone
in my personal history.
I guess that success really went to my head.
Because after basking in the glory of my newfound,
short-lived normalcy; I had the urge to break some
new ground. I thought I’d do something I barely
ever did before – break the silence and socialize,
start another conservation rather than just waiting
for something I can reply to.
“Getting late for work?” I asked. It felt like a
normal thing to say after she wanted to know the
time, and then immediately I thought it might have
been a personal question and maybe an
inappropriate thing to ask.
“No I don’t have work on Saturdays”, She
replied. “I was just out for a walk. What about you?”
My heart that was practically beatboxing at this
point, felt a bit relieved by the fact that my
companion did not feel offended by my question.
I answered, “3
rd
year medical college student. I
was on my way to, uh, some paperworks before the
next month’s exam”. I felt part proud, part ashamed
of how I diplomatically left out the information that
I’m quite possibly the worst student in my class.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
“Wow. So you’re almost a doctor.”
“Yup. Almost a doctor, already a patient“, I tried
to smile nervously while keeping my eyes locked on
to the street. “At this rate, I’ll probably need a
permanent bed at our hospital ward before I finish
the degree. “
She took a 2–3 second pause before replying
“Yeah I’ve heard med school can be very stressful.
But you’ve come this far, right? I’m sure you’ll do
great with the rest of your time too.”
“Thanks”, I smiled, this time less nervously. “So
what do you do?”
“I’m a teacher at a private primary school, mostly
teach kids in class 1 and 2.”
“Impressive. How do you keep your cool around
a room full of hyperactive trouble machines? I once
taught a kid of class 6, and it felt like losing my sanity
by the minute!”
She laughed for the first time, and for some
reason, the banging and beatboxing of my heart
made a shocking return. Her voice sounded like
music I’d never heard before, it didn’t sound, but
rather it felt; as if in a world rapidly sinking into an
ocean of falling rain, her laughter felt like an island
The Raindrop
emerging from the depths. In the constant rattles of
the June clouds crashing onto earth, her voice felt
like a warm, comforting echo.
“It does feel like that sometimes. A lot of times,
In fact. But I could never imagine a life away from
it. Everyday I come back home from school, tired
and happy to finally be home. And yet, every
Thursday night, I can’t wait til Sunday so that I can
see my kids again.”
“Aww. That’s very sweet“, I smiled again, this
time not nervously at all.
“And most importantly, being around them
makes me feel like I’m actually.. living, almost as if
their innocence is contagious.”
“I understand.”, I sighed, still staring at the
street, with my smile now poisoned with a pinch of
gloom. “Growing up is the most brutal scam ever.
We are born as humans, then grow up into being
machines.”
She replied sharing a similar gloom in her smile
as well “Exactly. We are taught specifically how to
survive and function, but barely any of us learn how
to live. That’s kind of the reason why I chose what I
do; to relive my own life through their lens, an d
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
maybe teach them to live better, so they don’t make
the same mistakes we did.”
“That’s... amazing really. Your students are lucky
to have you.”
“Thank you.”
She returned the politeness after a few seconds
of silence, “Your patients will be lucky to have you
too”.
During that short-lived silence, I was absent-
mindedly staring at 3 silhouettes approaching from
a distance. From what I could guess from their vague
shapes – the tall one in the middle was probably a
man holding an umbrella with a smaller humanoid
shape by each side, most likely a father with two of
his kids. The rain was so dense and heavy that those
3 figures almost seemed like shadows; frail, barely
existing shadows almost getting swallowed by a
cosmic beast made of liquid shards.
The voice of my new friend brought my mind
back to my body.
I laughed, filled with shame and flattered by this
person’s lack of knowledge about me.
The Raindrop
“My patients will be lucky if they manage to
survive my treatment at all, ‘cause looking at how
things are going, I’ll either be the world’s worst
doctor or not a doctor at all.”
“Why? Are you like, a backbencher type of
student?”
“Calling me a backbencher would be an
understatement. If you put a bench 5 miles outside
our college boundaries, that bench would have my
name written on it“, I replied, masking my insecurity
with a poorly manufactured chuckle.
She laughed too, hard to say if it was also
artificial or not.
“Don’t you enjoy what you study in med school?”
“It’s not that I like something else and dislike
medicine. In fact I find medical subjects more
fascinating than almost anything else. But still I just,
don’t feel anything in my heart to study or even do
anything. It feels like the all the possible option s are
bad and even the best option I have which is
medicine, is something I have to painfully drag
myself through.
I don’t think anything even stands for anything,
so I may as well be lying in my bed all day. Even
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
though that wouldn’t have much meaning either. I
don’t even know what I want or like, if that makes
any sense. “
The girl looked at me for a moment and replied,
“I understand.”
The next couple of seconds seemed unnaturally
long as we sat silently, while the rainfall continued its
loud orchestra as to intentionally highlight the
silence even more. Did I just ruin the vibe and make
it awkward? Yeah probably. But again, being a social
butterfly was never my thing anyway so I shouldn’t
be surprised.
“You know, I had this kid in my class last year.
Always making trouble, almost never doing his
homework or classwork. His exam grades were
always near the bottom. So I did what I had to do –
talked to him, tried to be his friend. He couldn’t
open up easily, but eventually he did. And it turns
out, he didn’t really have anything wrong with him.
In fact, I don’t think any child ever has anything
wrong with them. It’s just that – they’re all unique.
You have communicate to them in their own
different ways. But once you do, you’ll see that
they’re all good, they’re all strong and bright. The
same was true for my kid from that class. All he
The Raindrop
needed was a little help, and I’m glad I could give it
to him.”
I just sat there and listened to her, eyes
downwards.
She continued, “I don’t really know much about
you, but I’m sure you’re strong too. Because
everyone is. I hope you’ll find that extra bit of
strength to get out of bed every morning, and
everything will make sense. Sometimes just showing
up is enough.”
I slowly turned my head to her and smiled,
“Thank you.”
She smiled back. “You’re welcome.”
The rain went on, with the sound of ten
thousand guns shooting straight down from the
heavens, as if someone upstairs is really pissed and
they’ve declared war. Some bird from a nearby tree
let out a few shouts. Perhaps it’s a battle cry, or
maybe a scream of agony from a victim of collateral
damage.
Through that raging wall of sound the voice of

'rain' in my poem, even though I’ve always been a
passionate rain-hater.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
Which means I'd been unknowingly enchanted
by the rain for a very long time, and this morning
was only an unexpected revelation.
Could there be any specific reason behind our
such obsession with the rain?
Maybe there is.
I always felt a certain connection to every
raindrop that I saw falling. I think they’re just like us
in a way.
We also fall from the heavens into this whirlpool
of madness, not because we choose to, rather
because the world around us wants us to; then we
get mixed and entangled with billions others just like
ourselves, who also fell from the sky against their
will, only to make a ripple just for a fleeting moment,
on the surface of a reluctant universe that has been
around for billions of years without us, and will
likely be around for billions more after we’ve left.
Then we flow towards wherever life and law
takes us. At some point we reach the sea, our journey
ends. But the remains we leave behind are just
enough to restart the cycle, for clouds to form and
thus new raindrops to fall, just like the ones that fell
before them, and the ones that will follow. Eons
The Raindrop
shall pass, as the cycle will keep repeating without
pause.
I looked at her as she slowly disappeared towards
the far end of what my eyes allowed me to see.
The last hour wasn’t exactly a very memorable
experience I think. Rather it was sufficiently
uneventful, just a regular day among the thousands
I left behind and the thousands I’ll probably find
ahead. But I have a feeling that I will remember this
particular morning for a long, long time.
I don’t know why though. Is it because of the
rain? Or the person I met? Or the time I spent with
her? Could be any of the above, or it could be none.
But what do I know? After all, I’m just a sentient
raindrop, ready to flow along the current to where
my river meets the sea.
Maybe Blade Runner was right. Maybe all these
moments really do get lost in time, like tears in the
rain.
But I hope this moment doesn’t.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
Greetings and gratitude from the
author:
Firstly I would like to apologize to all the readers
for making them sit through what you just read. I
understand that it might not have been easy.
I have received many good-willed and well
appreciated criticisms from some readers that—
most of the conversation in the ‘story’ was carried
out by the protagonist and very little is spoken by
the female side-character. I’m also aware that the
conversation is exhaustingly long and one-sided
which makes the dialogue very unnatural and
unrealistic. However this choice of over-
clarification and precision over concise, dramatic
realism – was very much intentional and was in fact
the whole point of this book.
This was originally not supposed to be (and still
isn’t) a story with characters and plot – rather an
essay which was supposed to contain all the logic in
favour of antinatalism. I had written that ‘essay’
long before I gave it the thin veil of a story, based
on the arguments I’ve had with dozens of different
people over the years.
The Raindrop
I’ve noticed that different individuals had
varying levels of intelligence and
understanding, had unique angles of tackling a
certain point, and required different styles and
lengths of explanations to deliver a certain message.
I’ve even been in situations where a breeder
presented a certain argument, I rebutted that with a
counterargument, only for that person to just
rephrase that exact same argument again a few
seconds later, as if my counterargument didn’t
register in their brain at all. That forced me to
reiterate my counterargument multiple times in
different ways using different words just hoping
they’d catch my point. So if you feel frustrated that
I have rephrased the same line way too many times
to the point where the dialogue sounded like a
bunch of separate paragraphs from different books
on the same topic clumsily stitched together – just
know that the same frustration exists in me as well.
I am a thinker, not an artist. So I wanted to make
sure that any possible argument that any reader
might present against antinatalism — should
already have a counterargument prepared in my
story.
I wanted the protagonist’s monologue to be
universal, exhaustive and to properly encompass all
these arguments in favour of antinatalism as clearly
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
as possible, often in unnecessarily great detail and
repetition, and using different metaphors and words
for the exact same point.
Thus the tiresome, unrealistically long replies of
the protagonist were necessary for covering all the
possible logic and reasoning . A ‘realistic’
conversation wouldn’t have contained as many
points, and the points wouldn’t be as detailed.
The book was meant to be a complete
antinatalist manifesto first and story second.
The first priority of my book was not to be a
story with a message, but to be a message disguised
as a story. Thoroughness and exposition were much
more important to me than plot and pacing.
So I would request the readers to kindly see my
writing for what it truly is – not a story but an essay
dressed in narrative clothing.
Besides there aren’t many sound arguments I
could think of in favour of procreation (natalism).
Since the whole point of the girl’s existence was to
only voice the logic behind natalism and I don’t
really see any logic behind it at all, thus I couldn’t
find much for the girl to say. This may or may not
be my shortcoming as a writer, and you may feel
disappointed if you were expecting a balanced
The Raindrop
dialogue between two real humans. I apologize if
that was the case.
Furthermore, most people on earth are already
‘breeders’ anyway and therefore will be
automatically supporting the girl and opposing the
guy. As a result there was almost no necessity to
defend the girl’s perspective whereas the
protagonist’s controversial opinions required a lot
more defending and explanation.
This reinforced the one-sided nature of the
dialogue even more, to the point where the girl feels
like just a literary device instead of an actual person
– which is exactly what happened here.
The main character of the story has even directly
stated that he’d defended his views against many
people before and is therefore ridiculously over-
prepared to refute almost any arguments imaginable
(much like the writer himself), whereas the girl was
pretty much caught off guard by the absurdity of
the topic.
I hope the deliberateness of these choices will
help to somewhat explain the unrealism of the
encounter.
Last but not least, I am very grateful to anyone
who took their valuable time to read this work.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
As this entire book including the writing,
formatting, cover designing etc. was completely
done by just one single person (i.e. me) with no
prior professional experience or paid software, it
may not have lived up to a certain standard most
readers would expect. That further strengthens my
gratitude towards my readers for enduring this
travesty.
This book means a lot to me, and even if just 1
person reads it in its entirety, I’ll find that to be
deeply meaningful and rewarding.
Thank you.

content: The Raindrop
By
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
First Edition
Published independently
Cover design by Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
This book aims to explore
philosophical concepts, encourage critical
thinking and express social commentary
using fiction as a narrative vessel.
The ideas presented here are meant to
be taken as the author’s personal views
rather than legal/medical/professional
advice or personal attacks targeted
towards any individual.
All characters, events and places
mentioned in the book are entirely
products of imagination, thus any
resemblance to actual places or people,
whether living or dead, is coincidental.
Copyright © 2026 Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
All rights reserved
“Those who aren’t eligible for the 2nd professional
exam have been advised to report at the community
medicine department at 11 AM.”
Waking up and seeing this message in the class
group chat is probably the worst way to start a rainy
morning.
It’s bad enough that the prof is hitting me twice
– once in the form of the supplementary exams that
I’ll have to retake, and then there’s the actual prof
two months later – and now it seems I’ll also have to
roam around the department a dozen times
throughout the next few days.
But to be brutally honest, I have no one else but
myself to blame for this. I treated the last one year
of med school like a merry-go-round for toddlers. I
failed one half of the exams and didn’t even bother
to show up for the other half. So I rightfully deserve
a good spanking from the college right about now.
The clock on my phone shows 10:11 AM, which
theoretically should be enough to make it to college
in time.
The Raindrop
But the college is fairly far away from my home, and
on top of that, it’ll likely take a while to find a ride
there thanks to the rain. Which means I’ll have to
sacrifice my breakfast as well as my comfy morning
nap.
I got up from my bed, more pissed off than usual
and went to the bathroom for the first step of my
daily routine – which is sitting in the toilet for 10
minutes while scrolling through brainrot memes and
pictures of raccoons. But my phone battery was at
1%, so I decided to plug it to the charger and then
do the unthinkable – peeing without a phone in
hand.
Washing my face and brushing my teeth after
waking up is one of my least favourite parts of the
day. That’s because I end up watching my ugly face
every time I’m doing that. I’ve thought about
removing the mirror from the bathroom wall a few
times, but I’m not exactly the boss around here.
When you’re a freeloader leeching off your parents,
you must make a few compromises.
I was halfway out the door before mom even
realized I’m up.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
“Where are you going?” She asked with visible
confusion in her eyes. “I thought you didn’t have any
classes for the next few days.”
“The nation’s brightest have been summoned to
college, ma. Gotta go.” went my monotone tin can
voice.
Mom totally ignored my low quality sarcasm and
asked, “Aren’t you going to eat something before you
go?”
“Nah. The world needs your son more than your
son needs his breakfast.
I’ll be back in an hour by the way. Don’t worry”
“Okay then. Remember to take the umbrella.”
“Yeah it’s in my bag”.
Though the last couple of days including the
previous night up to this morning were quite rainy,
it thankfully wasn’t raining when I reached the street.
But that didn’t stop me from getting drenched
anyway. The water-clogged street was playing its role
pretty well. I thought of rolling up the sleeves of
my pants, but they were too tight for that. It seems
Being a stupid brick-brain is really taking a toll on
me today.
The Raindrop
Just when I thought I couldn’t be fucked up any
more, the rain started again. No light drizzle, no
warnings – just a straight up full throttle shower out
of nowhere.
A shallow “Fuck my life” came out of my mouth
like it was on autopilot. It’s been less than an hour
since my day began and it already feels like a hidden
camera prank, conducted by God himself.
I rushed into a departmental store and opened
my backpack to take out the umbrella, only to
discover I’m carrying a perfectly empty bag.
Perfect. Just perfect. After all, why would you
even check your bag before getting out, right?
It’s a fortunate tragedy that I can’t choke myself
to death with my own hands. Otherwise this circus
would have been long over by now.
As standing here and giving myself a silent hate
speech won’t magically teleport me anywhere, so I
started walking. I could have went back home to
fetch the umbrella though, but I was already getting
late for college, plus there would be a guaranteed
case of mom lecturing me about what a clumsy
moron I am.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
Since there’s no need to hear something I already
know, so I started walking towards the college
instead.
I looked down at my wrist watch. Through the
wet, clouded crystal, the analog dial showed it was
10:50. Today’s the 2nd or 3rd day I’m wearing this
watch, and it might be the last day too based on how
much rainwater the poor thing is drinking. It was
advertised to be water resistant though, but I highly
doubt a 400 taka quartz watch with “Rollex” written
on it would be a testament to business integrity.
The street’s pretty much empty aside from the
occasional one or two rickshaws passing by, all with
passengers on them.
There aren’t any pedestrians anywhere in sight. I
guess no one’s in the mood for swimming today.
I wasn’t either. But since when does life give a
shit about our what we want anyway?
Life isn’t some sandal shop on the footpath that
you can bargain your way through.
Rather it feels like a giant machine to me. We
humans are like the nuts and bolts on it.
The Raindrop
Our only purpose – is getting screwed. Both
literally and figuratively.
Why do students still have to manually attend
exams, I wondered while cruising through the knee -
level water. How much longer do we have to wait
until someone invents a machine that can scan our
brain and instantly reveal what we know, without
making us take any written or oral tests? Just imagine
how many hours that would save in everyone’s life.
A device like that sounds impossible now, but it may
exist somewhere in the distant future. After all, if I
were alive a hundred years ago and my friend told
me about a small rectangular piece of metal and
plastic that can let me talk to and see someone
standing on the other side of the planet, I’d probably
say, “Dude, have you been smoking those purple
mushrooms again?”
Yet that little machine is pretty much everywhere
right now.
It’s crazy how drastic the change of time can be.
Every 10 year old child today knows that the
earth moves round the sun. But Aristarchus got
cancelled by everyone, just for saying that same thing
two thousand years back.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
In today’s world, a guy who doesn’t believe in
germs will be unanimously labelled as crazy, and a
doctor will probably be put in jail for not taking
proper antiseptic precautions.
But when Dr Semmelweise, in the 19th century,
told us about germs and suggested that doctors
should wash their hands before medical procedures,
he received quite an unwelcoming reception.
And as a reward for his courage to stand up and
the ingenuity of his discovery, he had his medical
degree nullified and died in a mental asylum. I’ve
even read that he was beaten up by some guard who
used to work there.
I wonder if the phrase “fortune favours the
brave” was invented before or after the death of
Semmelweise. If it’s the latter, then the guy who
came up with this proverb could have used some
serious re-education.
The remorseless rain and the splashing noise that
arose with every step I took provided a good
background music for my train of thought. The
water was flowing in from the opposite direction,
caressing my legs with all the filth it’s carrying, and
just passing me by without showing any kind of
regret or sympathy.
The Raindrop
As I kept cutting through the opposing waves, I
imagined if Aristarchus or Semmelweise also felt the
exact same way. Except in their case, the oncoming
waves were made of humans, bigger and scarier; and
the dryness of their clothes wasn’t the only thing at
stake.
It baffles me that people still use the logic ‘If
everyone has been doing something, then it must be
right’. I mean, it’s pretty obvious that what the
society thinks to be true is a relative and dynamic
thing. It changes with time. What was right to them
in the last millennia, would be considered a lunatic
delusion or a crime today. So I don’t see why people
would take the society’s approval as a standard to
justify their acts. In a world where insanity is the
norm – rationality would be seen as a sickness.
But again, what do I know? I am just a fool who
goes out on a rainy day with an empty bag on his
shoulders. Who am I to question the humanity’s
collective intelligence?
An auto-rickshaw passed me by from behind
suddenly. It was going towards my medical college.
But as it was already filled with passengers, it didn’t
serve me any purpose – other than splashing some
dirty water on me of course.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
By the way, even if we do have a machine that
can figure out our knowledge by scanning our brains,
what would that be called?
Brain Scanner? Neh. Sounds way too lazy.
Neural Network Navigator?
This one’s clearly cooler. But the abbreviation
would be NNN and that might create some very
awkward confusions.
Cerebral Circuit Reader? Good, but the sci -fi
vibe of this one is too on the nose.
How about, Student Hospitable Automated
Machine for Examination?
Sounds like something a second grader would
come up with.
But on the flip side, it abbreviates to S.H.A.M.E,
which perfectly sums up the viva experience of most
med students. So my vote would definitely be on this
one.
A few steps ahead, there was a bench at the side
of the road with a shade on top. I was already getting
late for class. But since walking at this rate would
The Raindrop
never take me to class on time anyway so I figured
the best move would probably be sitting here and
waiting for a local auto.
There was a girl sitting there all by herself near
the far end of the bench. She was a bit older than
me, probably 25–27 years old, with a small purse on
her lap, a shopping bag and a bouquet of flowers
laying next to her on the bench.
She looked pretty beautiful too. If someone with
actual literary talent was here, he’d probably drop a
two and a half page long hymn about the
mesmerising beauty of this young lady.
Like how she had the eyes of a deer, roaming the
gardens of paradise; with a glance sharp as razors
and yet as soft as the fabric of dreams, and the lips
like the petals of a divine flower, and a smile that
shines, and glows and gleams; and how she had the
heart like the sky, so full of love and kind; and a
voice like a harp, raining bliss upon my mind —
that kind of corny stuff.
But since I’m a good for nothing brat with a PhD
in being talentless, I’ll just spare the details here.
But one thing that struck me the most was a dark,
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
shiny and irregular scar, most likely from a burn,
extending from the right side of her face all the way
down to her neck before disappearing underneath
her dress. It’s like someone drew a rough map of hell
on a portrait of heaven, almost as to intentional ly
mar the beauty of it – only to fail miserably. That
mark could not even put a dent on how stunning she
looked, rather it strangely complemented her
majesty. It was as if she was wearing it as a piece of
jewellery, and it didn’t feel out of place at the
slightest. She looked just as pure and elegant as the
flowers put next to her.
When I, a quite visually repulsive man, with his
villainous look further intensified with the
‘Drenched Crow’ appearance, went under the shade
and sat a few feet away from the girl, with no other
people anywhere nearby; that must have felt a bit
uncomfortable to her. And considering the things
that happen in this world I can’t even blame her for
being scared. Although she did seem very composed
and unaffected by my arrival. Brave girl. Or maybe
she just sensed that a scrawny twig like me couldn’t
be a threat to anyone even if it wanted to. I don’t
know.
Sitting on the bench instead of walking through
a pool of noxious water may be more comfortable,
but it sure was more boring too.
The Raindrop
I have a beautiful companion here to chat with.
But that’s of no good to me because I have the social
skills of a comatose rock. Naturally I just awkwardly
sat there staring at the clogged up street and
rethinking all my life choices.
“What time is it?”
My mind went temporarily blank and my heart
decided to punch me in the chest really hard. I wasn’t
expecting this girl to talk to me, because almost no
girl ever has spoken to me on her own.
Also I wasn’t expecting her voice to be this
beautiful as well.
With my brain going haywire inside my skull, I
hastily reached into my pocket to take my phone out.
My heart plunged down 3 feet into some physics-
defying abyss inside my chest when I noticed my
phone is not inside my pocket.
Shit! Did I drop it on the street? How am i going
to find it with the whole road bathing under 6 inches
of water? Is it – oh wait. I remembered. I had left
my phone charging back home because it was low
on battery. The sigh of relief accompanied another
epiphany – I had my wrist watch on. When I looked
at my watch, I learned that it was still telling the same
time as it had shown a while ago – 10:50.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
It seems the 400 taka quartz watch with “Rollex”
written on it wasn’t a testament to business integrity
after all.
I thought I’d lie to her and tell her an
approximated time based on what I saw the last time
I checked and roughly how long had passed since
then, because I didn’t want to look like a fool who
didn’t bring his phone with him and was also wearing
a cheap watch that drowned to death.
But then I thought, maybe the exact time might
be very important to her and an inaccurate answer
might end up messing with her schedule. I chose
honesty instead.
“Sorry, I don’t have my phone with me and my
watch got broken.“I tried to hide my insecurity with
an awkward smile. “But if it helps, the last time I
saw it working was 20–30 minutes ago and it was
10:50 AM back then.“
“Oh. Okay. Thank you “.
Speaking 2 sentences like a normal human being
may not sound like a lot, but for me – it was
exhilarating. Most of the conversations I’ve had
were online, and the contents of my conversation
never failed to get myself tagged as a raging
psychopath. Therefore giving a normal reply to a
The Raindrop
pretty girl asking the time was quite a great milestone
in my personal history.
I guess that success really went to my head.
Because after basking in the glory of my newfound,
short-lived normalcy; I had the urge to break some
new ground. I thought I’d do something I barely
ever did before – break the silence and socialize,
start another conservation rather than just waiting
for something I can reply to.
“Getting late for work?” I asked. It felt like a
normal thing to say after she wanted to know the
time, and then immediately I thought it might have
been a personal question and maybe an
inappropriate thing to ask.
“No I don’t have work on Saturdays”, She
replied. “I was just out for a walk. What about you?”
My heart that was practically beatboxing at this
point, felt a bit relieved by the fact that my
companion did not feel offended by my question.
I answered, “3rd year medical college student. I
was on my way to, uh, some paperworks before the
next month’s exam”. I felt part proud, part ashamed
of how I diplomatically left out the information that
I’m quite possibly the worst student in my class.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
“Wow. So you’re almost a doctor.”
“Yup. Almost a doctor, already a patient“, I tried
to smile nervously while keeping my eyes locked on
to the street. “At this rate, I’ll probably need a
permanent bed at our hospital ward before I finish
the degree. “
She took a 2–3 second pause before replying
“Yeah I’ve heard med school can be very stressful.
But you’ve come this far, right? I’m sure you’ll do
great with the rest of your time too.”
“Thanks”, I smiled, this time less nervously. “So
what do you do?”
“I’m a teacher at a private primary school, mostly
teach kids in class 1 and 2.”
“Impressive. How do you keep your cool around
a room full of hyperactive trouble machines? I once
taught a kid of class 6, and it felt like losing my sanity
by the minute!”
She laughed for the first time, and for some
reason, the banging and beatboxing of my heart
made a shocking return. Her voice sounded like
music I’d never heard before, it didn’t sound, but
rather it felt; as if in a world rapidly sinking into an
ocean of falling rain, her laughter felt like an island
The Raindrop
emerging from the depths. In the constant rattles of
the June clouds crashing onto earth, her voice felt
like a warm, comforting echo.
“It does feel like that sometimes. A lot of times,
In fact. But I could never imagine a life away from
it. Everyday I come back home from school, tired
and happy to finally be home. And yet, every
Thursday night, I can’t wait til Sunday so that I can
see my kids again.”
“Aww. That’s very sweet“, I smiled again, this
time not nervously at all.
“And most importantly, being around them
makes me feel like I’m actually.. living, almost as if
their innocence is contagious.”
“I understand.”, I sighed, still staring at the
street, with my smile now poisoned with a pinch of
gloom. “Growing up is the most brutal scam ever.
We are born as humans, then grow up into being
machines.”
She replied sharing a similar gloom in her smile
as well “Exactly. We are taught specifically how to
survive and function, but barely any of us learn how
to live. That’s kind of the reason why I chose what I
do; to relive my own life through their lens, an d
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
maybe teach them to live better, so they don’t make
the same mistakes we did.”
“That’s... amazing really. Your students are lucky
to have you.”
“Thank you.”
She returned the politeness after a few seconds
of silence, “Your patients will be lucky to have you
too”.
During that short-lived silence, I was absent-
mindedly staring at 3 silhouettes approaching from
a distance. From what I could guess from their vague
shapes – the tall one in the middle was probably a
man holding an umbrella with a smaller humanoid
shape by each side, most likely a father with two of
his kids. The rain was so dense and heavy that those
3 figures almost seemed like shadows; frail, barely
existing shadows almost getting swallowed by a
cosmic beast made of liquid shards.
The voice of my new friend brought my mind
back to my body.
I laughed, filled with shame and flattered by this
person’s lack of knowledge about me.
The Raindrop
“My patients will be lucky if they manage to
survive my treatment at all, ‘cause looking at how
things are going, I’ll either be the world’s worst
doctor or not a doctor at all.”
“Why? Are you like, a backbencher type of
student?”
“Calling me a backbencher would be an
understatement. If you put a bench 5 miles outside
our college boundaries, that bench would have my
name written on it“, I replied, masking my insecurity
with a poorly manufactured chuckle.
She laughed too, hard to say if it was also
artificial or not.
“Don’t you enjoy what you study in med school?”
“It’s not that I like something else and dislike
medicine. In fact I find medical subjects more
fascinating than almost anything else. But still I just,
don’t feel anything in my heart to study or even do
anything. It feels like the all the possible option s are
bad and even the best option I have which is
medicine, is something I have to painfully drag
myself through.
I don’t think anything even stands for anything,
so I may as well be lying in my bed all day. Even
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
though that wouldn’t have much meaning either. I
don’t even know what I want or like, if that makes
any sense. “
The girl looked at me for a moment and replied,
“I understand.”
The next couple of seconds seemed unnaturally
long as we sat silently, while the rainfall continued its
loud orchestra as to intentionally highlight the
silence even more. Did I just ruin the vibe and make
it awkward? Yeah probably. But again, being a social
butterfly was never my thing anyway so I shouldn’t
be surprised.
“You know, I had this kid in my class last year.
Always making trouble, almost never doing his
homework or classwork. His exam grades were
always near the bottom. So I did what I had to do –
talked to him, tried to be his friend. He couldn’t
open up easily, but eventually he did. And it turns
out, he didn’t really have anything wrong with him.
In fact, I don’t think any child ever has anything
wrong with them. It’s just that – they’re all unique.
You have communicate to them in their own
different ways. But once you do, you’ll see that
they’re all good, they’re all strong and bright. The
same was true for my kid from that class. All he
The Raindrop
needed was a little help, and I’m glad I could give it
to him.”
I just sat there and listened to her, eyes
downwards.
She continued, “I don’t really know much about
you, but I’m sure you’re strong too. Because
everyone is. I hope you’ll find that extra bit of
strength to get out of bed every morning, and
everything will make sense. Sometimes just showing
up is enough.”
I slowly turned my head to her and smiled,
“Thank you.”
She smiled back. “You’re welcome.”
The rain went on, with the sound of ten
thousand guns shooting straight down from the
heavens, as if someone upstairs is really pissed and
they’ve declared war. Some bird from a nearby tree
let out a few shouts. Perhaps it’s a battle cry, or
maybe a scream of agony from a victim of collateral
damage.
Through that raging wall of sound the voice of

'rain' in my poem, even though I’ve always been a
passionate rain-hater.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
Which means I'd been unknowingly enchanted
by the rain for a very long time, and this morning
was only an unexpected revelation.
Could there be any specific reason behind our
such obsession with the rain?
Maybe there is.
I always felt a certain connection to every
raindrop that I saw falling. I think they’re just like us
in a way.
We also fall from the heavens into this whirlpool
of madness, not because we choose to, rather
because the world around us wants us to; then we
get mixed and entangled with billions others just like
ourselves, who also fell from the sky against their
will, only to make a ripple just for a fleeting moment,
on the surface of a reluctant universe that has been
around for billions of years without us, and will
likely be around for billions more after we’ve left.
Then we flow towards wherever life and law
takes us. At some point we reach the sea, our journey
ends. But the remains we leave behind are just
enough to restart the cycle, for clouds to form and
thus new raindrops to fall, just like the ones that fell
before them, and the ones that will follow. Eons
The Raindrop
shall pass, as the cycle will keep repeating without
pause.
I looked at her as she slowly disappeared towards
the far end of what my eyes allowed me to see.
The last hour wasn’t exactly a very memorable
experience I think. Rather it was sufficiently
uneventful, just a regular day among the thousands
I left behind and the thousands I’ll probably find
ahead. But I have a feeling that I will remember this
particular morning for a long, long time.
I don’t know why though. Is it because of the
rain? Or the person I met? Or the time I spent with
her? Could be any of the above, or it could be none.
But what do I know? After all, I’m just a sentient
raindrop, ready to flow along the current to where
my river meets the sea.
Maybe Blade Runner was right. Maybe all these
moments really do get lost in time, like tears in the
rain.
But I hope this moment doesn’t.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
Greetings and gratitude from the
author:
Firstly I would like to apologize to all the readers
for making them sit through what you just read. I
understand that it might not have been easy.
I have received many good-willed and well
appreciated criticisms from some readers that—
most of the conversation in the ‘story’ was carried
out by the protagonist and very little is spoken by
the female side-character. I’m also aware that the
conversation is exhaustingly long and one-sided
which makes the dialogue very unnatural and
unrealistic. However this choice of over-
clarification and precision over concise, dramatic
realism – was very much intentional and was in fact
the whole point of this book.
This was originally not supposed to be (and still
isn’t) a story with characters and plot – rather an
essay which was supposed to contain all the logic in
favour of antinatalism. I had written that ‘essay’
long before I gave it the thin veil of a story, based
on the arguments I’ve had with dozens of different
people over the years.
The Raindrop
I’ve noticed that different individuals had
varying levels of intelligence and
understanding, had unique angles of tackling a
certain point, and required different styles and
lengths of explanations to deliver a certain message.
I’ve even been in situations where a breeder
presented a certain argument, I rebutted that with a
counterargument, only for that person to just
rephrase that exact same argument again a few
seconds later, as if my counterargument didn’t
register in their brain at all. That forced me to
reiterate my counterargument multiple times in
different ways using different words just hoping
they’d catch my point. So if you feel frustrated that
I have rephrased the same line way too many times
to the point where the dialogue sounded like a
bunch of separate paragraphs from different books
on the same topic clumsily stitched together – just
know that the same frustration exists in me as well.
I am a thinker, not an artist. So I wanted to make
sure that any possible argument that any reader
might present against antinatalism — should
already have a counterargument prepared in my
story.
I wanted the protagonist’s monologue to be
universal, exhaustive and to properly encompass all
these arguments in favour of antinatalism as clearly
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
as possible, often in unnecessarily great detail and
repetition, and using different metaphors and words
for the exact same point.
Thus the tiresome, unrealistically long replies of
the protagonist were necessary for covering all the
possible logic and reasoning . A ‘realistic’
conversation wouldn’t have contained as many
points, and the points wouldn’t be as detailed.
The book was meant to be a complete
antinatalist manifesto first and story second.
The first priority of my book was not to be a
story with a message, but to be a message disguised
as a story. Thoroughness and exposition were much
more important to me than plot and pacing.
So I would request the readers to kindly see my
writing for what it truly is – not a story but an essay
dressed in narrative clothing.
Besides there aren’t many sound arguments I
could think of in favour of procreation (natalism).
Since the whole point of the girl’s existence was to
only voice the logic behind natalism and I don’t
really see any logic behind it at all, thus I couldn’t
find much for the girl to say. This may or may not
be my shortcoming as a writer, and you may feel
disappointed if you were expecting a balanced
The Raindrop
dialogue between two real humans. I apologize if
that was the case.
Furthermore, most people on earth are already
‘breeders’ anyway and therefore will be
automatically supporting the girl and opposing the
guy. As a result there was almost no necessity to
defend the girl’s perspective whereas the
protagonist’s controversial opinions required a lot
more defending and explanation.
This reinforced the one-sided nature of the
dialogue even more, to the point where the girl feels
like just a literary device instead of an actual person
– which is exactly what happened here.
The main character of the story has even directly
stated that he’d defended his views against many
people before and is therefore ridiculously over-
prepared to refute almost any arguments imaginable
(much like the writer himself), whereas the girl was
pretty much caught off guard by the absurdity of
the topic.
I hope the deliberateness of these choices will
help to somewhat explain the unrealism of the
encounter.
Last but not least, I am very grateful to anyone
who took their valuable time to read this work.
Nafiz - Bin - Hafiz
As this entire book including the writing,
formatting, cover designing etc. was completely
done by just one single person (i.e. me) with no
prior professional experience or paid software, it
may not have lived up to a certain standard most
readers would expect. That further strengthens my
gratitude towards my readers for enduring this
travesty.
This book means a lot to me, and even if just 1
person reads it in its entirety, I’ll find that to be
deeply meaningful and rewarding.
Thank you.
