runs.text: The Worn Out Script
Exhausted, I stand in front of my door, trying to remember where I placed my keys as I
search through my pockets. I emptied them, but I didn’t find them. So I dump everything
from my backpack onto my front doormat, eyes hunting. Finally, I find them and shove
everything back in the bag haphazardly.
Minx, my adorable tuxedo cat, comes sprinting down the hallway, nearly smashing into
the couch and missing it by an inch, before reaching me. I crouch down to catch her as
she crashes into my arms, meowing like she hasn’t seen me in 10 years.
“Hi, baby,” I murmur, lips brushing against her little forehead, watching her eyes flutter
closed with delight. I drop my bag on the floor, letting exhaustion take over as I carry her
to the bedroom. I place her on the bed, watching her curl into a ball on top of the
blankets, before pulling away into the silence of the bathroom.
I turn the tap on, slipping out of my clothes, before entering the stream of lukewarm
water. Steam rolls like thick fog, causing the mirror to steam up. Water cascades down
my back, but I don’t really feel it. My eyes drift to the mirror, trailing the droplets
slipping down.
My throat burns for a moment, a lump forming— before it disappears as if it had only
been a phantom ache.
I step out, the cold air hitting my wet skin like a sharp, biting chill. I stand there for a
second, enjoying the way my skin prickles against the cold. Then, my mind pulls me back
into reality, so I grab my towel, drying myself off. I slip on my worn T-shirt and pull on
my cotton shorts over my legs, the waistband resting snugly on my hips.
I slip into the bed, switching the bedside lamp off. I watch the room instantly plunge into
darkness, the shadows in the room getting consumed. The silence is
loud
—loud with
every word I swallowed back today. I guess this is the cost of keeping such a big secret to
myself.
I had moved away for a reason. To make hiding easier. But it didn’t work, not really. I
just feel more lonely now, more deceitful and pathetic.
A different neighborhood with a different set of walls surrounding me, suffocating me,
but that’s all it is. I’m still under the same sky; I’m still living in this oppressive place.
You can’t outrun a whole country when you don’t have the money to buy a plane ticket.
So I’m still here, still pretending, still smiling like nothing has changed, still speaking
from an old script that I finally want to alter, trapped in an endless loop of pretense.
My phone lies untouched on the nightstand, vibrating occasionally as my concerned
family texts me, but I don’t have the energy to reply. Not tonight. They have been
checking on me more frequently since I moved, especially my mom.
The night before I left my family home, my belongings neatly packed into cardboard
boxes, my mom had sat me down to talk. “I’m worried, honey. You were never one to
make such rash decisions. Are you really sure moving away is a good decision? Are you
really okay? You’re responsible and mature, I know that, but I feel like you’re hiding a
part of you from us,” she had said, but I knew. Her love would never outweigh the
traditional views that have been pushed upon her for decades, views that would cloud her
judgment if I ever told her.
My heart feels heavy— heavy with the burden of the secret, heavy with the pretense that
is starting to feel like chains tied around me, suffocating my senses, trapping me in this
situation longer.
I try to shut my brain off, closing my eyes, trying to force myself to sleep. Yet sleep
eludes me. The minutes bleed by, filling the silence with deliberation. Beside me, Minx
shifts, pressing into my hip, letting a soft sigh out, as she stretches one paw out on my
stomach. She’s the only thing that feels real, the only thing that isn’t complicated right
now.
However, the peace doesn’t remain for much longer. My phone rings, the screen lighting
up as a shrill, overpowering ringtone fills the room in place of the silence, startling both
of us. I quickly pick it up, my mind begging for the sound to stop. It’s Mom. I sigh and
decide to answer.
“Hi, mom,” I murmur, my hand combing through my hair, pushing it off my forehead, as
I sit up, nudging back until the headboard presses against my back.
“Hi, honey, how are you? I couldn’t stop thinking about you… My eyes keep going to
your bedroom door, as if you’ll come out, but then you don’t, and I just… Needed to talk
to you,” my mom speaks, her voice crackling through the speaker.
A heavy silence stretches between us, the status of the line filling the quiet as I think of a
response that wouldn’t sound heavy. “...I’m fine, mom,” I whisper, the words tasting like
burnt toast, chalky and bitter.
“Are you really?” I hear her say. “Yes, mom, I promise. You should sleep now that you
know how I’m doing,” I tell her, attempting to subtly redirect the conversation towards
something light.
“Okay, honey. Love you, don’t stay up too late,” she rasps.
“Yes, mom, don’t worry. Love you too,” I breathe, pressing the ‘end call’ button.
I drop my phone into the covers, watching the screen turn dark, plummeting the room
back into blackness. I take one deep breath, my lungs filling with oxygen, and I breathe
out. I repeat. One deep inhale and one deep exhale. Until my mind clears just enough for
me to be able to lie back down.
However, as soon as my head hits the pillow again, my mind is filled with those thoughts.
I think I realised back in high school. I was 16, in a co-educational school. I had dated a
boy back when I was 14; stupid, but it made me realise things. After the breakup, my best
friend, Neela, had supported me through it. 14-year-old me felt heartbroken as if the
ground beneath my feet had shifted, and her kind words helped.
Except at one point, I stopped thinking about that guy, or anything at all. Neela clouded
my mind 24/7— her smiles lingered in my memory, and her giggles made my heart race.
I was confused at first, thinking the universe was playing a dumb yet cruel joke.
But the feelings had remained.
Every time her fingers brushed against mine when she wanted to take my notes, every
time she teased me for forgetting a test date, every time she helped me with chapters I
didn’t understand, every touch left a lingering warmth that terrified me to my very core.
In a country where everyone was taught to go down the traditional way, which is to get
married to the opposite sex of your parents’ selection, and have children to keep your
legacy alive. Oh, forgive me, I meant, to keep the
man’s
legacy alive. To ensure the
patriarchal society keeps
breathing
It was a slow, agonising journey. The confusion morphed into a permanent panic. I spent
months trying to convince myself this was a phase, that this was a temporary feeling that
would eventually disappear. I just felt grateful for her support; that’s what I told myself.
I tried to find logic in this feeling; I really did. I thought it was a normal side effect of
teenage heartbreak, hiding this massive truth from everyone I loved.
For 2 whole years, I pretended everything was okay. I learned to laugh things off, to
pretend I still wanted to go down that conservative path, when my family joked about my
future marriage, all while a quiet, painful warmth and joy bloomed in my chest when
Neela did so much as smile at me.
But the facade could only last for so long.
My heart ached with adoration. It didn’t help that she was a touchy person; she would
constantly hug me or kiss my cheek. And so one day, as a fresh 16-year-old, I decided to
write my feelings on paper as well as I could articulate them, and buy her favorite
flowers, carnations, with my pocket money. I picked a day for us to hang out, ensuring
the weather would be cool, even buying a fancy picnic basket just for that day, and texted
her, ‘
Hey, bubbles, let’s hang out on Nov. 24, I have something for you
The anticipation was killing me. When the day finally came, I had worn a pink top that
she had once said looked like it was made for me, white baggy jeans, and dusty pink
sneakers. I remember that day so well.
She had arrived 3 minutes early, but fortunately, I knew her so well by now that I had
already prepared everything—a blue picnic blanket perfectly splayed on the ground, my
shoes neatly placed beside said blanket, and the picnic basket containing the food I had
worked hard to buy and make. It wasn’t a lot, really; it was just 4 grilled cheese
sandwiches, a packet of her favorite potato crisps, her favorite cherry lime soda, and 4
chocolate chip brownies.
We had laughed over dumb inside jokes while munching on the food. Eventually, it got
cooler, the wind breezing past, causing her hair to fly into her face. I had put it behind her
ear gently, as if she was made of spun glass. The gold flecks in her pretty eyes had
glittered, the Sun emphasizing the gorgeous spark in her eyes.
The conversation had died down; she froze for a minute, watching me in confusion as I
pulled the letter and flower bouquet out. “What is it?” she whispered as I handed them to
her, her eyes flickering from the gifts to my face, trying to read the situation.
“Read it,” I had told her, almost entirely confident she reciprocated my feelings.
She had opened it slowly, her eyes flickering over the words I had spent an hour writing. I
waited, almost smugly waiting, thinking she would accept my proposal. And then, she
said, “I’m sorry, Adi, I didn’t–I didn’t realize you felt that way, or I wouldn’t have
behaved that way. I am like that with everyone, you know that… I’m sorry. I don’t feel
that way. Don’t worry, though, Adrita. I won’t tell anyone unless you feel comfortable.
And I do still want to be friends… I’m so sorry.” Her eyes filled with what I could only
describe as pitying politeness as she placed the letter in my hands.
My hands had shaken as my fingers closed around the paper. The cool November breeze
suddenly felt numbing against my skin. I didn’t cry; I didn’t even tear up. The shock was
too consuming for me at that moment. Instead, I started grabbing my things, shoving the
leftover food into the picnic basket haphazardly. I just needed to move. I needed to hide
before my face gave me away, before the facade would crack.
That’s all I remember—that’s all I
want
to remember.
I stare up at the dark ceiling now, the pitch-black of my bedroom bleeding through the
memory. It’s funny. It’s funny how you can move to a completely different neighborhood,
buy a different set of walls, and yet you’re still trapped in the exact memory you can be
desperate to escape, inside your head.
The letter is long gone, burned into ashes I had thrown in the trash can. The carnations
are dead; they
have
been for almost 8 years now.
And yet, the rejection still
screams
in the dark at 3:00 AM.

runs.text: in dreams
in dreams we’re together
in dreams i don’t have to wait for the distance to end
wait for me to comprehend
if it’s really love
or just another messed up pretend
in dreams
i’m with you and you’re with me
not just physically
but also in a sense that we both feel seen
in dreams
we’re closer
and there’s no deadline for us to end
or spare of time we need to bargain
just to see a glimpse of each other
in dreams
we’re holding hands and nothing tragic has happened to us
yet
in dreams
in loving you, i don’t hold back
i let it consume me
instead of contemplating on whatever we lack
in dreams
i’m holding you while i sleep
mumbling how you’re someone i want to keep
in my life
forever
in my dreams
i hug you and you hug me back
and we stay like this until the very end
in my dreams
you’re in my arms
until the dream ends
and this turns into another one of those scenes
that i constantly play in my head

title: Lovelorn
author: Tea Time
imageAlt: Cover image for Lovelorn

runs.text: Lovelorn
Be my poem
Thrill me with all you have
Let my forlorn melodies evoke
and whispers I never spoke.
I have never been a lover
Never been a poet
Yet when you look for my line,
I picture you as my valentine.
My every restraint disappear
whenever you are closer.
You are my bliss of aurora,
my moon in melancholy.
Under crystalline stars
Oh, How seraphic is my ingénue!
My thirst is sacred begonia,
weeping in my wistful bones.
Courage falling short to confess,
my sorrow grows spineless.
Tell me, for never promising forever
My piteous patience, am I a sinner?
The moon forgot my window
You are my bittersweet Mona Lisa
Am I allowed to love,
or being a lovelorn is my curse?

title: Human Judgement: Beyond Borders
author: Sagnik Saha
imageAlt: Cover image for Human Judgement: Beyond Borders

runs.text: Human Judgement: Beyond Borders
Humans, naturally, are inclined to judge everything, ranging from quality of everyday items to a
person's character. It's in their nature to put labels on everything. But, sometimes, it's taken too
far. They can never be absolutely sure about their decisions, regardless of how foolproof they
think their judging methods are. Judging humans is a complex matter, which most people don't
take seriously. But there are many flaws, even in the way you see other people yourselves.
Say, you meet a new person. His name's Fred. He seems pretty nice to you. Now, you might
assume that he's a pretty good human from your viewpoint. But, do you really think you're
absolutely correct about your hypothesis? Yes, you might be correct and he might be a great
person. But he also might be a serial killer or a downright evil person. Maybe he acted nice only
to you. Or maybe, he's neither a perfect person you imagined, nor a downright evil human, maybe
your limited knowledge of him makes your judgement incomplete. Taking this case in mind, I urge
you to question yourself if you can ever be always correct in your assumptions about other
people.
People unknowingly and sometimes unintentionally judge others without the full knowledge of
them based on things that might sometimes be unreliable as a judging factor.
Actions and intentions are some of the most common ways that people are judged. If a person is
known for doing good things, people regard him as sincere, while if a person is known for his evil
actions, he's known as malevolent. But it doesn't always justify everything. If a person planning
to murder someone accidentally saves someone else, he's known as 'good' while having
intentions of cruelty. While if a person who tries to help someone accidentally causes harm to
him, he's shown to be 'bad' when he didn't have any intention of committing harm. It essentially
causes unfairness to many. In this way, intentions and actions contradict each other, as, while
intentions point a person's character to one side, actions can point to another. In cases like these,
simple moral labels like 'bad' or 'good' don't work.
Another hidden force is the reason for this. In many outcomes, moral luck plays a significant role.
Factors beyond a person's control influence how their reason and conduct are judged. Two people
trying to do the same thing with the same intention can sometimes lead to different outcomes
for both, with moral luck ultimately at the root for this. There's no possible way to control moral
luck, and it's why unfairness and uncertain judgements happen frequently. Let's say, two drunk
drivers are driving back to their homes. One makes it back safely without any consequences, while
the other crashes into a pedestrian and commits murder. Both committed the same wrongdoing,
but their outcomes came out different. Moral luck is one of the biggest factors in these kinds of
events. We can never possibly judge a person absolutely correctly due to the randomness of
moral luck, and how even with proper responsibility, significantly worse outcomes happen.
Circumstances are possibly one of the most deciding factors in a person's judgement. Sometimes,
people can't control the outcome. Even if they do everything right, forces beyond their control
somehow force them to do something unwillingly. This can shape a person's identity and
reputation for many people if the outcome is devastating.
Ken Kaneki, from Tokyo Ghoul, never planned or willed to be a ghoul. But, due to forces beyond
his control, a surgery was made to transport another ghoul's organs into his body and transform
him into a half-ghoul to save his life was completed, which unknowingly ruined his life. His hunger
for human flesh in this new biological existence is not due to his will or desires, but the outcome
of the whole event resulted in his body structure to change and require human flesh. This is all
due to circumstances beyond his control, which were never chosen or even wanted by him. This
new biological form creates a conflict between his morality and identity.
However, Kaneki also changes through his time in his new form. At first, he repeatedly tried to
prevent himself from gorging on humans or in the least, not slay them. But gradually, his actions
become more indefensible and brutal, with even his morality and identity changing. This creates
an important question, should people be judged as the current form they are in without
consideration for their pasts and circumstances?
Imagine, a bright student scores 80% on a test and an average student also scores the same.
However, people are dissatisfied with the bright student while praising the average one. People's
expectations before something cause this to happen. If a person expects someone to perform
something perfectly beforehand, then he'll be disappointed if that person does it a little
imperfectly. While, if a person expects someone else to do something with not much quality, he'll
be surprised if that person manages to do it with the almost perfect quality. Even though the
outcomes are the same, people's expectations changed the judgement of one person from
another.
A soldier valiantly fights for his country in a war. After the end of the war, people of his homeland
immensely praise him and he receives overwhelming admiration and gratitude. While in the
enemy country, he's seen as an embodiment of evil, a mass murderer who committed homicide
on numerous people. The soldier does exactly the same thing, but the judgements he receives
from people are different. The actions and intentions don't change, only the perspective changes.
One person can receive vastly different opinions from different groups of people, without ever
changing anything about himself, all because of the change of perspective and the people who
judge him.
Now, digging into deeper and more questionable territories, Lelouch Vi Britannia from Code
Geass is one of the most intriguing characters in anime. He perfectly captures the moral dilemma
and question of, 'What happens when someone knowingly chooses morally questionable actions
for their pursuit of a greater good?'. He may have noble intentions, but, his methods are
irredeemably cruel and questionable. Even though his ultimate objective is world peace between
Britain and all the other territories, his actions undeniably cause immense suffering. This leads to
people condemning him without fully knowing his motivations. But, should people forgive him
after discovering his reasons, even after causing huge casualties? Can his objective truly justify his
actions? This creates a moral dilemma, where one might be confused on what to judge Lelouch
on. Lelouch is here, undeniably an anomaly in this case, where one cannot really judge him
correctly based on one singular aspect of his character without taking in mind his other traits.
Taking Lelouch's case into considerstion, I'd like to ask you, should we change our opinion on
others if we know the intentions behind their actions? Lelouch committed many almost
indefensible acts, including numerous war crimes and mass genocides. But, if we knew
beforehand that he had noble intentions of peace for all, should we change our opinion on him?
Even though his intentions are clearly for the greater good of humanity, should we change our
view of him, and directly reduce the effect of his actions by justifying it with his intentions? This
creates a genuinely interesting dilemma that can reveal a deeply fascinating layer to human
judgement.
Moreover, this creates another layer we could explore. Say, one person knows only about
Lelouch's atrocities, while another knows about both his motivations and actions. With the
difference in knowledge, most of the time, there is going to be an obvious difference between
their judgement of him. But, just because we know more of a person, does it mean that we should
change our original view on him, or is it just attempts to sympathize with his actions and justify
our existing prejudices? None of the additional information we know about him can ever change
the actions he did, so why should we also change our opinion on him? Is the extra information
we acquire on someone actually relevant evidence to maybe understanding their actions, or are
those just evidence we show to sympathize with and reinforce our existing judgement? This is a
deeply compelling layer that is worth exploring, and I'd like you to question yourself on these and
judge how confident you are in judging another person.
Returning to Fred's case in the beginning, let's say, we have vast information on his character. If
he has, say, done some cruel acts but with some understandable reasons behind it, should we
justify his actions? Is understanding someone's actions really equivalent to justifying his actions
as a whole? One can judge another's action, their responsibility in an action, or the person's
whole character. So, in the end, the judgements can also be unique based on what one judges.
And, if we change our opinion of him with the extra evidence, is it a sign of intelligence or
deception by persuasion? Can we ever really separate our personal feeling towards someone
from affecting our rational judgement of that person? Say, we disliked Lelouch, would it affect our
judgement of him? Say, the people he killed were our loved ones, should we be able to justify our
change of opinion on him? The evidence we acquire to judge a person can also ultimately lead to
us using it as attempts to strengthen our biases towards that person.
Ultimately, the final question I'd like to ask you after reading all of this is, even after understanding
all this, are you confident enough that your judgement on anyone is justified? Judgements can be
separately incomplete, biased and morally unjustified. While one's judgement of another person
can any of these, their judgement might not be inherently incorrect too. So, if I were to effectively
rephrase my original question, it would be, are you really confident enough and have enough
rational evidence to defend your judgement on anyone is actually justifiable in an overall sense?

content: Forever
"I love you with all my existence Rabea, you were the only one who never feared."

It is the hour of midnight, endless darkness surrounds Rabea. Inside an apartment the only source of light is the moonlight from the window that befalls her face. On her lap is the man she loves, her husband and in front of her stands an entity that wears his face and preaches about his love for her. Long black hair like his, same white Panjabi and the same prominent features yet his eyes are the one feature that sets them apart. The entity bears ruby red glistening eyes devouring her in his gaze in devotion. She looks at him with eyes of anger and disgust; his obsession wrapped in a cloth of love can’t melt her. She then looks down at her lap at her husband’s lifeless pale face with a soft gaze. He breathes heavily for some air as blood oozes down his nose, eyes and the corners of his mouth. She brushes his hair with her fingers gently, holds his hand and tells him it's alright. Yet the traces of tears in her cheeks say differently. The entity standing Infront of her breaths heavily, clenches his fist looking down at him. Fighting for life he finally is defeated by his destiny. Rabea screams in agony and pain holding him. The entity gives her a moment to grieve then speaks.

"You love him? I will be him; I will stay with you forever wearing the face you can never forget. Just tell me, you love me. Just tell me that you desire me the way I do. Lie if needed. I beg of you, my love."

The entity kneels on one knee beside Rabea and holds her left hand while her right one is still over her husband's chest. The eyes of the entity are teary and soft for her, yet for him every breath of her screams pure hatred. She spits in his face, her jaw clenched, her lips moving, eyes red, traces of tears on her cheeks. Instead of anger tears pour down his eyes as he listens to her with devotion.

" You have killed my father whose sole purpose was to save me, my mother lost her sanity. She repeats your name like a chant. Afjal, Afjal, Ajfal. My entire childhood went by carrying the weight off restrictions and talismans. And now, you have killed the only man that was brave enough to love me. How can you love someone if you ruin them? How can you demand love from me when all you have done made me miserable."

She yells at him and frees her hand. He stands up, a flick of his wrist is all it took, a simple gesture yet the force behind it is absolute. In unbridled rage he sends the body of her husband flying across the living room slammed at the wall from her lap. Rage leaves her body, it shivers in fear. She stands up and takes a few calculated steps back. He paces fast towards her in speed of wind, his hands gripped tight on her forearm.
‘I am the head of a qabalah; I can have anything the world has to offer but you are all I desire.’
‘Why?’  in a faint whisper with her eyes locked with his, she says.

‘You don’t remember, do you?... That one stormy night in your village…. 15 years ago…. when you were 15, angry with your mother, you ran away from home and took shelter in a manor….You were the one who was not afraid.’

A distant forgotten memory flashes before her eyes. One mistake of hers sailed her life’s boat to a storm that left her and those around her in shambles. That night in a conflict with her mother over discontinuing her studies and forcing marriage upon her she left her home in midst of a heavy storm. In search of shelter soaked and shivering she took shelter in an abandoned decaying manor house in the woods that was the portal of his world to hers. When she first saw him, he stepped out of a portal inside the manor, with the flick of his finger he removed a rock from his path in anger. In his human form he seemed about 4-5 years older than her. Long hair, sturdy, standing tall in a long white tunic that fitted him well. Utmost captivating man she had ever seen in her village. He noticed instantly hiding behind a pillar watching it all yet instead of fear he sees excitement in those eyes of hers. He could not help but smile, all his rage left him. In the blink of an eye he vanished, she looked around cluelessly. Over her left shoulder she felt a cold wind, a chill ran down her spine.

‘You shouldn’t have seen that, kiddo’ a whisper heard in her left ear was enough for her to look back. There he was standing four feet away from her, looking at her up and down with a smirk, his hands behind his back.
‘You are a jinn? I have heard stories of your kind from my Nanu.’
‘Anyone would’ve fainted, yet you stand before me with a smile, with fascination all over your face. Are you not afraid?’
Rabea nodded her head right to left to right with a smile.
‘I was always fascinated by your kind; always wanted to see for myself what I only heard about but could never express because my nanu would get angry with me. I miss her.’
‘She died a year ago?’
‘How do you know?’
‘One of my capabilities.’

And right before her eyes he transformed into her grandmother. With open arms he looked at her with a smile. In tears of joy, she hugged him, he wrapped his arms around her. Her smell mesmerized him so did her valiant nature, he never thought as the promised leader of his qabalah, so powerful, he could ever desire something so futile, an ordinary woman. After a long hug she looked back to look at her nanu but saw him smiling instead. Flustered, she took a few steps back yet smiled afterwards and he smiled back at her.
‘What more would you like to see?’

They talked for a while, showed her many of his capabilities sitting at a corner of the manor. The storm cleared, yet a bigger one was forged. She fell asleep resting her head over his shoulder, he admired her, fell for her. The villagers discovered her asleep in the manor alone, a place they called the jiner akhara. No one was willing to go there but upon her father’s request they did and discovered her unconscious. All her life she thought that was a dream and after a while she forgot all about it. But Afjal could never, he remained close to her than her own shadow and whomever dared to get closer ended up destroyed. She looks at her husband’s dead body then locks eyes with him; her eyes filled with terror and tears.
‘It all happened because of me, my father, Abdullah. They all died because of me. Now, it all ends with me.’

She frees herself swiftly, stands six feet away from him yet her body faces him. From the side table nearest to her she grabs a glass vase and smashes it on the wall, holds it so close to her neck that it pierces her flesh.

‘If you move even a centimeter I will shove the entire thing in my throat. Your kind has sworn upon an oath to destroy mine, a being like you can never love, all you know is to destroy and extort. I have lost so many things; I can’t live like this, a puppet of someone’s desire.’
She screams her heart out still holding the broken vase close and slowly pushing it into her flesh. Afjal’s ruby red eyes are tearfully filled with concern and pain.
‘Stop, I can’t see you like this.’
‘With you I will forever be miserable.’
‘I love you… I will prove it…I will leave.’

Afjal brings forth his left arm, clenches his fist and then slowly releases it and looks back at Abdullah’s lifeless body. Rabea breaths heavily yet slowly and observes it all, her eyes on Abdullah. The absolute stillness of the room shatters with a convulsive heave of Abdullah, his chest jolts upward, a rattling sound in his throat as his lungs expand and he breaths through his nose and mouth as his life finds its way back to him. His eyes wander around; he whispers Rabea’s name with such a frequency what only Afjal could hear.

Rabea’s grip on the glass loosens, it shatters and turns to powder in collision with the ground. She runs to Abdullah, sits by his side and calms him down, tapping chest slowly. Then after a moment she slowly turns her head to look back, he is gone.
Time passed by and it all felt like a forgotten nightmare to her. Rabea now lives in a new house with Abdullah. They have hired a Raqi who visits them often to inspect their house.
‘The house is free from any paranormal, it has been 2 years. I believe there is no need for any further visit, Mr. Abdullah. I must leave now.’
Lastly observing their living room, the Raqi stands up and says goodbye to both.
‘Let me escort you to the corridor hujur.’ Abdullah offers. The Raqi flashes a grin to Abdullah at the gate, the color of his iris flashes red for a moment then stabilizes.
‘The whole Qaabilah is waiting for your return my lord, for you to lead us all into excellence. You must keep your promise. Humans are short lived; you must return to your world when she dies.’

He leaves, walks towards the road ahead for 5 minutes and vanishes in thin air. Afjal closes the gate and enters the house to see Rabea waiting for him at lunch table. She smiles at him from a distance; he smiles back at her. She runs and hugs him.
‘I thought the miseries were never ending, it all feels like a dream still.’
He ruffles her hair softly, her face buried in his chest, his arms wrapped around her. His eyes change to its natural ruby red color.
‘It is not a dream. I love you. You are safe here with me. We are together…Forever.’

title: The Chameleon
author: Fahmiah Fahreen
imageAlt: Cover image for The Chameleon

runs.text: The boat rumbled and yawned as we started across the creek.
I cupped my hands around the dewy railing, my heart a living thing in my chest as we glided along the
silky green water, the reflections of the trees surrounding us crinkling and curling up as the boat made its
way majestically through them.
The guide’s booming words through the loudspeaker acted as a confirmation of everyone’s anticipation.
“We will now be starting our journey through the Sundarbans. If you step onto the deck, you will see a
whole lot of things on either side of you that you might want to capture in your cameras. Enjoy!”
Sati had a routine. She woke up everyday before the roosters could call, quickly brushed her hair down
while the first lights of dawn tried to crack through the dark interior of the hut, then tiptoed out, before
breaking into a run at a safe distance from where her parents slept.
She’d skip across the warm earth, her feet crunching the fallen leaves and leaving the dust in small
whirlpools as she reached the water.
Sometimes, a lot of times, she could catch the boat.
At least she could see the thing cutting slowly and contentedly through the green water, opening the
curtains to daylight as it made the fog make way for it. She could watch the people on the railings outside,
some who looked a lot like herself, and others who didn’t. Baba called them bideshis, said it was for them
the boats were made, the tracks cleared, the treetops cleared of nests to make the small wooden houses
with trailing rope ladders.
He said it was for these people, standing wide eyed at the boats, that he had to go out to the forest
everyday.
Sati, having turned just nine this year, didn’t understand half the things Baba said. She also didn’t
understand why before Baba left every morning, Ma stood before him, her lips moving rapidly in prayers
incomprehensive to Sati as she ran her hand repeatedly over Baba’s head and blew on it at regular
intervals.
She didn’t understand the relief Ma tried to hide when Baba came home every evening.
She didn’t get it. Baba was supposed to come home, was he not?
Today, Sati was lucky. She reached the bank just as the boat hummed through the canopy clad water. She
watched it for a while, before the first ray of sun warned her of her parent’s waking. She fox-walked
through the trees again, unbeknownst of the fact that someone on the boat was watching her retreat.
I put my binoculars down as the little girl disappeared back into the trees.
She’d almost scared me when she peeked through the trees, watching us with close set, stealthy eyes. You’d
think she was a spy if it wasn’t for the curiosity and fascination etched across her little face.
The guide was saying that the boat would be anchored shortly, and we’d start our short trek through one
of the less dense parts of the forest. We were recommended to gather our supplies.
Retrieving my backpack from the storage inside the boat, I found myself wondering if I would see the girl
again.
Sati sat alone on the withering grass, turning one of the dried tendrils over her fingers.
Beside her sat her father’s tools for honey collecting: an old wicker basket, a small machete. In her hands,
she held the smoker.
Baba himself was wringing out a thin gamchha before wrapping it around his face: his main source of
protection.
She was happy today, because Baba was taking her with him. He wouldn’t dare do this in most cases, but
today they were to go to a much lighter stretch of forest, and she had been begging him to take her for
ages.
Ma wasn’t very happy about this. Sati could tell from her clouded face as she watched Baba take Sati by
the hand and walk her away from the safety of her home.
They got to the spot before the other baowalis did, and Sati made herself comfortable on a seat of dry
leaves as Baba inspected the trees.
Sati wondered why this part of the forest looked so well groomed compared to the others.
The answer presented itself shortly enough, the sound of collective footsteps and exaggerated gasps
making its entrance.
The track had extended into a stretch of damp land clouded by trees. The guide was explaining how this
was a popular spot for villagers making a livelihood out of collecting honey. We took careful steps through
the trees.
We stopped before a collection of shorter greens with long, slitted leaves pouring out and tangling with
one another. It was hard paying any attention to the guide with the constant jittery conversations within the
group, and I found myself staring blankly at the tongue like leaves.
Then the leaves crackled, and the chameleon showed.
I gasped.
The creature was quite invisible among the green around it, and its constantly darting bulging beads of
eyes were the only thing that gave it away.
As I watched, stripes seemed to materialize on its coarse skin, and one long limb stretched out to a thin
branch nearby. The next second, it disappeared.
I fished out and flipped through the little brochure in my pocket.
There were no mentions of chameleons there…
“Do you want to hold it?”
I jumped and looked to my side. The girl I’d seen in the morning stood there, her hands tucked under the
folds of her faded frock.
“I…you can?” I asked, and she nodded enthusiastically.
She parted the branches a little, and the chameleon reappeared.
Making a soft clicking sound with her tongue, the girl stretched out a hand. The chameleon remained quite
still as one finger tickled its back, then curled up under its belly. She quickly drew her hand back, and I
saw the chameleon be drawn along with it, its split claws grasping her finger for a hold. Before my eyes,
its color changed from leafy green to a muted brown, and then slowly to a more charcoal shade. Dark
navy stripes with turquoise highlights materialized around its body, yellow spots bubbling towards its belly.
It opened its jaw wide, and its eyes darted around maniacally.
“Are you sure this is safe?” I asked, watching its tiny teeth.
She grinned. “Don’t worry, he’s just a little scared. He’s not used to so many people.”
She gently blew across its back, and with fascination, I watched its color lighten until it was back to the
original grass green.
“He’s a young one.” The girl deduced. “Hold?”
She held the creature out, and I quickly shook my head.
Slightly crestfallen, she let the chameleon scamper back into the leaves. We watched as it quickly made
itself invisible again.
“SATI!” A man’s voice growled, and the girl jumped. Her confident exterior disappeared, crumpled up with
apprehension and tucked away inside her tiny form as she nimbly made her way to the voice’s source, a
baowali who seemed to be her father by the way he wrapped her thin forearm with a rough, protective
hand and took her away.
The chameleon had appeared again. As it seemed to notice me, its back curled, and it quickly climbed
back into the depths of the tree. I couldn’t help thinking I’d seen this same movement just a few moments
ago.
As we boarded back to our boat, I saw her again. She meandered through the crowd, going up to tired
tourists with a pitiful expression. Then she hefted multiple backpacks too big for her and trudged down to
the boat as the tourists who had given her their burden splashed their faces with water and sauntered
along the bank. The girl reappeared beside them, and I saw her face light up as they handed her a few
crinkled notes.
As she stood by a corner fumbling with the notes, I went up to her.
“What’s your name?” I asked, and she started, quickly tucking away the money in a knot at the hem of her
frock.
“Sati.” She stammered as she answered me.
I didn’t know what else to say.
She seemed desperate to get away, and so I left her.
This was the second time she reminded me of the chameleon.
The boat started again to take us away from this beautiful place, I pictured the chameleon again. The way
it sat hugging the branches with a false sense of security. I wondered if it knew there were people around
it, all around it, that could pluck him away at their choice simply for their own entertainment. How many
times, I wondered, did a human being feel the same way, surrounded by people who they knew were there
just to take advantage of them, prise them away from their comfort for other people’s satisfaction? How
many times did I feel like that? Countless. Since childhood. In school. Outside. Fighting tooth and nail just to
be able to take a flight across the world to another country to make others proud of me. Isn’t it the same? I
wondered where the chameleon came from. If it remembered what home felt like. If it could ever go back.
I walked up to the deck and looked out. The trees, sturdy and motionless as it seemed rooted to the
ground, seemed to sway slightly to acknowledge me. Was this home, then?
And a little further from them, sitting alone on the sand, was a girl named Sati. She looked up as I stood
there, and got to her feet. With a thin, frail hand, she waved. I waved back, and her lips broke into a
small, but real smile. The chameleon had changed colors again, different from the shy, scared girl
desperately leading life to one that had found her home beside the green waters of Sundarbans, who
could be happy at the smallest things in life. Was that not the life every person lives? As the boat gently
glided away, I wrapped my hands around the railing, another chameleon in this world where you were
forced to change constantly to find a home that’s yours. Is that not what makes life worth living?
