tourists with a pitiful expression. Then she hefted multiple backpacks too big for her and trudged down to
the boat as the tourists who had given her their burden splashed their faces with water and sauntered
along the bank. The girl reappeared beside them, and I saw her face light up as they handed her a few
crinkled notes.
As she stood by a corner fumbling with the notes, I went up to her.
“What’s your name?” I asked, and she started, quickly tucking away the money in a knot at the hem of her
frock.
“Sati.” She stammered as she answered me.
I didn’t know what else to say.
She seemed desperate to get away, and so I left her.
This was the second time she reminded me of the chameleon.
The boat started again to take us away from this beautiful place, I pictured the chameleon again. The way
it sat hugging the branches with a false sense of security. I wondered if it knew there were people around
it, all around it, that could pluck him away at their choice simply for their own entertainment. How many
times, I wondered, did a human being feel the same way, surrounded by people who they knew were there
just to take advantage of them, prise them away from their comfort for other people’s satisfaction? How
many times did I feel like that? Countless. Since childhood. In school. Outside. Fighting tooth and nail just to
be able to take a flight across the world to another country to make others proud of me. Isn’t it the same? I
wondered where the chameleon came from. If it remembered what home felt like. If it could ever go back.
I walked up to the deck and looked out. The trees, sturdy and motionless as it seemed rooted to the
ground, seemed to sway slightly to acknowledge me. Was this home, then?
And a little further from them, sitting alone on the sand, was a girl named Sati. She looked up as I stood
there, and got to her feet. With a thin, frail hand, she waved. I waved back, and her lips broke into a
small, but real smile. The chameleon had changed colors again, different from the shy, scared girl
desperately leading life to one that had found her home beside the green waters of Sundarbans, who
could be happy at the smallest things in life. Was that not the life every person lives? As the boat gently
glided away, I wrapped my hands around the railing, another chameleon in this world where you were
forced to change constantly to find a home that’s yours. Is that not what makes life worth living?

title: The Things We Buried…
author: Fatiha Nufaisa Zara
imageAlt: Cover image for The Things We Buried…

runs.text: The Things We Buried…
Chapter 1 : The Basket
“Aunt Anne!”
My voice echoed through the upstairs hallway.

I had been cleaning the spare room for almost an hour, and I was beginning to regret every decision that had led me there. Dust covered the shelves, old boxes were stacked against the walls, and the curtains looked as though they had not been washed since the beginning of time.
Then I noticed a basket tucked beneath the wooden table.
It was old. Not just old in the way that made something look antique, but old in the way that made you wonder how many secrets it had witnessed.
A thin layer of dust covered its lid. I pulled it out, sneezed twice and carefully lifted the cover.
Inside were a few yellowed photographs, a folded piece of fabric and a thick, dark-green book.
It looked like a diary.
“Aunt Anne!” I called again.
She appeared in the doorway, wiping her hands on her apron.
“What happened now?”
“What’s this?”
The moment she saw the basket, her expression changed. It was subtle, but I noticed it. Her eyes lingered on the book before moving towards me.
“Where did you find that?”
“Under the table.”
She stepped closer and ran her fingers along the basket’s handle.
“That basket was given to me the night you came to live with us,” she said quietly.
I looked up. “The night I was handed to you?”
She nodded.
I knew very little about that night. According to Aunt Anne, I had been brought to her as a baby. My mother had already passed away, and my father was unable to take care of me.
My father.
Sky Blake.
The man who had been in prison for thirteen years.
The man accused of killing the grandparents of my best friends. Harper and Hank.
I had never known him well enough to hate him properly. I had only known the stories people told about him.
“Can I look inside?” I asked.
Aunt Anne hesitated.
Then she nodded. “I suppose it’s time you did.”
I lifted the book. Its cover was worn, and the corners had begun to curl. There was no title, only a small silver design pressed into the leather.
I opened it.
Nothing happened.
Then I noticed a small lock near the spine.
“It’s locked?”
“Apparently,” Aunt Anne murmured.
I tried 123. Nothing.
333. Nothing.
378. Nothing.
I was about to give up when I noticed four numbers faintly scratched near the lock.
I entered them.
Click.
The lock opened.
My stomach tightened.
The first page was almost empty. In the centre, written in elegant handwriting, were five words:
For my dear Amelia.
I stared at them.
The handwriting looked strangely familiar. I could not explain why, but something about the shape of the letters reminded me of my own.
I turned the page.
6 November 1998.
The date was more than twenty years old.
I read the first sentence.
If you are reading this, then perhaps I finally have a chance to tell you everything.
I stopped.
Everything?
I glanced towards the doorway. Aunt Anne had already returned downstairs, leaving me alone with the diary.
For the next few minutes, I examined every page. Some were filled with handwriting, others had photographs tucked between them. A few pages appeared to have been carefully removed.
One photograph caught my attention.
Four boys stood together outside what looked like an old railway station. They were laughing, their arms around one another.
On the back, someone had written:
RAIDER-BOYS. Forever, even when the world tries to separate us.
I recognised one of them.
Sky.
My father.
I turned the photograph over again, hoping to find more information. Instead, I noticed something written beneath the original message, almost too faint to read.
Four boys. Four promises. One unforgivable secret.
I shut the diary.
For the first time in my life, I wondered whether the man in prison was really the person I thought he was.
And, more importantly, who had decided that I should never know the truth?
Chapter 2 : The Boy Who Wrote to Tomorrow
6 November 1998  Friday
Dear future child,
I have absolutely no idea whether you will ever read this.
For all I know, you might hate reading. You might prefer sports, music or spending your days arguing with people over things that do not matter. You might even be nothing like me.
Actually, I hope you are nothing like me.
Today, Josh caught me writing in this diary. He laughed so loudly that I nearly threw my pen at him.
“What are you writing, Shakespeare?” he asked.
“Something important.”
“A love letter?”
I told him to shut up.
He took the diary from me before I could stop him and read the first line aloud. Apparently, the idea of me writing to a child I haven’t even met is the funniest thing he has ever heard.
Joshua Forest Palmer. A complete idiot.
Sky’s diary continued for several pages.
He described his friends as though he were introducing them to someone who would one day become part of their lives.
There was Josh, the loud one, who played football, wore glasses and had an unfortunate habit of falling for girls who barely acknowledged him. His latest obsession was Lisa Edwards.
Then there was River Lane, the calmest person Sky knew. River spent more time with books than people, but he had a surprisingly fierce protective side.
Polo was the quietest of the group. He hated attention, avoided arguments and somehow managed to eat more than everyone else combined.
And then there was Sky himself.
Funny. Rebellious. Fond of football and music. The sort of person who could make an entire room laugh while keeping every real emotion locked away.
Together, they called themselves the RAIDER-BOYS.
Amelia read the entry again, then looked at the photograph from Chapter 1.
They looked ordinary.
Just four boys who believed their friendship would last forever.
It was strange to think that one of them would eventually be accused of killing another’s parents.
The diary continued.
There is a girl named Magdalene.
I have known her since middle school. She has dirty-blonde hair and blue eyes that make it difficult to remember what I was saying whenever she looks at me.
She is kind, clever and far too patient with me.
Josh thinks I should tell her how I feel. I think Josh should spend less time giving advice and more time figuring out why Lisa refuses to sit beside him.
But perhaps one day I will be brave enough.
I don’t know what my future looks like. I don’t know whether Magdalene will be part of it.
I do know one thing, though.
If I ever have a daughter, I want her to grow up knowing that home is somewhere she can be herself.
I want her to make mistakes without being terrified of them. I want her to disagree with me without worrying that I will stop loving her.
I want to be the kind of father I never had.
Amelia paused.
For a moment, the diary no longer felt like an old object belonging to a stranger.
It felt like a message.
A message from someone who had imagined her long before she existed.
She turned to the final paragraph.
There is one place the four of us go whenever we need to escape everything. The old railway station, Platform Four. We carved our names beneath the bench.
If you ever find yourself there, remember that the people who know you best are not always the people you should trust the most.
I hope I get to meet you one day.
Love,
Sky.
Amelia sat very still.
She read the last sentence twice.
Then a third time.
She had spent thirteen years believing her father was a monster.
But monsters did not usually write letters to children they had not yet met.
At least, she had never imagined they did.
Chapter 3 : People Aren’t Always Who They Seem to Be
The following morning, I took the diary to school.
Not because I intended to show it to everyone, but because there was one person who would know exactly what to do with it.
Susan Garcia.
Susan collected information the way other people collected stickers. If something happened in our town, she probably knew about it before the people involved did.
I found her in the library, surrounded by books and a notebook.
“You look like you’ve discovered a dead body,” she said without looking up.
“Not exactly.”
I placed the diary on the table.
Her eyes immediately moved towards it.
“Where did you get that?”
“My father’s.”
She looked at me properly.
“Your father?”
I nodded.
Susan knew about Sky. Everyone knew about Sky. I rarely discussed him, and my friends had learned not to ask unnecessary questions.
I explained how I had found the diary, how it had been locked and what I had read so far.
Susan listened without interrupting.
When I finished, she slowly closed her notebook.
“We should look him up.”
I frowned. “Who?”
“Your father. The case. The newspaper articles. Everything.”
Within twenty minutes, we were sitting in front of an old computer in the town library’s archive room.
The first article appeared almost immediately.
BLAKE CONVICTED IN PALMER FAMILY DEATHS
I felt my throat tighten.
The article described the deaths of Henry and Margaret Palmer, Josh’s parents. Their home had been destroyed by a fire on 3 April 2006. Sky Blake had later confessed to being responsible.
The article included an old photograph of the house.
I stared at it.
“That’s where Harper and Hank’s grandparents lived,” I whispered.
Susan nodded.
A second article caught our attention.
It mentioned that witnesses had reported seeing another vehicle near the property that night. The driver had never been identified publicly.
“Wait,” I said.
Susan leaned closer.
“Read that again.”
She did.
An unidentified vehicle was reportedly seen leaving the property shortly before emergency services arrived.
“Why wasn’t that investigated?” I asked.
“Maybe it was. The article doesn’t say.”
I began scrolling through the archive.
There were several reports, but one detail kept appearing: Sky had refused to explain his actions beyond his confession.
No motive.
No argument.
No clear explanation.
Just a confession.
That afternoon, Harper and Hank found us in the library.
Harper glanced at the open article.
“What are you doing?”
I tried to close the screen, but she had already seen the headline.
“Seriously, Amelia?”
Hank stood behind her, looking at the photograph.
“That’s our grandparents’ house.”
“I know,” I said quietly.
Harper folded her arms.
“Why are you looking into it?”
“Because I found my father’s diary.”
“And?”
“And something doesn’t make sense.”
She looked at me for a long moment.
“My father says your father killed them.”
“I know what your father says.”
“Then why are you doing this?”
“Because I don’t want to spend my entire life believing something just because everyone repeats it.”
Harper looked away.
Hank, who had remained silent, finally spoke.
“Maybe we should find out what happened.”
Harper turned towards him, surprised.
I looked back at the computer.
At the bottom of the article was a small detail I had missed earlier.
A witness had mentioned a man wearing a silver ring.
I remembered something from the photograph in Sky’s diary.
And suddenly, I had another reason to keep reading.
Chapter 4 : His Family
7 November 1998  Saturday
Dear future child,
There are things about my family that I have never told anyone outside the RAIDER-BOYS.

My family believes that being different is something to be ashamed of. They have rules for everything: how we speak, what we believe, who we spend time with and what kind of people we are allowed to respect.
They call it tradition.
I call it a cage.
There are seven scars across my back. I will not explain how they got there today. Perhaps one day I will.
My older brother, Richard, agrees with them. He thinks the way our family lives is perfectly normal. He has always been Father’s favourite.

He wears a silver ring with a compass engraved on it. He never takes it off. I used to think it looked impressive. Now I think it looks like a reminder that he always wants to know which direction everyone else should follow.
I hope you never meet people who confuse fear with respect.
Amelia stopped reading.
Richard Blake.
She knew the name.
Aunt Anne had mentioned him once, years ago, but whenever Amelia asked about her father’s family, the conversation somehow changed.
She continued.
Magdalene came to me today asking for help with her mathematics homework.
I have decided that mathematics is suddenly my favourite subject.
I have known her since middle school. She has been one of my closest friends for years, and I cannot understand why telling her how I feel seems more frightening than anything else.
Josh says I am being ridiculous.
Josh also got rejected by Lisa again, so I am not taking relationship advice from him.
River says I should be honest. Polo says I should stop worrying and eat something.
They are both probably right.
Sometimes I wonder whether I will ever be able to leave this house and live the way I want.
I want a family of my own one day. A daughter, perhaps.
And if I have one, I want her to know that love should never feel like a punishment.
Richard told me something tonight.
He said that friends are weaknesses.
I asked him whether that meant he had ever had any.
He did not find it funny.
The entry ended there.
Amelia closed the diary and stared at the ceiling.
She had expected to find memories, perhaps a few photographs or stories about her parents.
She had not expected to find a description of someone who seemed so different from the man everyone claimed her father was.
That evening, she searched the family photographs Aunt Anne kept in the cabinet.
There were pictures of Sky as a teenager, Sky with Magdalene, and Sky standing beside an older boy.
The older boy wore a silver ring.
A compass.
Amelia picked up the photograph and turned it over.
On the back, someone had written:
Richard and Sky Blake. Brothers, despite everything.
The handwriting was Aunt Anne’s.
She carried it downstairs.
“Who is Richard?”
Aunt Anne froze.
“Where did you find that?”
“In the cabinet.”
For a moment, neither of us spoke.
Then she took the photograph from my hand.
“Your father’s brother.”
“Where is he now?”
Aunt Anne looked towards the window.
“I don’t know.”
But something in her voice told me she remembered exactly where he was.
And something in her expression told me she was afraid of him.
Chapter 5 : Platform Four
I decided to visit the old railway station on Saturday.
I did not tell Aunt Anne where I was going.
I knew she would ask questions, and I was beginning to realise that questions were the one thing the adults in my life disliked most.
The station was nearly abandoned. The ticket office had been closed for years, and weeds had grown between the cracked platforms.
I walked towards Platform Four, holding Sky’s diary in my bag.
The photograph had shown a bench beneath an old clock. I found it near the end of the platform.
It was still there.
The wooden surface was weathered, and one of its legs leaned slightly to the side. I crouched to examine the underside.
Four names had been carved into the wood.
SKY. JOSH. RIVER. POLO.
Beneath them were four small symbols.
A star.
A wave.
A circle.
A compass.
I traced the compass with my finger.
Richard’s ring.
I pulled the diary from my bag and opened it to the second entry. There was a small drawing in the corner of the page: a wave beside a number. 4.
I turned back towards the bench.
A loose wooden panel sat beneath the seat. I tugged at it, and it came away with a quiet scrape.
Inside was a small metal box.
My hands were shaking by the time I opened it.
There was a photograph, an old key and a folded piece of paper.
The photograph showed the four boys again, but this time someone else stood behind them.
An older boy.
His face was partly hidden by the shadow of the clock.
He wore a silver compass ring.
Richard.
The note was written in a different hand.
If Sky’s daughter ever comes looking, tell her the truth was never kept in one place.
The river remembers what the station forgets.
I read it twice.
Then I heard footsteps.
I turned sharply.
A woman in a long blue coat was standing at the other end of the platform. She appeared to be watching me.
“Hello?” I called.
She did not answer.
Instead, she turned and walked away.
I hurried after her, but by the time I reached the station entrance, she had disappeared.
“Amelia!”
I turned.
Nathan, Susan, Harper and Hank were approaching. Grace and Rover were behind them.
“You said you were coming here alone,” Nathan complained.
“I did.”
“Then why did you leave a message in the group chat saying you found something?”
“I didn’t.”
Susan’s expression changed.
She showed me her phone.
A message had been sent from my account.
Platform Four. Come before the truth disappears.
I stared at it.
“I didn’t send that.”
Harper looked towards the empty platform.
“Then who did?”
Nobody answered.
I showed them the box and the photograph.
Hank picked it up.
“That’s my dad.”
He pointed towards Josh, who stood beside Sky in the picture.
Harper examined the back.
There was writing beneath the photograph.
The four of us knew. The four of us stayed silent.
“Your father knew something,” I said.
Hank slowly lowered the picture.
“Then maybe it’s time he told us.”
I looked at the note again.
The river remembers.
For the first time, I had a destination.
Chapter 6 : The Day You Arrived
2 April 2006 — Sunday
Dear Amelia,
Today, I became a father.
I have written those words several times, but they still do not feel real.
Your mother held you first. She was exhausted, but she smiled when she looked at you. I don’t think I have ever seen anything more beautiful.
You have tiny hands, a little nose and grey eyes that seem far too serious for someone who has only just arrived.
I was terrified of holding you.
Not because I thought you would break, but because I finally understood how much a person could love someone they had only just met.
Your mother says you have my eyes.
I hope you have her courage.
We decided to name you Amelia.

I keep looking at you and wondering what kind of person you will become. Will you enjoy music? Will you be stubborn? Will you make friends easily? Will you ask too many questions, just like your mother?
Whatever happens, I promise to be there.
I promise.
The entry continued with a photograph of a baby wrapped in a pale blanket.
Amelia touched the edge of the picture.
She had seen photographs of herself as a baby, but never this one.
It was taken from above. Her tiny hand was curled around someone’s finger.
The next paragraph was written later that evening.
Josh called.
Something has happened at his parents’ house. He sounded frightened, and I could barely understand what he was saying.
Magdalene told me not to go.
She said we had just brought a child into the world and that I should not run towards every problem as though it were mine to solve.
She is right.
But Josh is my best friend.
I told her I would return before morning.
She looked at me for a long time before handing me this diary.
“One day, Amelia deserves the truth,” she said.
I told her that I would tell her myself.
I don’t know why she looked so sad.
Amelia turned the page.
There was a sentence written in the bottom corner, almost hidden by the photograph.
If anything happens, Anne knows what to do.
Amelia frowned.
Aunt Anne.
She read the sentence again.
Then she closed the diary and called her aunt.
“Anne?”
Her aunt appeared in the doorway.
“What is it?”
“Why did my father mention you in his diary?”
Aunt Anne’s face lost its colour.
She sat down slowly.
“Because he trusted me.”
“Why?”
“Amelia…”
“What happened on the night I was born?”
Aunt Anne looked at the diary.
Then at me.
“I think,” she whispered, “you should ask Uncle Troy.”
“Why?”
“Because he was there too.”
Chapter 7 : The River Remembers
The river mentioned in the note was not difficult to find.
It ran along the eastern side of town, behind a row of old buildings. I had been there plenty of times with my friends, but I had never known it was connected to my father’s past.
River Lane lived nearby.
His name was almost too perfect.
According to Sky’s diary, River had always been the quietest member of the RAIDER-BOYS. Finding him, however, proved more difficult than I expected.
We eventually discovered a small bookbinding shop near the river.
An old man sat behind the counter, repairing the spine of a book.
“Can I help you?” he asked.
I took the photograph from my bag.
His hands stopped moving.
“Where did you get that?”
“From my father’s diary.”
He looked at me carefully.
“Who is your father?”
I swallowed.
“Sky Blake.”
For a moment, the only sound in the room was the ticking of a clock.
Then the old man stood.
“You’re his daughter.”
I nodded.
He looked away.
“I wondered when this day would come.”
His name was River Lane.
He invited us into the back room. The walls were covered with shelves, and old photographs hung above a desk.
One of them showed the RAIDER-BOYS standing outside the same railway station.
“Your father kept everything,” River said. “Photographs, letters, ticket stubs. He was sentimental, even when he pretended not to be.”
“Did he kill Josh’s parents?”
River did not answer immediately.
Instead, he walked towards a cabinet and opened a drawer.
He took out a small envelope.
“Your father gave me this before he was arrested. He told me not to open it unless someone came looking for the truth.”
“Why didn’t you give it to the police?”
“Because I was afraid.”
He handed the envelope to me.
My name was written across it.
For Amelia.
Inside was a letter.
If you have reached River, you are already closer to the truth than I ever thought you would be.
There is something I need you to understand.
Josh was at the Palmer house that night.
But being there and being responsible are not the same thing.
I made a promise to protect someone. I kept that promise, even when it cost me everything.
River knows what happened after I left the house. Polo knows what happened before I arrived.
Find Polo.
And Amelia, if you ever meet a woman wearing a blue coat, do not be afraid of her.
I looked up.
“The woman at the station?”
River’s expression changed.
“You saw her?”
“Who is she?”
“I think,” he said slowly, “you are going to have to find that out yourself.”
He handed me another photograph.
This one showed Sky standing outside the Palmer house.
It was dated 3 April 2006.
But Sky was not alone.
Behind him stood a man wearing a silver compass ring.
Richard.
I looked at River.
“Why was my uncle there?”
River closed his eyes.
“Because some secrets are passed down through families, Amelia. And some people will do anything to keep them buried.”
Chapter 8: What I Swore to Protect
3 April 2006 Monday
Dear Amelia,
I am writing this with a hand that refuses to stay still.
I went to the Palmer house.
The place was already surrounded by people. I could hear sirens from the road. Josh was outside, looking as though the whole world had collapsed around him.
He kept repeating the same sentence.
“I didn’t mean for any of this to happen.”
I asked him what he meant.
He told me he had gone there to confront his parents. They had discovered something he was trying to hide from them, and the argument had turned into something neither of us could undo.
But Josh was not alone when he arrived.
He said Richard had been there earlier.
Richard.
My brother.
I did not want to believe him.
Then I saw the ring.
The silver compass ring was lying near the back gate. One of its edges was damaged.
I recognised it immediately.
I picked it up.
Josh begged me not to tell anyone that Richard had been there. He said Richard knew where his children lived.
I thought of Harper and Hank.
I thought of you.
I thought of Magdalene.
And I understood why Josh was frightened.
I could have gone to the police. I should have gone to the police.
Instead, I made a decision that I will spend the rest of my life regretting.
I told them I was responsible.
I thought I could keep Richard away from all of you if I gave him one person to blame.
I was wrong.
I am not writing this to excuse myself. I am writing it because I need you to know that I loved you enough to make a terrible choice, but I should have trusted the truth to protect us.
I told River what I had found. Polo has something else.
If one day you read this, please do what I could not.
Do not let someone else’s silence become your story.
The final lines were written in a different pen.
Magdalene knows.
She has to leave tonight.
Anne will keep Amelia safe.
I will find my way back to you both.
I promise.
Amelia’s hands trembled as she finished reading.
The diary had changed everything.
Her father had confessed to the deaths, but he had not written that he had killed anyone. Instead, he had described finding a ring that belonged to his brother.
Richard had been at the house.
And her mother had known.
The next morning, Amelia visited Uncle Troy.
He was sitting in the garden, repairing an old radio.
I placed the diary beside him.
“I know about Richard.”
He slowly put down his tools.
“And I know my mother didn’t just disappear.”
He looked at me.
I waited.
Finally, he spoke.
“Your mother was alive when she left.”
The words seemed to drain the air from the room.
“What?”
“She was frightened, Amelia. She had seen something that could put you in danger. Sky asked Anne to take you somewhere safe.”
“Then why did everyone tell me she was dead?”
Troy looked towards the house.
“Because we believed it was the only way to keep you safe.”
I stood up.
“You let me grow up thinking my mother was dead.”
“I know.”
“And you let me believe my father was a monster.”
Troy had no answer.
I picked up the diary.
“Where is Polo?”
He looked at me for a long moment.
“Near the old clocktower.”
Chapter 9 : The Missing Name
The clocktower stood at the edge of town.
It had not worked in years, but Polo had once loved repairing clocks. According to River, he had kept a small workshop beneath it.
We found him there on a rainy afternoon.
He was older now, with silver in his hair and round glasses resting low on his nose.
When I introduced myself, he stared at me.
Then he smiled sadly.
“Sky’s daughter.”
I nodded.
He looked at Harper and Hank.
“And the Palmer children.”
Nobody spoke.
Polo invited us inside.
The workshop was filled with clocks. Some ticked loudly, others had stopped at different times. On the wall hung a photograph of the RAIDER-BOYS.
I recognised the four faces immediately.
“You all knew,” I said.
Polo nodded.
“We knew enough.”
“Then why did you stay silent?”
His expression hardened.
“Because I was a coward.”
He reached beneath his desk and pulled out a wooden box.
Inside was a small tape recorder, several photographs and a sealed envelope.
“I recorded something that night,” he said.
“Why?”
“I was testing an old recorder. I used to collect sounds from the railway station. I didn’t realise it had captured a conversation until later.”
He placed a cassette into the machine.
A moment of static filled the room.
Then came the sound of two men speaking.
One voice belonged to Josh.
The other was unfamiliar to me.
Until it wasn’t.
I recognised it from the family photographs.
Richard.
The recording was unclear, but certain words came through.
“You were supposed to get rid of the evidence.”
Then Josh:
“I never asked you to do this.”
And Richard again:
“You think your little family is safe? You should have stayed out of it.”
The recording stopped.
Harper covered her mouth.
Hank looked furious.
“That’s my father’s voice,” he whispered.
Polo nodded.
“I kept the tape because I knew Sky hadn’t told us everything. But I didn’t know how to help him.”
I opened the sealed envelope.
Inside was a torn diary page.
The handwriting was Sky’s.
Richard was there. I saw him.
I know what he did, and I know why he did it.
But he knows about Amelia.
He knows about Magdalene.
If I speak, he will come for the people I love.
At the bottom of the page was another sentence.
The woman in blue has the rest.
I looked at the others.
“The woman from the station.”
Polo nodded.
“She has been waiting a long time.”
He handed me a final note.
It contained only one line.
Platform Four. Tomorrow morning. Come before the first train.
I stared at the words.
“Who wrote this?”
Polo didn’t answer.
Instead, he looked at the door.
A small blue flower had been placed on the windowsill.
Its petals were still wet from the rain.
I picked it up.
I had seen that flower before.
It was pressed between the pages of my father’s diary on the very first night I found it.
And suddenly I understood.
The person who had left the clues had been close to me all along.
Chapter 10 : For My Dear Amelia
I arrived at Platform Four just before sunrise.
The station was almost completely silent. A thin layer of fog hung above the tracks, and the old clock still showed the same time it had shown in Sky’s photograph.
I carried the diary in my arms.
For once, I was not alone.
Nathan, Susan, Harper, Hank, Grace and Rover waited near the entrance. River and Polo stood a little farther away.
They had promised not to let me face whatever was coming by myself.
I walked towards the old bench.
Someone was already there.
A woman stood with her back to me, wearing a long blue coat.
My heart began to pound.
“Hello?” I whispered.
The woman turned.
For a moment, I couldn’t breathe.
Her hair was darker than I expected. There were faint lines around her eyes, and she looked older than the woman in the photographs.
But her eyes..
Blue.
The same blue I had seen in the few pictures of my mother.
She took one careful step towards me.
“Amelia?”
I couldn’t answer.
She lifted a trembling hand to her mouth.
“Oh, my darling.”
The diary slipped slightly in my arms.
I knew that voice.
Not because I remembered hearing it as a child, but because I had heard it in every story Aunt Anne refused to finish.
“Mother?”
She nodded.
And then I was running.
I don’t remember crossing the distance between us. I don’t remember dropping the diary or hearing the others move behind me.
I only remember her arms around me.
For thirteen years, I had believed there was an empty space in my life that could never be filled.

I had imagined what my mother might have looked like. Whether she would have liked my drawings. Whether she would have brushed my hair when I was younger. Whether she would have remembered my birthday.
Now she was standing in front of me.
And she was crying.
“I thought you were dead,” I whispered.
“I know.”
“You let me believe that.”
Her face crumpled.
“I am so sorry.”
I pulled away just enough to look at her.
“Why?”
She took a deep breath.
“Because I saw what happened that night, Amelia. I saw Richard leave the Palmer house. I knew what he had done, and he knew I had seen him.”
She explained that Richard had been using the Palmer family to hide his dishonest dealings. Henry and Margaret had discovered what he was doing and planned to expose him.
Richard confronted them.
The situation ended in tragedy.
Josh had arrived at the house afterwards. Sky had followed him, discovered Richard’s involvement and found the damaged compass ring.
Magdalene had witnessed Richard leaving the property.
Sky knew that if the truth came out immediately, Richard would target their families. He would go after Josh’s children, Amelia and Magdalene.
So Sky confessed.
He believed that prison would keep Richard focused on him while Magdalene and Amelia were hidden somewhere safe.
But he had never planned for thirteen years of silence.
“Why didn’t you come back?” I asked.
“I wanted to. Every birthday, every first day of school, every time I saw a little girl who looked your age, I wanted to come home.”
She reached into her coat and pulled out a small envelope.
“Your father asked me to give you this when you were old enough to understand.”
I opened it.
Inside was a letter.
My dear Amelia,
If your mother has given you this letter, then you have finally found the truth.
I am sorry I wasn’t there to watch you grow up. I am sorry I missed your first words, your birthdays, your school performances and all the little things that make up a childhood.
I need you to know that I never stopped being your father.
I know you have probably heard terrible things about me. Some of them are true. I lied. I kept secrets. I made decisions that hurt people who trusted me.
But I never stopped loving you.
Your mother did not leave because she didn’t want you. She left because she wanted you to have a future.
And if there is one thing I hope you learn from all of this, it is that love should never require someone to disappear.
I hope you have friends who stand beside you when the truth becomes difficult.
I hope you never become afraid of asking questions.
And I hope that one day, when you are ready, you will let me know what kind of person you have become.
I have imagined meeting you a thousand times.
I wonder whether you laugh like your mother.
I wonder whether you are stubborn like me.
Most of all, I wonder whether you will forgive me.
With all the love I have,
Dad.
I pressed the letter against my chest.
For a while, nobody spoke.
Then Harper stepped forward.
She looked at my mother, then at me.
“My father needs to tell us everything,” she said.
“He does,” Magdalene replied.
Hank took his sister’s hand.
“And your father deserves the chance to tell his side.”
I looked at them.
For thirteen years, our families had been separated by a story none of us had questioned.
Now we finally had a chance to write a different one.
The recording, the photographs and Richard’s damaged ring were turned over to the authorities.
River and Polo gave their statements. Magdalene explained what she had witnessed, and Josh finally admitted everything he had kept hidden.
The investigation was reopened.
It took months.
There were interviews, documents and hearings. There were days when I thought nothing would change. But this time, the truth had witnesses.
Richard was arrested, and Sky’s conviction was overturned.
The day Sky came home, the sky was unusually clear.
I stood at the front gate with Aunt Anne, Uncle Troy, Nora and my friends.
A car stopped outside.
The door opened.
And there he was.
My father.
He looked older than the boy in the photographs. His hair had darkened with grey, and his face carried the years he had spent away from us.
For a moment, neither of us moved.
Then he smiled.
“Amelia?”
I ran towards him.
He caught me in his arms, holding me as though he had been waiting for that moment his entire life.
“I missed you,” I whispered.
He closed his eyes.
“I missed you more than you could ever know.”
My mother joined us, and for the first time, the three of us stood together.
Behind us, Josh approached Sky.
The two men looked at each other for a long moment.
Then Josh stepped forward.
“I should have told the truth.”
Sky shook his head.
“We both should have.”
Josh’s eyes filled with tears.
“I owe you my life.”
“No,” Sky replied quietly. “You owe your children the truth.”
Harper and Hank stood beside them.
And I realised something.
The RAIDER-BOYS had once promised to stay together forever.
They had failed each other, hurt each other and spent years living with a secret.
But their children had found the pieces they had lost.
That evening, I returned to my room.
The diary lay open on my desk.
I turned to the first page.
For my dear Amelia.
I finally recognised the handwriting.
It was my mother’s.
But beneath the dedication, there was another sentence I had never noticed before. It was written so faintly that the letters almost disappeared into the paper.
The password was never meant to be a secret.
I smiled through my tears
The date I was born.
My mother had chosen it.
I turned to the last page of the diary. There was a photograph tucked inside it.
It showed my parents standing together outside the old railway station. My father was laughing, and my mother was holding his hand.
On the back, Sky had written:
One day, I hope we can all stand here again.
I placed the photograph beside my bed.
For years, I had thought my story began with a missing mother and a father behind bars.
I was wrong.
It began with four boys who made a promise, a girl who refused to let a secret remain buried, and two parents who loved their daughter enough to make choices they could never take back.
The truth had taken thirteen years to find its way home.
But it had found us.
And this time, nobody was leaving.
For my dear Amelia.
You were loved before you even knew what love was.
And you always will be.

content: The Things We Buried…
Chapter 1 : The Basket
“Aunt Anne!”
My voice echoed through the upstairs hallway.

I had been cleaning the spare room for almost an hour, and I was beginning to regret every decision that had led me there. Dust covered the shelves, old boxes were stacked against the walls, and the curtains looked as though they had not been washed since the beginning of time.
Then I noticed a basket tucked beneath the wooden table.
It was old. Not just old in the way that made something look antique, but old in the way that made you wonder how many secrets it had witnessed.
A thin layer of dust covered its lid. I pulled it out, sneezed twice and carefully lifted the cover.
Inside were a few yellowed photographs, a folded piece of fabric and a thick, dark-green book.
It looked like a diary.
“Aunt Anne!” I called again.
She appeared in the doorway, wiping her hands on her apron.
“What happened now?”
“What’s this?”
The moment she saw the basket, her expression changed. It was subtle, but I noticed it. Her eyes lingered on the book before moving towards me.
“Where did you find that?”
“Under the table.”
She stepped closer and ran her fingers along the basket’s handle.
“That basket was given to me the night you came to live with us,” she said quietly.
I looked up. “The night I was handed to you?”
She nodded.
I knew very little about that night. According to Aunt Anne, I had been brought to her as a baby. My mother had already passed away, and my father was unable to take care of me.
My father.
Sky Blake.
The man who had been in prison for thirteen years.
The man accused of killing the grandparents of my best friends. Harper and Hank.
I had never known him well enough to hate him properly. I had only known the stories people told about him.
“Can I look inside?” I asked.
Aunt Anne hesitated.
Then she nodded. “I suppose it’s time you did.”
I lifted the book. Its cover was worn, and the corners had begun to curl. There was no title, only a small silver design pressed into the leather.
I opened it.
Nothing happened.
Then I noticed a small lock near the spine.
“It’s locked?”
“Apparently,” Aunt Anne murmured.
I tried 123. Nothing.
333. Nothing.
378. Nothing.
I was about to give up when I noticed four numbers faintly scratched near the lock.
I entered them.
Click.
The lock opened.
My stomach tightened.
The first page was almost empty. In the centre, written in elegant handwriting, were five words:
For my dear Amelia.
I stared at them.
The handwriting looked strangely familiar. I could not explain why, but something about the shape of the letters reminded me of my own.
I turned the page.
6 November 1998.
The date was more than twenty years old.
I read the first sentence.
If you are reading this, then perhaps I finally have a chance to tell you everything.
I stopped.
Everything?
I glanced towards the doorway. Aunt Anne had already returned downstairs, leaving me alone with the diary.
For the next few minutes, I examined every page. Some were filled with handwriting, others had photographs tucked between them. A few pages appeared to have been carefully removed.
One photograph caught my attention.
Four boys stood together outside what looked like an old railway station. They were laughing, their arms around one another.
On the back, someone had written:
RAIDER-BOYS. Forever, even when the world tries to separate us.
I recognised one of them.
Sky.
My father.
I turned the photograph over again, hoping to find more information. Instead, I noticed something written beneath the original message, almost too faint to read.
Four boys. Four promises. One unforgivable secret.
I shut the diary.
For the first time in my life, I wondered whether the man in prison was really the person I thought he was.
And, more importantly, who had decided that I should never know the truth?
Chapter 2 : The Boy Who Wrote to Tomorrow
6 November 1998  Friday
Dear future child,
I have absolutely no idea whether you will ever read this.
For all I know, you might hate reading. You might prefer sports, music or spending your days arguing with people over things that do not matter. You might even be nothing like me.
Actually, I hope you are nothing like me.
Today, Josh caught me writing in this diary. He laughed so loudly that I nearly threw my pen at him.
“What are you writing, Shakespeare?” he asked.
“Something important.”
“A love letter?”
I told him to shut up.
He took the diary from me before I could stop him and read the first line aloud. Apparently, the idea of me writing to a child I haven’t even met is the funniest thing he has ever heard.
Joshua Forest Palmer. A complete idiot.
Sky’s diary continued for several pages.
He described his friends as though he were introducing them to someone who would one day become part of their lives.
There was Josh, the loud one, who played football, wore glasses and had an unfortunate habit of falling for girls who barely acknowledged him. His latest obsession was Lisa Edwards.
Then there was River Lane, the calmest person Sky knew. River spent more time with books than people, but he had a surprisingly fierce protective side.
Polo was the quietest of the group. He hated attention, avoided arguments and somehow managed to eat more than everyone else combined.
And then there was Sky himself.
Funny. Rebellious. Fond of football and music. The sort of person who could make an entire room laugh while keeping every real emotion locked away.
Together, they called themselves the RAIDER-BOYS.
Amelia read the entry again, then looked at the photograph from Chapter 1.
They looked ordinary.
Just four boys who believed their friendship would last forever.
It was strange to think that one of them would eventually be accused of killing another’s parents.
The diary continued.
There is a girl named Magdalene.
I have known her since middle school. She has dirty-blonde hair and blue eyes that make it difficult to remember what I was saying whenever she looks at me.
She is kind, clever and far too patient with me.
Josh thinks I should tell her how I feel. I think Josh should spend less time giving advice and more time figuring out why Lisa refuses to sit beside him.
But perhaps one day I will be brave enough.
I don’t know what my future looks like. I don’t know whether Magdalene will be part of it.
I do know one thing, though.
If I ever have a daughter, I want her to grow up knowing that home is somewhere she can be herself.
I want her to make mistakes without being terrified of them. I want her to disagree with me without worrying that I will stop loving her.
I want to be the kind of father I never had.
Amelia paused.
For a moment, the diary no longer felt like an old object belonging to a stranger.
It felt like a message.
A message from someone who had imagined her long before she existed.
She turned to the final paragraph.
There is one place the four of us go whenever we need to escape everything. The old railway station, Platform Four. We carved our names beneath the bench.
If you ever find yourself there, remember that the people who know you best are not always the people you should trust the most.
I hope I get to meet you one day.
Love,
Sky.
Amelia sat very still.
She read the last sentence twice.
Then a third time.
She had spent thirteen years believing her father was a monster.
But monsters did not usually write letters to children they had not yet met.
At least, she had never imagined they did.
Chapter 3 : People Aren’t Always Who They Seem to Be
The following morning, I took the diary to school.
Not because I intended to show it to everyone, but because there was one person who would know exactly what to do with it.
Susan Garcia.
Susan collected information the way other people collected stickers. If something happened in our town, she probably knew about it before the people involved did.
I found her in the library, surrounded by books and a notebook.
“You look like you’ve discovered a dead body,” she said without looking up.
“Not exactly.”
I placed the diary on the table.
Her eyes immediately moved towards it.
“Where did you get that?”
“My father’s.”
She looked at me properly.
“Your father?”
I nodded.
Susan knew about Sky. Everyone knew about Sky. I rarely discussed him, and my friends had learned not to ask unnecessary questions.
I explained how I had found the diary, how it had been locked and what I had read so far.
Susan listened without interrupting.
When I finished, she slowly closed her notebook.
“We should look him up.”
I frowned. “Who?”
“Your father. The case. The newspaper articles. Everything.”
Within twenty minutes, we were sitting in front of an old computer in the town library’s archive room.
The first article appeared almost immediately.
BLAKE CONVICTED IN PALMER FAMILY DEATHS
I felt my throat tighten.
The article described the deaths of Henry and Margaret Palmer, Josh’s parents. Their home had been destroyed by a fire on 3 April 2006. Sky Blake had later confessed to being responsible.
The article included an old photograph of the house.
I stared at it.
“That’s where Harper and Hank’s grandparents lived,” I whispered.
Susan nodded.
A second article caught our attention.
It mentioned that witnesses had reported seeing another vehicle near the property that night. The driver had never been identified publicly.
“Wait,” I said.
Susan leaned closer.
“Read that again.”
She did.
An unidentified vehicle was reportedly seen leaving the property shortly before emergency services arrived.
“Why wasn’t that investigated?” I asked.
“Maybe it was. The article doesn’t say.”
I began scrolling through the archive.
There were several reports, but one detail kept appearing: Sky had refused to explain his actions beyond his confession.
No motive.
No argument.
No clear explanation.
Just a confession.
That afternoon, Harper and Hank found us in the library.
Harper glanced at the open article.
“What are you doing?”
I tried to close the screen, but she had already seen the headline.
“Seriously, Amelia?”
Hank stood behind her, looking at the photograph.
“That’s our grandparents’ house.”
“I know,” I said quietly.
Harper folded her arms.
“Why are you looking into it?”
“Because I found my father’s diary.”
“And?”
“And something doesn’t make sense.”
She looked at me for a long moment.
“My father says your father killed them.”
“I know what your father says.”
“Then why are you doing this?”
“Because I don’t want to spend my entire life believing something just because everyone repeats it.”
Harper looked away.
Hank, who had remained silent, finally spoke.
“Maybe we should find out what happened.”
Harper turned towards him, surprised.
I looked back at the computer.
At the bottom of the article was a small detail I had missed earlier.
A witness had mentioned a man wearing a silver ring.
I remembered something from the photograph in Sky’s diary.
And suddenly, I had another reason to keep reading.
Chapter 4 : His Family
7 November 1998  Saturday
Dear future child,
There are things about my family that I have never told anyone outside the RAIDER-BOYS.

My family believes that being different is something to be ashamed of. They have rules for everything: how we speak, what we believe, who we spend time with and what kind of people we are allowed to respect.
They call it tradition.
I call it a cage.
There are seven scars across my back. I will not explain how they got there today. Perhaps one day I will.
My older brother, Richard, agrees with them. He thinks the way our family lives is perfectly normal. He has always been Father’s favourite.

He wears a silver ring with a compass engraved on it. He never takes it off. I used to think it looked impressive. Now I think it looks like a reminder that he always wants to know which direction everyone else should follow.
I hope you never meet people who confuse fear with respect.
Amelia stopped reading.
Richard Blake.
She knew the name.
Aunt Anne had mentioned him once, years ago, but whenever Amelia asked about her father’s family, the conversation somehow changed.
She continued.
Magdalene came to me today asking for help with her mathematics homework.
I have decided that mathematics is suddenly my favourite subject.
I have known her since middle school. She has been one of my closest friends for years, and I cannot understand why telling her how I feel seems more frightening than anything else.
Josh says I am being ridiculous.
Josh also got rejected by Lisa again, so I am not taking relationship advice from him.
River says I should be honest. Polo says I should stop worrying and eat something.
They are both probably right.
Sometimes I wonder whether I will ever be able to leave this house and live the way I want.
I want a family of my own one day. A daughter, perhaps.
And if I have one, I want her to know that love should never feel like a punishment.
Richard told me something tonight.
He said that friends are weaknesses.
I asked him whether that meant he had ever had any.
He did not find it funny.
The entry ended there.
Amelia closed the diary and stared at the ceiling.
She had expected to find memories, perhaps a few photographs or stories about her parents.
She had not expected to find a description of someone who seemed so different from the man everyone claimed her father was.
That evening, she searched the family photographs Aunt Anne kept in the cabinet.
There were pictures of Sky as a teenager, Sky with Magdalene, and Sky standing beside an older boy.
The older boy wore a silver ring.
A compass.
Amelia picked up the photograph and turned it over.
On the back, someone had written:
Richard and Sky Blake. Brothers, despite everything.
The handwriting was Aunt Anne’s.
She carried it downstairs.
“Who is Richard?”
Aunt Anne froze.
“Where did you find that?”
“In the cabinet.”
For a moment, neither of us spoke.
Then she took the photograph from my hand.
“Your father’s brother.”
“Where is he now?”
Aunt Anne looked towards the window.
“I don’t know.”
But something in her voice told me she remembered exactly where he was.
And something in her expression told me she was afraid of him.
Chapter 5 : Platform Four
I decided to visit the old railway station on Saturday.
I did not tell Aunt Anne where I was going.
I knew she would ask questions, and I was beginning to realise that questions were the one thing the adults in my life disliked most.
The station was nearly abandoned. The ticket office had been closed for years, and weeds had grown between the cracked platforms.
I walked towards Platform Four, holding Sky’s diary in my bag.
The photograph had shown a bench beneath an old clock. I found it near the end of the platform.
It was still there.
The wooden surface was weathered, and one of its legs leaned slightly to the side. I crouched to examine the underside.
Four names had been carved into the wood.
SKY. JOSH. RIVER. POLO.
Beneath them were four small symbols.
A star.
A wave.
A circle.
A compass.
I traced the compass with my finger.
Richard’s ring.
I pulled the diary from my bag and opened it to the second entry. There was a small drawing in the corner of the page: a wave beside a number. 4.
I turned back towards the bench.
A loose wooden panel sat beneath the seat. I tugged at it, and it came away with a quiet scrape.
Inside was a small metal box.
My hands were shaking by the time I opened it.
There was a photograph, an old key and a folded piece of paper.
The photograph showed the four boys again, but this time someone else stood behind them.
An older boy.
His face was partly hidden by the shadow of the clock.
He wore a silver compass ring.
Richard.
The note was written in a different hand.
If Sky’s daughter ever comes looking, tell her the truth was never kept in one place.
The river remembers what the station forgets.
I read it twice.
Then I heard footsteps.
I turned sharply.
A woman in a long blue coat was standing at the other end of the platform. She appeared to be watching me.
“Hello?” I called.
She did not answer.
Instead, she turned and walked away.
I hurried after her, but by the time I reached the station entrance, she had disappeared.
“Amelia!”
I turned.
Nathan, Susan, Harper and Hank were approaching. Grace and Rover were behind them.
“You said you were coming here alone,” Nathan complained.
“I did.”
“Then why did you leave a message in the group chat saying you found something?”
“I didn’t.”
Susan’s expression changed.
She showed me her phone.
A message had been sent from my account.
Platform Four. Come before the truth disappears.
I stared at it.
“I didn’t send that.”
Harper looked towards the empty platform.
“Then who did?”
Nobody answered.
I showed them the box and the photograph.
Hank picked it up.
“That’s my dad.”
He pointed towards Josh, who stood beside Sky in the picture.
Harper examined the back.
There was writing beneath the photograph.
The four of us knew. The four of us stayed silent.
“Your father knew something,” I said.
Hank slowly lowered the picture.
“Then maybe it’s time he told us.”
I looked at the note again.
The river remembers.
For the first time, I had a destination.
Chapter 6 : The Day You Arrived
2 April 2006 — Sunday
Dear Amelia,
Today, I became a father.
I have written those words several times, but they still do not feel real.
Your mother held you first. She was exhausted, but she smiled when she looked at you. I don’t think I have ever seen anything more beautiful.
You have tiny hands, a little nose and grey eyes that seem far too serious for someone who has only just arrived.
I was terrified of holding you.
Not because I thought you would break, but because I finally understood how much a person could love someone they had only just met.
Your mother says you have my eyes.
I hope you have her courage.
We decided to name you Amelia.

I keep looking at you and wondering what kind of person you will become. Will you enjoy music? Will you be stubborn? Will you make friends easily? Will you ask too many questions, just like your mother?
Whatever happens, I promise to be there.
I promise.
The entry continued with a photograph of a baby wrapped in a pale blanket.
Amelia touched the edge of the picture.
She had seen photographs of herself as a baby, but never this one.
It was taken from above. Her tiny hand was curled around someone’s finger.
The next paragraph was written later that evening.
Josh called.
Something has happened at his parents’ house. He sounded frightened, and I could barely understand what he was saying.
Magdalene told me not to go.
She said we had just brought a child into the world and that I should not run towards every problem as though it were mine to solve.
She is right.
But Josh is my best friend.
I told her I would return before morning.
She looked at me for a long time before handing me this diary.
“One day, Amelia deserves the truth,” she said.
I told her that I would tell her myself.
I don’t know why she looked so sad.
Amelia turned the page.
There was a sentence written in the bottom corner, almost hidden by the photograph.
If anything happens, Anne knows what to do.
Amelia frowned.
Aunt Anne.
She read the sentence again.
Then she closed the diary and called her aunt.
“Anne?”
Her aunt appeared in the doorway.
“What is it?”
“Why did my father mention you in his diary?”
Aunt Anne’s face lost its colour.
She sat down slowly.
“Because he trusted me.”
“Why?”
“Amelia…”
“What happened on the night I was born?”
Aunt Anne looked at the diary.
Then at me.
“I think,” she whispered, “you should ask Uncle Troy.”
“Why?”
“Because he was there too.”
Chapter 7 : The River Remembers
The river mentioned in the note was not difficult to find.
It ran along the eastern side of town, behind a row of old buildings. I had been there plenty of times with my friends, but I had never known it was connected to my father’s past.
River Lane lived nearby.
His name was almost too perfect.
According to Sky’s diary, River had always been the quietest member of the RAIDER-BOYS. Finding him, however, proved more difficult than I expected.
We eventually discovered a small bookbinding shop near the river.
An old man sat behind the counter, repairing the spine of a book.
“Can I help you?” he asked.
I took the photograph from my bag.
His hands stopped moving.
“Where did you get that?”
“From my father’s diary.”
He looked at me carefully.
“Who is your father?”
I swallowed.
“Sky Blake.”
For a moment, the only sound in the room was the ticking of a clock.
Then the old man stood.
“You’re his daughter.”
I nodded.
He looked away.
“I wondered when this day would come.”
His name was River Lane.
He invited us into the back room. The walls were covered with shelves, and old photographs hung above a desk.
One of them showed the RAIDER-BOYS standing outside the same railway station.
“Your father kept everything,” River said. “Photographs, letters, ticket stubs. He was sentimental, even when he pretended not to be.”
“Did he kill Josh’s parents?”
River did not answer immediately.
Instead, he walked towards a cabinet and opened a drawer.
He took out a small envelope.
“Your father gave me this before he was arrested. He told me not to open it unless someone came looking for the truth.”
“Why didn’t you give it to the police?”
“Because I was afraid.”
He handed the envelope to me.
My name was written across it.
For Amelia.
Inside was a letter.
If you have reached River, you are already closer to the truth than I ever thought you would be.
There is something I need you to understand.
Josh was at the Palmer house that night.
But being there and being responsible are not the same thing.
I made a promise to protect someone. I kept that promise, even when it cost me everything.
River knows what happened after I left the house. Polo knows what happened before I arrived.
Find Polo.
And Amelia, if you ever meet a woman wearing a blue coat, do not be afraid of her.
I looked up.
“The woman at the station?”
River’s expression changed.
“You saw her?”
“Who is she?”
“I think,” he said slowly, “you are going to have to find that out yourself.”
He handed me another photograph.
This one showed Sky standing outside the Palmer house.
It was dated 3 April 2006.
But Sky was not alone.
Behind him stood a man wearing a silver compass ring.
Richard.
I looked at River.
“Why was my uncle there?”
River closed his eyes.
“Because some secrets are passed down through families, Amelia. And some people will do anything to keep them buried.”
Chapter 8: What I Swore to Protect
3 April 2006 Monday
Dear Amelia,
I am writing this with a hand that refuses to stay still.
I went to the Palmer house.
The place was already surrounded by people. I could hear sirens from the road. Josh was outside, looking as though the whole world had collapsed around him.
He kept repeating the same sentence.
“I didn’t mean for any of this to happen.”
I asked him what he meant.
He told me he had gone there to confront his parents. They had discovered something he was trying to hide from them, and the argument had turned into something neither of us could undo.
But Josh was not alone when he arrived.
He said Richard had been there earlier.
Richard.
My brother.
I did not want to believe him.
Then I saw the ring.
The silver compass ring was lying near the back gate. One of its edges was damaged.
I recognised it immediately.
I picked it up.
Josh begged me not to tell anyone that Richard had been there. He said Richard knew where his children lived.
I thought of Harper and Hank.
I thought of you.
I thought of Magdalene.
And I understood why Josh was frightened.
I could have gone to the police. I should have gone to the police.
Instead, I made a decision that I will spend the rest of my life regretting.
I told them I was responsible.
I thought I could keep Richard away from all of you if I gave him one person to blame.
I was wrong.
I am not writing this to excuse myself. I am writing it because I need you to know that I loved you enough to make a terrible choice, but I should have trusted the truth to protect us.
I told River what I had found. Polo has something else.
If one day you read this, please do what I could not.
Do not let someone else’s silence become your story.
The final lines were written in a different pen.
Magdalene knows.
She has to leave tonight.
Anne will keep Amelia safe.
I will find my way back to you both.
I promise.
Amelia’s hands trembled as she finished reading.
The diary had changed everything.
Her father had confessed to the deaths, but he had not written that he had killed anyone. Instead, he had described finding a ring that belonged to his brother.
Richard had been at the house.
And her mother had known.
The next morning, Amelia visited Uncle Troy.
He was sitting in the garden, repairing an old radio.
I placed the diary beside him.
“I know about Richard.”
He slowly put down his tools.
“And I know my mother didn’t just disappear.”
He looked at me.
I waited.
Finally, he spoke.
“Your mother was alive when she left.”
The words seemed to drain the air from the room.
“What?”
“She was frightened, Amelia. She had seen something that could put you in danger. Sky asked Anne to take you somewhere safe.”
“Then why did everyone tell me she was dead?”
Troy looked towards the house.
“Because we believed it was the only way to keep you safe.”
I stood up.
“You let me grow up thinking my mother was dead.”
“I know.”
“And you let me believe my father was a monster.”
Troy had no answer.
I picked up the diary.
“Where is Polo?”
He looked at me for a long moment.
“Near the old clocktower.”
Chapter 9 : The Missing Name
The clocktower stood at the edge of town.
It had not worked in years, but Polo had once loved repairing clocks. According to River, he had kept a small workshop beneath it.
We found him there on a rainy afternoon.
He was older now, with silver in his hair and round glasses resting low on his nose.
When I introduced myself, he stared at me.
Then he smiled sadly.
“Sky’s daughter.”
I nodded.
He looked at Harper and Hank.
“And the Palmer children.”
Nobody spoke.
Polo invited us inside.
The workshop was filled with clocks. Some ticked loudly, others had stopped at different times. On the wall hung a photograph of the RAIDER-BOYS.
I recognised the four faces immediately.
“You all knew,” I said.
Polo nodded.
“We knew enough.”
“Then why did you stay silent?”
His expression hardened.
“Because I was a coward.”
He reached beneath his desk and pulled out a wooden box.
Inside was a small tape recorder, several photographs and a sealed envelope.
“I recorded something that night,” he said.
“Why?”
“I was testing an old recorder. I used to collect sounds from the railway station. I didn’t realise it had captured a conversation until later.”
He placed a cassette into the machine.
A moment of static filled the room.
Then came the sound of two men speaking.
One voice belonged to Josh.
The other was unfamiliar to me.
Until it wasn’t.
I recognised it from the family photographs.
Richard.
The recording was unclear, but certain words came through.
“You were supposed to get rid of the evidence.”
Then Josh:
“I never asked you to do this.”
And Richard again:
“You think your little family is safe? You should have stayed out of it.”
The recording stopped.
Harper covered her mouth.
Hank looked furious.
“That’s my father’s voice,” he whispered.
Polo nodded.
“I kept the tape because I knew Sky hadn’t told us everything. But I didn’t know how to help him.”
I opened the sealed envelope.
Inside was a torn diary page.
The handwriting was Sky’s.
Richard was there. I saw him.
I know what he did, and I know why he did it.
But he knows about Amelia.
He knows about Magdalene.
If I speak, he will come for the people I love.
At the bottom of the page was another sentence.
The woman in blue has the rest.
I looked at the others.
“The woman from the station.”
Polo nodded.
“She has been waiting a long time.”
He handed me a final note.
It contained only one line.
Platform Four. Tomorrow morning. Come before the first train.
I stared at the words.
“Who wrote this?”
Polo didn’t answer.
Instead, he looked at the door.
A small blue flower had been placed on the windowsill.
Its petals were still wet from the rain.
I picked it up.
I had seen that flower before.
It was pressed between the pages of my father’s diary on the very first night I found it.
And suddenly I understood.
The person who had left the clues had been close to me all along.
Chapter 10 : For My Dear Amelia
I arrived at Platform Four just before sunrise.
The station was almost completely silent. A thin layer of fog hung above the tracks, and the old clock still showed the same time it had shown in Sky’s photograph.
I carried the diary in my arms.
For once, I was not alone.
Nathan, Susan, Harper, Hank, Grace and Rover waited near the entrance. River and Polo stood a little farther away.
They had promised not to let me face whatever was coming by myself.
I walked towards the old bench.
Someone was already there.
A woman stood with her back to me, wearing a long blue coat.
My heart began to pound.
“Hello?” I whispered.
The woman turned.
For a moment, I couldn’t breathe.
Her hair was darker than I expected. There were faint lines around her eyes, and she looked older than the woman in the photographs.
But her eyes..
Blue.
The same blue I had seen in the few pictures of my mother.
She took one careful step towards me.
“Amelia?”
I couldn’t answer.
She lifted a trembling hand to her mouth.
“Oh, my darling.”
The diary slipped slightly in my arms.
I knew that voice.
Not because I remembered hearing it as a child, but because I had heard it in every story Aunt Anne refused to finish.
“Mother?”
She nodded.
And then I was running.
I don’t remember crossing the distance between us. I don’t remember dropping the diary or hearing the others move behind me.
I only remember her arms around me.
For thirteen years, I had believed there was an empty space in my life that could never be filled.

I had imagined what my mother might have looked like. Whether she would have liked my drawings. Whether she would have brushed my hair when I was younger. Whether she would have remembered my birthday.
Now she was standing in front of me.
And she was crying.
“I thought you were dead,” I whispered.
“I know.”
“You let me believe that.”
Her face crumpled.
“I am so sorry.”
I pulled away just enough to look at her.
“Why?”
She took a deep breath.
“Because I saw what happened that night, Amelia. I saw Richard leave the Palmer house. I knew what he had done, and he knew I had seen him.”
She explained that Richard had been using the Palmer family to hide his dishonest dealings. Henry and Margaret had discovered what he was doing and planned to expose him.
Richard confronted them.
The situation ended in tragedy.
Josh had arrived at the house afterwards. Sky had followed him, discovered Richard’s involvement and found the damaged compass ring.
Magdalene had witnessed Richard leaving the property.
Sky knew that if the truth came out immediately, Richard would target their families. He would go after Josh’s children, Amelia and Magdalene.
So Sky confessed.
He believed that prison would keep Richard focused on him while Magdalene and Amelia were hidden somewhere safe.
But he had never planned for thirteen years of silence.
“Why didn’t you come back?” I asked.
“I wanted to. Every birthday, every first day of school, every time I saw a little girl who looked your age, I wanted to come home.”
She reached into her coat and pulled out a small envelope.
“Your father asked me to give you this when you were old enough to understand.”
I opened it.
Inside was a letter.
My dear Amelia,
If your mother has given you this letter, then you have finally found the truth.
I am sorry I wasn’t there to watch you grow up. I am sorry I missed your first words, your birthdays, your school performances and all the little things that make up a childhood.
I need you to know that I never stopped being your father.
I know you have probably heard terrible things about me. Some of them are true. I lied. I kept secrets. I made decisions that hurt people who trusted me.
But I never stopped loving you.
Your mother did not leave because she didn’t want you. She left because she wanted you to have a future.
And if there is one thing I hope you learn from all of this, it is that love should never require someone to disappear.
I hope you have friends who stand beside you when the truth becomes difficult.
I hope you never become afraid of asking questions.
And I hope that one day, when you are ready, you will let me know what kind of person you have become.
I have imagined meeting you a thousand times.
I wonder whether you laugh like your mother.
I wonder whether you are stubborn like me.
Most of all, I wonder whether you will forgive me.
With all the love I have,
Dad.
I pressed the letter against my chest.
For a while, nobody spoke.
Then Harper stepped forward.
She looked at my mother, then at me.
“My father needs to tell us everything,” she said.
“He does,” Magdalene replied.
Hank took his sister’s hand.
“And your father deserves the chance to tell his side.”
I looked at them.
For thirteen years, our families had been separated by a story none of us had questioned.
Now we finally had a chance to write a different one.
The recording, the photographs and Richard’s damaged ring were turned over to the authorities.
River and Polo gave their statements. Magdalene explained what she had witnessed, and Josh finally admitted everything he had kept hidden.
The investigation was reopened.
It took months.
There were interviews, documents and hearings. There were days when I thought nothing would change. But this time, the truth had witnesses.
Richard was arrested, and Sky’s conviction was overturned.
The day Sky came home, the sky was unusually clear.
I stood at the front gate with Aunt Anne, Uncle Troy, Nora and my friends.
A car stopped outside.
The door opened.
And there he was.
My father.
He looked older than the boy in the photographs. His hair had darkened with grey, and his face carried the years he had spent away from us.
For a moment, neither of us moved.
Then he smiled.
“Amelia?”
I ran towards him.
He caught me in his arms, holding me as though he had been waiting for that moment his entire life.
“I missed you,” I whispered.
He closed his eyes.
“I missed you more than you could ever know.”
My mother joined us, and for the first time, the three of us stood together.
Behind us, Josh approached Sky.
The two men looked at each other for a long moment.
Then Josh stepped forward.
“I should have told the truth.”
Sky shook his head.
“We both should have.”
Josh’s eyes filled with tears.
“I owe you my life.”
“No,” Sky replied quietly. “You owe your children the truth.”
Harper and Hank stood beside them.
And I realised something.
The RAIDER-BOYS had once promised to stay together forever.
They had failed each other, hurt each other and spent years living with a secret.
But their children had found the pieces they had lost.
That evening, I returned to my room.
The diary lay open on my desk.
I turned to the first page.
For my dear Amelia.
I finally recognised the handwriting.
It was my mother’s.
But beneath the dedication, there was another sentence I had never noticed before. It was written so faintly that the letters almost disappeared into the paper.
The password was never meant to be a secret.
I smiled through my tears
The date I was born.
My mother had chosen it.
I turned to the last page of the diary. There was a photograph tucked inside it.
It showed my parents standing together outside the old railway station. My father was laughing, and my mother was holding his hand.
On the back, Sky had written:
One day, I hope we can all stand here again.
I placed the photograph beside my bed.
For years, I had thought my story began with a missing mother and a father behind bars.
I was wrong.
It began with four boys who made a promise, a girl who refused to let a secret remain buried, and two parents who loved their daughter enough to make choices they could never take back.
The truth had taken thirteen years to find its way home.
But it had found us.
And this time, nobody was leaving.
For my dear Amelia.
You were loved before you even knew what love was.
And you always will be.
