runs.text: The Fox Lady
A few millennia ago, in a year when volcanoes had turned farming lands to ash,
tsunamis flooded settlements, forests burned down, cold winds slashed across skin,
life… was on the brink of extinction. Creatures forgot their differences and
gathered to scavenge the remains to survive. Every new day was a threat, a face
melting in the scorching hot lava, a body shattering in the cold, a close one buried
in a watery grave. Hope was never the reason to stay alive. Fear was. The fear of
pain, the fear of death, the fear of… darkness.
Then, one day, the earth shook violently. The ground cracked. Volcanoes
erupted throughout the lands viciously; tsunamis rose higher than ever, and black
clouds covered the sky. At a time like this, the living could do nothing more than
stare. It was over. Suddenly, ice erupted from the ground, appearing from thin air,
barricading against the lava like a shield. Roaring fires fought back the tsunamis.
Water flooded into the forest, putting out their fires in an instant. A physical force
pulled the crust back together and sealed it. The ocean and volcanoes calmed. The
skies cleared. The rays of sunshine were like a balm that the living forgot long
before. And descending before them was a living, yet unlike any creature they had
ever seen. A kitsune. Or as they called her:
The Fox Lady
Towering at eight feet tall, she stood on two legs with the undeniable shape
and white fur of a fox, yet the gait of a woman of confidence and power. Her nine
tails flowed in sync behind her. Red markings accentuated her fur, most hidden by
clothes of such luxury only seen before in imaginations. Yet her eyes and her
gentle smile… reflected the warmth of a mother.
“Fear not,” she said, her voice echoing through the forest.
Gently, her feet touched the newly growing grass. She softly walked closer
toward the last remaining faction, who were gathered and stared at her in disbelief,
stopping a fair distance before them.
“For I have come to guide you. I hope to bring back the peace this realm lost
long ago.”
She swept her arm toward the crowd, and everyone felt their bodies sting but
only for a few seconds. When they straightened again, everyone realized their
wounds had healed. She smiled.
“Let me help. You all have suffered much through these godforsaken
decades.”
Her actions and voice captured the crowd immediately. She flowed through the
lands. Levitated above the waters. Everywhere she walked, the grass became
greener, the waters became calmer, the trees sang. Within a few years, the land
became almost a paradise. Families started. Settlements were being built. Crops
were being farmed. People laughed and roamed easily in peace, after decades of
suffering.
Among them was a little boy, no older than ten, perhaps. Curious, eyes full
of wonder, always peeking at her from behind a wall. He wore simple clothing.
Had nothing but a simple bow on his back. His hunting was sloppy. His every step
was anxious and nervous, wandering around the crowd, always trying to hide. She
noticed, of course. She smiled every time, and every time the boy would run away
when their eyes met. It amused her, and worried her.
It was a regular night like any other. The villagers were asleep. The kitsune
gently floated around humming a lullaby. Then her ears quivered. She looked
around and found the boy shivering around a fire that was barely burning. Her
lullaby ceased, and she landed on the soft ground. Her paws barely made a sound
as she walked over, her tails swaying behind her. The boy, as soon as he noticed
her, tried to scramble up and run. But this time she caught his arm.
“Easy, little one,” she said, gently pulling him to her side and sitting down.
Her tails gently wrapped around the boy like a blanket. Her hand went through his
hair, softly massaging his scalp. “Now, is that not better?” She smiled.
The boy didn’t reply, only averted his gaze. But she didn’t miss the flush on
his cheeks. It made her chuckle. She gazed at the fire, and it suddenly became
stronger, eliciting a wide-eyed gasp from the boy. She let the silence linger until
she felt the boy completely still in her tails.
“May I ask your name, little one?” she finally asked.
The boy tensed. Her expression softened.
“Shh, it is okay to be anxious. No need to pressure yourself. Just…
be
if you
want to for a while.”
Silence passed again, the only sound being that of the distant crickets and
the fire spitting out sparks.
“Frater…” the boy murmured shyly.
She smiled. “Frater, such a wonderful name. I… am Amri Kyōso. You may
call me Amri, dear.”
His face flushed again. She chuckled, the soft rumbling travelling down her
body into his. He averted his gaze again. She leaned down and gently nudged his
head with her snout.
“I do not mean to make you uncomfortable, Frater. I simply wish to know…
why a wonderful boy like you is roaming the nights alone and shivering. May I
know?” she asked softly.
He hesitated, snuggling in a bit closer. She welcomed it.
“I… don’t… have anyone to go to,” Frater finally replied, his voice close to
a whisper.
Her face instantly softened, the playfulness turning to maternal concern.
“Oh, poor dear. What about your guardians?”
The boy tensed again, tears rolling down his face. She instantly tightened her
tails a fraction more, gently wrapping her arms around and nuzzling her snout into
his hair.
“Shh, it’s okay. You are not required to tell me if you find the memory to be
a burden.”
Silence passed again. Frater sobbed gently, snuggling in as close as he could.
He breathed shakily, and finally spoke.
“They… died. In… a blizzard two years ago,” he said, wiping his tears.
“You should have come and spoken to me. Some here must be delighted to
have you.”
Frater shook his head. “No. T-They… offered. I-I don’t… want to.”
“Why not?”
“Because…” He exhaled shakily. “No home… feels comfortable.”
Amri sighed. “Ah, so you find difficulty reciprocating the warmth you lost.
Then you carry a heavy burden, Frater.”
He nodded. Silence passed again as Amri thought. Then she smiled again.
“How about… here? How do you find this warmth?”
He went silent again, his face flushing a bit deeper. “Better…” he muttered
shyly.
Amri chuckled, then gently used a paw to turn his head to meet her eyes.
“Then will you… let my warmth take care of you?”
His eyes widened. “But—”
“Ah ah,” Amri gently shushed him with her paw. “I would be nothing short
of content to do so.” The vulnerability in her face was practically shining now.
“You see, I have been… alone… for so long. Time has lost meaning for me. I have
always… found a strength in leadership, but have also yearned for companionship.
Someone I can simply converse or laugh with is… more than enough. As
temporary as it may be. Will you allow me that grace?”
For a while, Frater just stared, eyes wide, then turned to the fire that still
burned brightly. But he snuggled closer, leaning his head against her. She smiled,
already knowing the answer she needed. She didn’t say anything, simply rubbed
his scalp with her arm.
“I…” Frater started. “What do I… have to live for at this point?”
Amri’s hand froze, settling into his hair. She looked up at the sky where the
stars twinkled particularly brightly tonight.
“That is… a heavy question,” she said. “Sometimes, I believe, you should
simply… live.
Consider
, and live.”
“Consider?”
Amri nodded, turning her gaze back to him. “Consider the people, the
ground, consider
you
. A blind path… or a path paved by others may not be as safe
for you as it was for them. So, we think, we gamble… we consider. Live as
you
not what others think you are.”
“Hm,”
Frater yawned. Amri smiled and gently angled his body in her tails so his
head would rest comfortably against her. She continued her soothing. His eyes
drooped until they slowly closed. His breathing evened out, and Amri simply sat
there, watching the boy in her arms.
Kyōsō(
狂騒
Ten years later, everything fell apart. The guidance that had once blessed the lands
now sought to purify it. Amri had never been one for violence, but what she had
seen turned her worldview on its axis.
As the years passed after she arrived, something shifted within the living.
They became aggressive. They became ungrateful. They… craved more, demanded
more. Greed, lust, fame, and hatred created factions, wars… and bloodshed. They
belittled her. Went against her guidance, suffered, and still went against her just for
power, just to keep themselves seated in a high place among their peers. They stole
from her. Her belongings, the gold she was once so graciously offered for her
guidance were taken and plundered. Her fur became disheveled, marred by blood
on several occasions when she had to intervene in a fight. In private, she found
herself panting, eyes wide, having witnessed more malice, more suffering. Yet, she
convinced herself.
“They—They needed it more than I did. T-They simply are lost. They just…
needed more concrete guidance. They… they…”
One night, the breaking point arrived. She called every faction together, for
the first time using a forceful air barrier to pull the leaders to the center, and
confronted them. Openly accused them, and for the first time… felt pure
frustration. But the crowd didn’t accept it. They turned on her. Called her a
monster. A corrupted deity. A conniving fox. A false guide. A failed god.
That was the night everything changed. Her power surged, and the years of
fury broke out. Her fur turned greyer. The red markings that once accentuated her
beauty now turned a glowing purple, settling themselves like scars on her skin. The
gentle synchronized sway of her tails became erratic and uncoordinated. Her soft
tone was gone, replaced by the one of a mother scorned. Her eyes turned from
ocean blue to violent red.
“This world… never needed guidance,” she rasped. Her glowing eyes
fixated on the crowd, now trembling before her. She bared her claws. “It needs…
purification.”
No one… left alive that night. No body was found after the barrier was
lifted, only blood… and rotting organs.
Two centuries passed since what became known as
The Great Massacre
, or what
she called it,
The Start of the Cleanse
. Since then, the world has become almost
deafeningly quiet. Not the quiet one might enjoy, but the quiet that makes you
check your back a dozen times before taking a step forward.
The noon sun shone across the forest high in the mountains, tanning the
skins of some dead bodies that were rotting away. Someone walked past that to
reach the top. A boy, most likely a man, probably in early adulthood. He wore an
all-black, long trench coat and pants, paired with dark brown boots. His hands were
covered with dark fingerless gloves, designed with intricate red markings of some
kind. A light beard and barely noticeable mustache were visible on his face. He
stopped. A light breeze whistled past, ruffling his hair, along with something else.
Something strong.
“Who walks there?” A voice boomed. “There is no use in hiding, human.”
He stood and simply waited. A figure approached him. A kitsune. Amri. She
floated toward him, the trees bending slightly to give her space. She stopped a few
feet away. Her claws were bared. Fresh streaks of blood still clung to her fur. The
purple markings glowed steady and faint. The power exuding from her was intense
and suffocating, but he stood unfazed. Amri’s eyes scanned the human for a
moment, as if waiting for a movement or assessing if the prey was worth her time.
“Speak,” she commanded finally. “For what purpose do you stand here?”
Silence passed for a moment. The man stared at her, then sighed.
“I… didn’t come here to fight or argue,” he said calmly. “I wish to talk.
About—”
“There is nothing to talk about,” Amri interrupted, her power surging a little.
Her eyes narrowed. “If you come to negotiate, it means you reject my ways, thus
making you nothing less than filth.”
She raised her arm toward the man. A small purple ball of energy formed in
her palm.
“Begone,” she said, and fired.
The ball of energy surged forward with unnatural speed, reaching the man in
mere milliseconds. The boy stood still and smiled. Then something sliced through
the air, cutting the ball in half. The halves split off and blasted two trees behind
him. Amri’s eyes widened in surprise.
“Apologies,” the man said. “It’s a… safety measure of sorts.”
A low growl rumbled in Amri’s throat. “I will not allow you to disrupt
divine judgement.”
She charged up more energy balls and shot them towards the man. The man
simply dodged and swerved, as if avoiding mere rocks. Finding no other choice,
she lunged with her claws bared, swiping viciously. Yet again, the man only
dodged each attack. Amri growled and finally took a step back, straightening.
“You are a formidable foe. In fact, I refuse to believe you are human at all,”
she said, clasping two paws together and sliding each across the other arm. Her
tails curled inward as a shimmering gold line appeared, before solidifying into a
divine spear. “Thus, I choose not to delay your inevitable.”
“The Vega Spear…” the man muttered, surprised.
A small smirk graced her face, but disappeared the next second. “You have a
keen eye. Like always, Frater.”
Frater smiled. “So you did recognize me, and yet you chose to kill?”
Amri didn’t answer and instead charged. There it was again, the slice
through the air. Her ears quivered, and she quickly leaned back mid-motion to
avoid it. Frater raised his arm and caught it. Slowly, the invisibility wore off to
reveal a sword. Amri took another step back.
“The Victus Sword,” she said. “But I sense magic imbued within it.”
“You would be correct,” Frater replied, bringing the sword up front. “I
tampered with it a little.” His eyes softened. “Amri, please, I simply wish to talk to
you.”
“And I have already told you,” she started, changing her form. Her tails
curled inward again, summoning several energy balls that hovered around her. “We
have nothing to talk about. This world requires purification.” The grip on her spear
tightened. “You of all should know that best, Frater.”
Before Frater could respond, she used the spear to guide a ball toward him.
Frater swerved. The ball grazed his sword and crashed on the ground. He broke
into a run. Amri followed, firing one ball after the other. Frater dodged, cut, or
parried each of them. They crashed and made a crater where they landed. Amri
growled, her frustration growing by the second. She charged another energy ball at
the tip of her spear, about to shoot. Then Frater looked over his shoulder. Amri
hesitated, meeting his eyes for a split second. The energy concentration flickered.
Frater then skidded to a halt and planted his sword in the ground. Amri’s eyes
narrowed, and she stopped too. A suffocating pressure suddenly built around them.
Amri’s tails drooped. The spear in her hand slowly disintegrated into golden mist.
She stared at her hand, then at the sky.
“A dampening barrier,” Amri muttered. “Smart choice.”
Frater let go of the sword and stepped forward. “Right, but don’t worry.” He
lifted his hand. A few weak sparks erupted before diminishing to smoke. “I can’t
do anything either.”
“I find myself curious as to how you gained such a powerful spell,” she said,
turning back to him. “It should be virtually impossible for a human.”
Frater smiled. “Lots of things seem impossible. Yet some still happen. I, for
one, never thought I’d get to see… this side of you,” he said, gesturing to her.
Amri snarled. “Do not compare me with such trivial matters! You do not
understand the weight I carry.”
“Hardly anyone does or ever will,” he admitted with a sigh. “Can we…
please… just sit and talk? That's all I want to do.”
Amri’s claws bared, arms rising halfway. “And why are you so adamant
about seeking this conversation?”
“Perhaps… to understand you, let's say.” He shrugged.
For a moment she stared at him, then finally lowered her arms with a sigh
and relaxed, though still cautious.
“Fine. I suppose, out of slight amusement at you containing me, I am
inclined to offer some of my time to you. But make no mistake.” Her eyes glowed
faintly. “I do not intend to let you live once this barrier recedes. And considering
how much it has to dampen to keep us powerless, it will not be long. So, for your
sake, I hope you are quick.”
Frater chuckled. “Don’t worry, we have plenty of time. And something tells
me you might enjoy it more than you’d want to admit.”
He walked past her and looked around the area, collecting broken pieces of
wood. Amri followed him around, eyeing him carefully, but also with, perhaps, a
slight bit of curiosity.
“What are you doing?” she asked finally.
Frater gathered the wood and set them properly. “Preparing a fire just in
case. The night gets awfully cold.” He stood up and turned to Amri. “Do you have
a hoe of sorts?”
“A… hoe?” Amri asked, confused.
Frater nodded.
Amri exhaled sharply and turned around. “Stay here.”
She walked away, returning a minute later with a rusty hoe. A streak of
blood stained the blade.
“It belonged to a greedy farmer,” she said, tossing it to the ground. “But he
and his family are no more. As deserved.”
Frater picked up the hoe. “His family?”
Amri crossed her arms. “Yes, snakes breed more snakes. His deeds would
only carry over if his close ones were not dealt with.”
“I see.”
He turned around and started plowing the ground. Amri tilted her head,
staring in utter bewilderment. She watched him silently, sweat forming on his
forehead as he worked diligently. After making a row, she finally stepped forward
to ask.
“Exactly what are you doing?”
“Planting. I thought that was pretty clear.”
“You said you wanted to talk.”
“I did. And I am right now. I just wanted to also show you something.”
“Show what?”
“You’ll see.”
Amri sighed and settled herself on a log, staring at him. Her tails hung
behind her, lifeless. She felt irritated, but staring at him after so many years kept
her still. It even made her chest ache ever so slightly. She watched patiently for
hours as he plowed into the dirt, finally stopping after the sixth row and pulling
seed packets from his pockets. Amri stood up and approached him again.
“How long will this barrier stand?” she asked.
“Until we’re done,” Frater replied, spreading seeds over the fields.
“And when is that?”
“After I talk to you.”
“You are being vague.”
“Isn’t that the point?”
He offered her a smile and continued working. She stood there. Frater
finished and dusted his hands a minute later, then walked past her. She turned, and
was caught off guard. A small cabin stood there.
“These crops will take some time. Care for some tea?” Frater said, already
unlocking the door.
“How did this get here?” she asked, walking to the door, eyeing the cabin
carefully.
“What do you mean? It has always been here, or has time dulled your
senses?” Frater said with a chuckle.
Amri gave him a low growl and headed inside behind him. It was very
modest. Just a bed, a small kitchen area, and a table. The window gave a perfect
view of the crops and the cliff beyond it. Small leaves were already sprouting out
in the field. The sun was getting lower as afternoon hit.
“Magic crops. They grow fast but contain fewer nutrients,” Frater said,
setting water to boil.
“But they drain the land, making it useless for at least a few years,” Amri
said.
Frater shrugged. “I mean… you aren’t really cultivating crops so…”
“The surrounding trees require nutrients, Frater,” Amri sighed. “Magic crops
seep those away.”
“Eh, it’ll be fine,” Frater dismissed.
He put the tea leaves in and watched the water boil, while Amri stared
outside. Though she couldn’t help but steal glances, as if trying to piece something
together. Her eyes, which she used to judge for two centuries, softened
imperceptibly. After a few minutes of silence, Frater came back with two cups and
passed one to Amri. He sat opposite her and looked towards the crops, which
already had green, lively leaves. The sun was starting to get low. Amri stared at her
tea for a moment. Frater sipped his.
“Why are you here now, Frater?” she finally asked softly.
“Is it a crime to visit someone who took care of you?” he said. “If so, then I
plead guilty.”
Amri’s grip on the cup tightened fractionally. Her tails quivered before going
still again. “You know what I mean, Frater.”
“Maybe I do,” he replied, taking another sip. “But what if I don’t want to
answer?” He gestured to her tea. “Come on, drink. I want you to tell me how it is.”
Amri sat silently for a moment longer, then finally took a big sip. “Good. A
little light, but good.”
“Ah, I can’t ever seem to hit your taste buds, huh.” He sighed. “Well, better
luck next time.”
Silence passed as both sipped their tea. Amri finished first and set her cup
down gently. Frater followed a moment later with a satisfied sigh. They stared at
the crops.
“Do you remember what you used to tell me often, Amri?” he finally asked,
turning to her.
Amri hummed, looking at her grey fur and purple markings on her arm.
“Guidance leads to peace. Peace leads to enlightenment. Enlightenment leads to
prosperity.” Then, her eyes hardened again. “I missed a few lines back then.
Prosperity… doesn’t follow all. This partiality creates imbalance. It spreads greed
and envy. Thus the struggle. Thus… the purification.” Her claws bared once more.
Frater leaned on his chair and shook his head. “No.”
Amri’s eyes snapped toward him, glowing faintly. “No?”
“That’s not what you used to often say to me,” he said, holding her gaze
before looking back out the window. “We guide each other. We seek each other.
For one year, or a thousand, guidance is something passed down. Never withheld.
But… a seeker must never seek the answers. Only the way towards it. A guide
must never mark. They must point. For only the person seeking, or the person
guiding, knows whether the path is true or false.”
Amri went entirely silent. She turned away, her jaw tensing.
Frater smiled. “Trying to find a flaw? Good luck. Believe me, I tried two
centuries ago.” He chuckled, then stood up. “Well, it’s harvest time. Come, let’s see
how these turned out. Boy, am I hungry.”
He walked past her, stretching his shoulders while Amri sat still. Her grip on
the cup was so tight the ceramic cracked. She breathed shakily, her tails curling
around her as her body began to tremble. With a sharp effort, she let go of the cup
and concentrated on her palm. Her teeth bared. At first, there were faint glows that
diminished quickly. Then finally, a small green energy aura developed in her hand.
She brought the hand up and covered her eyes. The shaking subsided. Her tails
uncurled, dropping lifelessly behind her, though her breathing remained ragged as
she stared at the fractured ceramic. She looked up. Frater was still there, bent over
the fields with two baskets beside him. Exhaling shakily, she stood up and stepped
out into the open air. The sun was setting, painting the sky in hues of red and
violet. She stared at the sky for a moment, then turned to him.
“Good… Good…” Frater muttered, pulling up one vegetable after the other.
Amri closed the distance until she stood almost beside him. Just then, he
uprooted a rotten vegetable, making him sigh.
“Ah, man,” he groaned, tossing it into a separate basket before straightening
his back. “Well, guess this entire row is worthless now.”
He went along the row and started uprooting each vegetable, throwing them
into the same basket as the rotten one. Even good ones. Amri watched for a
moment, confused. Then finally stepped forward.
“What are you doing?”
“Hm?” Frater stopped and turned. “Throwing away the bad veggies. I
thought that was obvious.”
“Those are not bad. Among the ones you threw, only a handful were. The
rest were fine.”
“Well, yes, but they came in contact with the bad ones. So, they are rotten
too, right?”
Amri gave him a look as if she had heard the dumbest question in her
lifetime. “Are you choosing to act unintelligent, Frater? Was this all to simply
annoy me?”
“No, I was just stating the truth.”
“That cannot be farther from the truth. A rot cannot spread if the source is
simply plucked and removed, treated even, if possible. Why waste valuable
resources when you could simply recover them?”
A smile graced Frater’s face. He stood up again. “I see. So how does that
justify… you?”
Amri’s eyes narrowed. “Pardon?” A rumble came from her throat.
Frater bent down to the baskets and separated the good and bad ones
properly this time, before continuing to harvest the remaining rows.
“This field is like the first village you founded,” he started. “You set the
seeds. You took care of them. When some undesirable sprouting happened, you
treated them. But somewhere along the way too many things became undesirable,
and you chose to pluck the entire field. But you see…” He stood up and faced her.
“You said it yourself. That’s just one veggie. Remove the others, and they’ll be
fine. One rotten veggie isn’t enough to ruin the field unless it lingers.”
Amri’s claws bared again, but she clenched her fists and held it in. “I know
what you are trying to imply,” she said calmly. “But the creatures here are not the
same.”
“Could be true.” Frater thought for a second. “Could you perhaps…
enlighten me?”
“Firstly, they are not simple vegetables that can be moved with ease.”
“I’m well aware. But I’m asking why the analogy doesn’t apply. Why does
that not apply to the living?” he asked. There was no mockery or smugness in his
voice, simply a genuine question.
Amri crossed her arms, her claws slightly digging into her fur. “H-Humans
and other living beings have complex emotions and desires, unlike a simple
composition of nutrients.”
“Then, do you mean to imply those cannot be controlled or guided?”
Amri finally snapped. “It’s not like I haven’t tried!” she snarled, her voice
rising. “THEY… were the ones who showed me they were beyond reasoning.
Beyond guidance. BEYOND EVERYTHING. I tried for decades! Offering advice,
turning a blind eye to their blatant greed, caring every bit as much as I could! And
THIS…” She balled her hands into fists before her, grinding her teeth. Her tail
started swaying erratically behind her. “This is what they turned me into,” she
hissed.
Frater remained entirely calm, watching her for a moment. He looked at the
carrot he was currently holding, then turned to her. “And you chose to care?”
Amri’s gaze snapped up to him. “Chose to—Of course I chose to care! I was
meant to care!”
Frater shook his head gently. “Amri, it’s not how or when you chose to care.
It’s
what
you chose to care about. You cared about what others saw your actions as.
You let them change you. In a way, I’d suppose you sought validation from them
even when you knew better. Now, was that because of your prolonged isolation, or
simply because you didn’t know better? I can’t really tell.”
Amri froze. Her eyes widened. She stared at him, her tails abruptly going
still and dropping to the ground. Her mouth remained open, but no words came
out. Frater simply smiled and crouched down again to harvest the remaining ones.
While Amri silently just stared. It was like she wanted to say something, but for the
first time, didn’t know what. Frater finally finished and quickly dug up a hole.
After dumping the rotten vegetables in, he covered them and carried the basket of
good vegetables back.
“Could you light the fire here, please? The one inside will take ages to cook
this,” he said.
Amri still stared at the same spot, unmoving. Frater sighed. He walked by
and set the basket inside before coming out and gently nudging her. Amri blinked
and snapped out of it, straightening. Frater gestured to the gathered logs. Amri
looked at the logs, then at him, and nodded. He smiled and went back into the
cabin. She turned to the logs again, her eyes misting slightly. A drop of blood
splattered on a log. She quickly wiped her mouth and found blood on her paws.
Suddenly, a sharp sting ran through her head, making her fall to her knees,
grasping her head. Flashes crossed her mind. The begging. The blood. The scream.
The kills. Her cold stare. She gritted her teeth and desperately focused, feeling
some energy spark in her palm, before finally igniting into that green aura. She
gasped as it flooded into her head, coughing and breathing shakily. It took her a
moment to stabilize, but she sat there, staring at the stacked logs. Gently, she
extended a hand and closed her eyes, breathing slower but still ragged. A few
sparks appeared at first, then finally the logs ignited into a bright fire. She exhaled
shakily and sat on the ground, using her tails to hold her body. Her hands trembled
slightly.
“What is happening?” she muttered, rubbing her head.
She crossed her legs and tried to be as straight as she could, closing her eyes
again. The gentle breeze ruffled her fur as she remained still. The purple scars
glowed faintly before settling again. Her ears perked up at the sound of footsteps.
“Oh, nice. You got the fire going,” Frater said, carrying a bowl of cut
vegetables.
He came forth and set up a pot above the fire. Amri didn’t speak, or rather,
for the first time, she felt exhausted to do so. She simply watched. He put in water
and waited for it to boil, then added spices before stirring and finally dropped in
the vegetables and covered the pot. He sat down close to Amri. The sun had set
completely by now. The darkness of the night enveloped them as the crickets began
to chirp. For a solid minute, there was just silence. Amri sniffed the air.
“You’re making a stew?” she asked, her voice lower than usual.
Frater nodded. “Yeah, it’s the only thing I know, since there was only one
person who taught me.”
A small smile graced her face, disappearing quickly. She curled up to her
knees, using her tails as a backrest as she started into the fire. Meanwhile, Frater
stared at the sky with a smile.
“Tell me, Frater,” Amri started.
“Hm?” Frater turned to her.
A moment of silence passed. “If I am not meant to guide or care, then what
am I? Simply a tired kitsune?” she asked, her scars dimming further.
Frater hummed, turning back to the sky. “I… honestly don’t know.” He
sighed. “I don’t have every answer after all.” He paused for a moment. “You know
something interesting? I’m really bad at barrier magic. So, I know you have
enough power to break this barrier in an instant. Yet, you didn’t. Why?”
Silence rang again. Amri shifted, curling her tails around her this time. “I…
do not know.”
“Valid,” Frater said. He raised his arm, and finally, the pressure from before
completely evaporated. “There. That’s much better,” he said, stretching a bit.
Amri didn’t move an inch, staring as if trying to track where the sparks
spitting out from the fire went. Frater let the silence linger.
“Can you tell me… what I should do?” she finally asked, her voice the
lowest it has been in two centuries.
Frater thought for a moment. “I can’t just tell you to become good again. I
can’t tell you to completely stop pillaging either. I know it’s not as easy or simple.
All I can tell you is… live. Consider, and live.”
Amri’s ears quirked up. “Consider… what exactly?”
“Now that’s up to you, isn’t it? What do
you
want to consider?”
Amri didn’t reply. But her grey fur was starting to recede a little, the white
flickering out. She looked at her hands, now fully white with those long-forgotten
red markings. Frater finally stood up and took the pot off the fire. He poured the
stew into two bowls and handed one to her. Amri stared at it for a moment before
finally accepting it, uncurling her tails from around her. She took a spoonful and
chewed slowly.
“Hm.” Frater’s eyes narrowed. “Something’s missing…”
“Salt,” Amri then said. “A little bit more salt.”
“Ah, you’re right!” Frater groaned. “I don’t know why, but I always get that
wrong. It’s like a serious curse!”
A moment of silence passed. Amri finally smiled, then chuckled, then
finally… laughed.
“I’m serious!” Frater said, smiling. He laughed too.
They calmed down a minute later and ate the stew quietly, setting their
bowls down. They sat there quietly for a moment, looking out to the horizon
beyond the cliff. Amri’s tail swayed gently behind her, the grey fur receding a bit
farther. Frater finally stood up and walked toward the cliff. Amri’s eyes widened,
as if sensing his departure. She quickly stood up too.
“Wait!” she called. It was instinctive this time.
He stopped, glancing over his shoulder. “Yeah?”
Amri found herself at a loss for words, trying to think quickly. She rested a
hand on her chest. “Earlier, you mentioned you wanted to talk so you could
understand me,” she said, her now blue eyes locking onto his. “Did you?”
“Maybe,” he replied, offering a gentle shrug.
“That’s a vague answer.”
“It’s meant to be. The only one who can truly understand you is… you.”
Another breeze blew. Frater turned to the view, taking a deep breath,
smiling. Amri hesitated for a moment, then took a step forward.
“Well,” he sighed softly. “It’s about time I leave for now.”
“Wait.” This time her hand reached out as she took another step closer.
He turned fully to face her. “Hm?”
A single tear broke free, slowly rolling down and wetting the fur on her
cheek. She reached out further, but stopped just short of touching, as if doing so
might do something she might not be able to handle anymore.
“Are you… real?” she whispered, her eyes boring into him as if trying to
decipher the answer.
Frater gave a small, wry smile. “Elaborate.”
“Don’t… act coy,” she snapped softly, a spark of her old fury reigniting,
before softening instantly. “I remember that night. I remember well, you dying in
my arms all those years ago. Speared through the chest. The very night everything
shattered.”
“I was protecting your hoard,” he said.
“I know what you were protecting!” She exhaled, her breath ragged, closing
her eyes for a fraction of a second, trying to anchor herself. “I buried you with my
own two hands. So I am asking once more. Are you… actually here?”
Frater stared at her for a moment, then met her eyes. “I could be. I could not
be. This could all be in your head, but why must it mean it’s not real? Your feelings
are real after all. So, I’ll leave that up to you to consider.”
Amri remained silent for a moment. Then, a soft, traitorous laugh bubbled
up in her throat. For the first time in two hundred years, a genuine smile graced her
face. A maternal smile.
“You’re weird, you know that?” she asked, finally touching his cheek.
Frater chuckled warmly, leaning into the touch. “Is that a bad thing?”
Amri closed her eyes and exhaled. “No, it had never been.”
But when she opened her eyes again, he was gone. She was alone, standing
at the edge, her hand holding nothing but air. Another tear rolled down her face.
“Farewell,” she muttered, sniffling.
She turned. The field, the fire, the cabin, the covered-up hole were still there.
Yet, the man who did them wasn’t. She looked at her hands. They were dirty. Her
fur still had more grey than white, more purple scars than red markings, but it was
a change. She walked around and wondered for a moment, touching everything. It
felt real, yet so surreal. She turned to the fields and noticed a single wheat stalk
swinging in the air, surrounded by weeds. Gently, she stepped forward and cut
them out, piling the dirt closer to the wheat. To her, this wasn’t just a plant. It was a
way forward.

content: The Fox Lady
A few millennia ago, in a year when volcanoes had turned farming lands to ash,
tsunamis flooded settlements, forests burned down, cold winds slashed across skin,
life… was on the brink of extinction. Creatures forgot their differences and
gathered to scavenge the remains to survive. Every new day was a threat, a face
melting in the scorching hot lava, a body shattering in the cold, a close one buried
in a watery grave. Hope was never the reason to stay alive. Fear was. The fear of
pain, the fear of death, the fear of… darkness.
Then, one day, the earth shook violently. The ground cracked. Volcanoes
erupted throughout the lands viciously; tsunamis rose higher than ever, and black
clouds covered the sky. At a time like this, the living could do nothing more than
stare. It was over. Suddenly, ice erupted from the ground, appearing from thin air,
barricading against the lava like a shield. Roaring fires fought back the tsunamis.
Water flooded into the forest, putting out their fires in an instant. A physical force
pulled the crust back together and sealed it. The ocean and volcanoes calmed. The
skies cleared. The rays of sunshine were like a balm that the living forgot long
before. And descending before them was a living, yet unlike any creature they had
ever seen. A kitsune. Or as they called her: The Fox Lady.
Towering at eight feet tall, she stood on two legs with the undeniable shape
and white fur of a fox, yet the gait of a woman of confidence and power. Her nine
tails flowed in sync behind her. Red markings accentuated her fur, most hidden by
clothes of such luxury only seen before in imaginations. Yet her eyes and her
gentle smile… reflected the warmth of a mother.
“Fear not,” she said, her voice echoing through the forest.
Gently, her feet touched the newly growing grass. She softly walked closer
toward the last remaining faction, who were gathered and stared at her in disbelief,
stopping a fair distance before them.
“For I have come to guide you. I hope to bring back the peace this realm lost
long ago.”
She swept her arm toward the crowd, and everyone felt their bodies sting but
only for a few seconds. When they straightened again, everyone realized their
wounds had healed. She smiled.
“Let me help. You all have suffered much through these godforsaken
decades.”
Her actions and voice captured the crowd immediately. She flowed through the
lands. Levitated above the waters. Everywhere she walked, the grass became
greener, the waters became calmer, the trees sang. Within a few years, the land
became almost a paradise. Families started. Settlements were being built. Crops
were being farmed. People laughed and roamed easily in peace, after decades of
suffering.
Among them was a little boy, no older than ten, perhaps. Curious, eyes full
of wonder, always peeking at her from behind a wall. He wore simple clothing.
Had nothing but a simple bow on his back. His hunting was sloppy. His every step
was anxious and nervous, wandering around the crowd, always trying to hide. She
noticed, of course. She smiled every time, and every time the boy would run away
when their eyes met. It amused her, and worried her.
It was a regular night like any other. The villagers were asleep. The kitsune
gently floated around humming a lullaby. Then her ears quivered. She looked
around and found the boy shivering around a fire that was barely burning. Her
lullaby ceased, and she landed on the soft ground. Her paws barely made a sound
as she walked over, her tails swaying behind her. The boy, as soon as he noticed
her, tried to scramble up and run. But this time she caught his arm.
“Easy, little one,” she said, gently pulling him to her side and sitting down.
Her tails gently wrapped around the boy like a blanket. Her hand went through his
hair, softly massaging his scalp. “Now, is that not better?” She smiled.
The boy didn’t reply, only averted his gaze. But she didn’t miss the flush on
his cheeks. It made her chuckle. She gazed at the fire, and it suddenly became
stronger, eliciting a wide-eyed gasp from the boy. She let the silence linger until
she felt the boy completely still in her tails.
“May I ask your name, little one?” she finally asked.
The boy tensed. Her expression softened.
“Shh, it is okay to be anxious. No need to pressure yourself. Just… be if you
want to for a while.”
Silence passed again, the only sound being that of the distant crickets and
the fire spitting out sparks.
“Frater…” the boy murmured shyly.
She smiled. “Frater, such a wonderful name. I… am Amri Kyōso. You may
call me Amri, dear.”
His face flushed again. She chuckled, the soft rumbling travelling down her
body into his. He averted his gaze again. She leaned down and gently nudged his
head with her snout.
“I do not mean to make you uncomfortable, Frater. I simply wish to know…
why a wonderful boy like you is roaming the nights alone and shivering. May I
know?” she asked softly.
He hesitated, snuggling in a bit closer. She welcomed it.
“I… don’t… have anyone to go to,” Frater finally replied, his voice close to
a whisper.
Her face instantly softened, the playfulness turning to maternal concern.
“Oh, poor dear. What about your guardians?”
The boy tensed again, tears rolling down his face. She instantly tightened her
tails a fraction more, gently wrapping her arms around and nuzzling her snout into
his hair.
“Shh, it’s okay. You are not required to tell me if you find the memory to be
a burden.”
Silence passed again. Frater sobbed gently, snuggling in as close as he could.
He breathed shakily, and finally spoke.
“They… died. In… a blizzard two years ago,” he said, wiping his tears.
“You should have come and spoken to me. Some here must be delighted to
have you.”
Frater shook his head. “No. T-They… offered. I-I don’t… want to.”
“Why not?”
“Because…” He exhaled shakily. “No home… feels comfortable.”
Amri sighed. “Ah, so you find difficulty reciprocating the warmth you lost.
Then you carry a heavy burden, Frater.”
He nodded. Silence passed again as Amri thought. Then she smiled again.
“How about… here? How do you find this warmth?”
He went silent again, his face flushing a bit deeper. “Better…” he muttered
shyly.
Amri chuckled, then gently used a paw to turn his head to meet her eyes.
“Then will you… let my warmth take care of you?”
His eyes widened. “But—”
“Ah ah,” Amri gently shushed him with her paw. “I would be nothing short
of content to do so.” The vulnerability in her face was practically shining now.
“You see, I have been… alone… for so long. Time has lost meaning for me. I have
always… found a strength in leadership, but have also yearned for companionship.
Someone I can simply converse or laugh with is… more than enough. As
temporary as it may be. Will you allow me that grace?”
For a while, Frater just stared, eyes wide, then turned to the fire that still
burned brightly. But he snuggled closer, leaning his head against her. She smiled,
already knowing the answer she needed. She didn’t say anything, simply rubbed
his scalp with her arm.
“I…” Frater started. “What do I… have to live for at this point?”
Amri’s hand froze, settling into his hair. She looked up at the sky where the
stars twinkled particularly brightly tonight.
“That is… a heavy question,” she said. “Sometimes, I believe, you should
simply… live. Consider, and live.”
“Consider?”
Amri nodded, turning her gaze back to him. “Consider the people, the
ground, consider you. A blind path… or a path paved by others may not be as safe
for you as it was for them. So, we think, we gamble… we consider. Live as you,
not what others think you are.”
“Hm,”
Frater yawned. Amri smiled and gently angled his body in her tails so his
head would rest comfortably against her. She continued her soothing. His eyes
drooped until they slowly closed. His breathing evened out, and Amri simply sat
there, watching the boy in her arms.
Kyōsō(狂騒)
Ten years later, everything fell apart. The guidance that had once blessed the lands
now sought to purify it. Amri had never been one for violence, but what she had
seen turned her worldview on its axis.
As the years passed after she arrived, something shifted within the living.
They became aggressive. They became ungrateful. They… craved more, demanded
more. Greed, lust, fame, and hatred created factions, wars… and bloodshed. They
belittled her. Went against her guidance, suffered, and still went against her just for
power, just to keep themselves seated in a high place among their peers. They stole
from her. Her belongings, the gold she was once so graciously offered for her
guidance were taken and plundered. Her fur became disheveled, marred by blood
on several occasions when she had to intervene in a fight. In private, she found
herself panting, eyes wide, having witnessed more malice, more suffering. Yet, she
convinced herself.
“They—They needed it more than I did. T-They simply are lost. They just…
needed more concrete guidance. They… they…”
One night, the breaking point arrived. She called every faction together, for
the first time using a forceful air barrier to pull the leaders to the center, and
confronted them. Openly accused them, and for the first time… felt pure
frustration. But the crowd didn’t accept it. They turned on her. Called her a
monster. A corrupted deity. A conniving fox. A false guide. A failed god.
That was the night everything changed. Her power surged, and the years of
fury broke out. Her fur turned greyer. The red markings that once accentuated her
beauty now turned a glowing purple, settling themselves like scars on her skin. The
gentle synchronized sway of her tails became erratic and uncoordinated. Her soft
tone was gone, replaced by the one of a mother scorned. Her eyes turned from
ocean blue to violent red.
“This world… never needed guidance,” she rasped. Her glowing eyes
fixated on the crowd, now trembling before her. She bared her claws. “It needs…
purification.”
No one… left alive that night. No body was found after the barrier was
lifted, only blood… and rotting organs.
Two centuries passed since what became known as The Great Massacre, or what
she called it, The Start of the Cleanse. Since then, the world has become almost
deafeningly quiet. Not the quiet one might enjoy, but the quiet that makes you
check your back a dozen times before taking a step forward.
The noon sun shone across the forest high in the mountains, tanning the
skins of some dead bodies that were rotting away. Someone walked past that to
reach the top. A boy, most likely a man, probably in early adulthood. He wore an
all-black, long trench coat and pants, paired with dark brown boots. His hands were
covered with dark fingerless gloves, designed with intricate red markings of some
kind. A light beard and barely noticeable mustache were visible on his face. He
stopped. A light breeze whistled past, ruffling his hair, along with something else.
Something strong.
“Who walks there?” A voice boomed. “There is no use in hiding, human.”
He stood and simply waited. A figure approached him. A kitsune. Amri. She
floated toward him, the trees bending slightly to give her space. She stopped a few
feet away. Her claws were bared. Fresh streaks of blood still clung to her fur. The
purple markings glowed steady and faint. The power exuding from her was intense
and suffocating, but he stood unfazed. Amri’s eyes scanned the human for a
moment, as if waiting for a movement or assessing if the prey was worth her time.
“Speak,” she commanded finally. “For what purpose do you stand here?”
Silence passed for a moment. The man stared at her, then sighed.
“I… didn’t come here to fight or argue,” he said calmly. “I wish to talk.
About—”
“There is nothing to talk about,” Amri interrupted, her power surging a little.
Her eyes narrowed. “If you come to negotiate, it means you reject my ways, thus
making you nothing less than filth.”
She raised her arm toward the man. A small purple ball of energy formed in
her palm.
“Begone,” she said, and fired.
The ball of energy surged forward with unnatural speed, reaching the man in
mere milliseconds. The boy stood still and smiled. Then something sliced through
the air, cutting the ball in half. The halves split off and blasted two trees behind
him. Amri’s eyes widened in surprise.
“Apologies,” the man said. “It’s a… safety measure of sorts.”
A low growl rumbled in Amri’s throat. “I will not allow you to disrupt
divine judgement.”
She charged up more energy balls and shot them towards the man. The man
simply dodged and swerved, as if avoiding mere rocks. Finding no other choice,
she lunged with her claws bared, swiping viciously. Yet again, the man only
dodged each attack. Amri growled and finally took a step back, straightening.
“You are a formidable foe. In fact, I refuse to believe you are human at all,”
she said, clasping two paws together and sliding each across the other arm. Her
tails curled inward as a shimmering gold line appeared, before solidifying into a
divine spear. “Thus, I choose not to delay your inevitable.”
“The Vega Spear…” the man muttered, surprised.
A small smirk graced her face, but disappeared the next second. “You have a
keen eye. Like always, Frater.”
Frater smiled. “So you did recognize me, and yet you chose to kill?”
Amri didn’t answer and instead charged. There it was again, the slice
through the air. Her ears quivered, and she quickly leaned back mid-motion to
avoid it. Frater raised his arm and caught it. Slowly, the invisibility wore off to
reveal a sword. Amri took another step back.
“The Victus Sword,” she said. “But I sense magic imbued within it.”
“You would be correct,” Frater replied, bringing the sword up front. “I
tampered with it a little.” His eyes softened. “Amri, please, I simply wish to talk to
you.”
“And I have already told you,” she started, changing her form. Her tails
curled inward again, summoning several energy balls that hovered around her. “We
have nothing to talk about. This world requires purification.” The grip on her spear
tightened. “You of all should know that best, Frater.”
Before Frater could respond, she used the spear to guide a ball toward him.
Frater swerved. The ball grazed his sword and crashed on the ground. He broke
into a run. Amri followed, firing one ball after the other. Frater dodged, cut, or
parried each of them. They crashed and made a crater where they landed. Amri
growled, her frustration growing by the second. She charged another energy ball at
the tip of her spear, about to shoot. Then Frater looked over his shoulder. Amri
hesitated, meeting his eyes for a split second. The energy concentration flickered.
Frater then skidded to a halt and planted his sword in the ground. Amri’s eyes
narrowed, and she stopped too. A suffocating pressure suddenly built around them.
Amri’s tails drooped. The spear in her hand slowly disintegrated into golden mist.
She stared at her hand, then at the sky.
“A dampening barrier,” Amri muttered. “Smart choice.”
Frater let go of the sword and stepped forward. “Right, but don’t worry.” He
lifted his hand. A few weak sparks erupted before diminishing to smoke. “I can’t
do anything either.”
“I find myself curious as to how you gained such a powerful spell,” she said,
turning back to him. “It should be virtually impossible for a human.”
Frater smiled. “Lots of things seem impossible. Yet some still happen. I, for
one, never thought I’d get to see… this side of you,” he said, gesturing to her.
Amri snarled. “Do not compare me with such trivial matters! You do not
understand the weight I carry.”
“Hardly anyone does or ever will,” he admitted with a sigh. “Can we…
please… just sit and talk? That's all I want to do.”
Amri’s claws bared, arms rising halfway. “And why are you so adamant
about seeking this conversation?”
“Perhaps… to understand you, let's say.” He shrugged.
For a moment she stared at him, then finally lowered her arms with a sigh
and relaxed, though still cautious.
“Fine. I suppose, out of slight amusement at you containing me, I am
inclined to offer some of my time to you. But make no mistake.” Her eyes glowed
faintly. “I do not intend to let you live once this barrier recedes. And considering
how much it has to dampen to keep us powerless, it will not be long. So, for your
sake, I hope you are quick.”
Frater chuckled. “Don’t worry, we have plenty of time. And something tells
me you might enjoy it more than you’d want to admit.”
He walked past her and looked around the area, collecting broken pieces of
wood. Amri followed him around, eyeing him carefully, but also with, perhaps, a
slight bit of curiosity.
“What are you doing?” she asked finally.
Frater gathered the wood and set them properly. “Preparing a fire just in
case. The night gets awfully cold.” He stood up and turned to Amri. “Do you have
a hoe of sorts?”
“A… hoe?” Amri asked, confused.
Frater nodded.
Amri exhaled sharply and turned around. “Stay here.”
She walked away, returning a minute later with a rusty hoe. A streak of
blood stained the blade.
“It belonged to a greedy farmer,” she said, tossing it to the ground. “But he
and his family are no more. As deserved.”
Frater picked up the hoe. “His family?”
Amri crossed her arms. “Yes, snakes breed more snakes. His deeds would
only carry over if his close ones were not dealt with.”
“I see.”
He turned around and started plowing the ground. Amri tilted her head,
staring in utter bewilderment. She watched him silently, sweat forming on his
forehead as he worked diligently. After making a row, she finally stepped forward
to ask.
“Exactly what are you doing?”
“Planting. I thought that was pretty clear.”
“You said you wanted to talk.”
“I did. And I am right now. I just wanted to also show you something.”
“Show what?”
“You’ll see.”
Amri sighed and settled herself on a log, staring at him. Her tails hung
behind her, lifeless. She felt irritated, but staring at him after so many years kept
her still. It even made her chest ache ever so slightly. She watched patiently for
hours as he plowed into the dirt, finally stopping after the sixth row and pulling
seed packets from his pockets. Amri stood up and approached him again.
“How long will this barrier stand?” she asked.
“Until we’re done,” Frater replied, spreading seeds over the fields.
“And when is that?”
“After I talk to you.”
“You are being vague.”
“Isn’t that the point?”
He offered her a smile and continued working. She stood there. Frater
finished and dusted his hands a minute later, then walked past her. She turned, and
was caught off guard. A small cabin stood there.
“These crops will take some time. Care for some tea?” Frater said, already
unlocking the door.
“How did this get here?” she asked, walking to the door, eyeing the cabin
carefully.
“What do you mean? It has always been here, or has time dulled your
senses?” Frater said with a chuckle.
Amri gave him a low growl and headed inside behind him. It was very
modest. Just a bed, a small kitchen area, and a table. The window gave a perfect
view of the crops and the cliff beyond it. Small leaves were already sprouting out
in the field. The sun was getting lower as afternoon hit.
“Magic crops. They grow fast but contain fewer nutrients,” Frater said,
setting water to boil.
“But they drain the land, making it useless for at least a few years,” Amri
said.
Frater shrugged. “I mean… you aren’t really cultivating crops so…”
“The surrounding trees require nutrients, Frater,” Amri sighed. “Magic crops
seep those away.”
“Eh, it’ll be fine,” Frater dismissed.
He put the tea leaves in and watched the water boil, while Amri stared
outside. Though she couldn’t help but steal glances, as if trying to piece something
together. Her eyes, which she used to judge for two centuries, softened
imperceptibly. After a few minutes of silence, Frater came back with two cups and
passed one to Amri. He sat opposite her and looked towards the crops, which
already had green, lively leaves. The sun was starting to get low. Amri stared at her
tea for a moment. Frater sipped his.
“Why are you here now, Frater?” she finally asked softly.
“Is it a crime to visit someone who took care of you?” he said. “If so, then I
plead guilty.”
Amri’s grip on the cup tightened fractionally. Her tails quivered before going
still again. “You know what I mean, Frater.”
“Maybe I do,” he replied, taking another sip. “But what if I don’t want to
answer?” He gestured to her tea. “Come on, drink. I want you to tell me how it is.”
Amri sat silently for a moment longer, then finally took a big sip. “Good. A
little light, but good.”
“Ah, I can’t ever seem to hit your taste buds, huh.” He sighed. “Well, better
luck next time.”
Silence passed as both sipped their tea. Amri finished first and set her cup
down gently. Frater followed a moment later with a satisfied sigh. They stared at
the crops.
“Do you remember what you used to tell me often, Amri?” he finally asked,
turning to her.
Amri hummed, looking at her grey fur and purple markings on her arm.
“Guidance leads to peace. Peace leads to enlightenment. Enlightenment leads to
prosperity.” Then, her eyes hardened again. “I missed a few lines back then.
Prosperity… doesn’t follow all. This partiality creates imbalance. It spreads greed
and envy. Thus the struggle. Thus… the purification.” Her claws bared once more.
Frater leaned on his chair and shook his head. “No.”
Amri’s eyes snapped toward him, glowing faintly. “No?”
“That’s not what you used to often say to me,” he said, holding her gaze
before looking back out the window. “We guide each other. We seek each other.
For one year, or a thousand, guidance is something passed down. Never withheld.
But… a seeker must never seek the answers. Only the way towards it. A guide
must never mark. They must point. For only the person seeking, or the person
guiding, knows whether the path is true or false.”
Amri went entirely silent. She turned away, her jaw tensing.
Frater smiled. “Trying to find a flaw? Good luck. Believe me, I tried two
centuries ago.” He chuckled, then stood up. “Well, it’s harvest time. Come, let’s see
how these turned out. Boy, am I hungry.”
He walked past her, stretching his shoulders while Amri sat still. Her grip on
the cup was so tight the ceramic cracked. She breathed shakily, her tails curling
around her as her body began to tremble. With a sharp effort, she let go of the cup
and concentrated on her palm. Her teeth bared. At first, there were faint glows that
diminished quickly. Then finally, a small green energy aura developed in her hand.
She brought the hand up and covered her eyes. The shaking subsided. Her tails
uncurled, dropping lifelessly behind her, though her breathing remained ragged as
she stared at the fractured ceramic. She looked up. Frater was still there, bent over
the fields with two baskets beside him. Exhaling shakily, she stood up and stepped
out into the open air. The sun was setting, painting the sky in hues of red and
violet. She stared at the sky for a moment, then turned to him.
“Good… Good…” Frater muttered, pulling up one vegetable after the other.
Amri closed the distance until she stood almost beside him. Just then, he
uprooted a rotten vegetable, making him sigh.
“Ah, man,” he groaned, tossing it into a separate basket before straightening
his back. “Well, guess this entire row is worthless now.”
He went along the row and started uprooting each vegetable, throwing them
into the same basket as the rotten one. Even good ones. Amri watched for a
moment, confused. Then finally stepped forward.
“What are you doing?”
“Hm?” Frater stopped and turned. “Throwing away the bad veggies. I
thought that was obvious.”
“Those are not bad. Among the ones you threw, only a handful were. The
rest were fine.”
“Well, yes, but they came in contact with the bad ones. So, they are rotten
too, right?”
Amri gave him a look as if she had heard the dumbest question in her
lifetime. “Are you choosing to act unintelligent, Frater? Was this all to simply
annoy me?”
“No, I was just stating the truth.”
“That cannot be farther from the truth. A rot cannot spread if the source is
simply plucked and removed, treated even, if possible. Why waste valuable
resources when you could simply recover them?”
A smile graced Frater’s face. He stood up again. “I see. So how does that
justify… you?”
Amri’s eyes narrowed. “Pardon?” A rumble came from her throat.
Frater bent down to the baskets and separated the good and bad ones
properly this time, before continuing to harvest the remaining rows.
“This field is like the first village you founded,” he started. “You set the
seeds. You took care of them. When some undesirable sprouting happened, you
treated them. But somewhere along the way too many things became undesirable,
and you chose to pluck the entire field. But you see…” He stood up and faced her.
“You said it yourself. That’s just one veggie. Remove the others, and they’ll be
fine. One rotten veggie isn’t enough to ruin the field unless it lingers.”
Amri’s claws bared again, but she clenched her fists and held it in. “I know
what you are trying to imply,” she said calmly. “But the creatures here are not the
same.”
“Could be true.” Frater thought for a second. “Could you perhaps…
enlighten me?”
“Firstly, they are not simple vegetables that can be moved with ease.”
“I’m well aware. But I’m asking why the analogy doesn’t apply. Why does
that not apply to the living?” he asked. There was no mockery or smugness in his
voice, simply a genuine question.
Amri crossed her arms, her claws slightly digging into her fur. “H-Humans
and other living beings have complex emotions and desires, unlike a simple
composition of nutrients.”
“Then, do you mean to imply those cannot be controlled or guided?”
Amri finally snapped. “It’s not like I haven’t tried!” she snarled, her voice
rising. “THEY… were the ones who showed me they were beyond reasoning.
Beyond guidance. BEYOND EVERYTHING. I tried for decades! Offering advice,
turning a blind eye to their blatant greed, caring every bit as much as I could! And
THIS…” She balled her hands into fists before her, grinding her teeth. Her tail
started swaying erratically behind her. “This is what they turned me into,” she
hissed.
Frater remained entirely calm, watching her for a moment. He looked at the
carrot he was currently holding, then turned to her. “And you chose to care?”
Amri’s gaze snapped up to him. “Chose to—Of course I chose to care! I was
meant to care!”
Frater shook his head gently. “Amri, it’s not how or when you chose to care.
It’s what you chose to care about. You cared about what others saw your actions as.
You let them change you. In a way, I’d suppose you sought validation from them
even when you knew better. Now, was that because of your prolonged isolation, or
simply because you didn’t know better? I can’t really tell.”
Amri froze. Her eyes widened. She stared at him, her tails abruptly going
still and dropping to the ground. Her mouth remained open, but no words came
out. Frater simply smiled and crouched down again to harvest the remaining ones.
While Amri silently just stared. It was like she wanted to say something, but for the
first time, didn’t know what. Frater finally finished and quickly dug up a hole.
After dumping the rotten vegetables in, he covered them and carried the basket of
good vegetables back.
“Could you light the fire here, please? The one inside will take ages to cook
this,” he said.
Amri still stared at the same spot, unmoving. Frater sighed. He walked by
and set the basket inside before coming out and gently nudging her. Amri blinked
and snapped out of it, straightening. Frater gestured to the gathered logs. Amri
looked at the logs, then at him, and nodded. He smiled and went back into the
cabin. She turned to the logs again, her eyes misting slightly. A drop of blood
splattered on a log. She quickly wiped her mouth and found blood on her paws.
Suddenly, a sharp sting ran through her head, making her fall to her knees,
grasping her head. Flashes crossed her mind. The begging. The blood. The scream.
The kills. Her cold stare. She gritted her teeth and desperately focused, feeling
some energy spark in her palm, before finally igniting into that green aura. She
gasped as it flooded into her head, coughing and breathing shakily. It took her a
moment to stabilize, but she sat there, staring at the stacked logs. Gently, she
extended a hand and closed her eyes, breathing slower but still ragged. A few
sparks appeared at first, then finally the logs ignited into a bright fire. She exhaled
shakily and sat on the ground, using her tails to hold her body. Her hands trembled
slightly.
“What is happening?” she muttered, rubbing her head.
She crossed her legs and tried to be as straight as she could, closing her eyes
again. The gentle breeze ruffled her fur as she remained still. The purple scars
glowed faintly before settling again. Her ears perked up at the sound of footsteps.
“Oh, nice. You got the fire going,” Frater said, carrying a bowl of cut
vegetables.
He came forth and set up a pot above the fire. Amri didn’t speak, or rather,
for the first time, she felt exhausted to do so. She simply watched. He put in water
and waited for it to boil, then added spices before stirring and finally dropped in
the vegetables and covered the pot. He sat down close to Amri. The sun had set
completely by now. The darkness of the night enveloped them as the crickets began
to chirp. For a solid minute, there was just silence. Amri sniffed the air.
“You’re making a stew?” she asked, her voice lower than usual.
Frater nodded. “Yeah, it’s the only thing I know, since there was only one
person who taught me.”
A small smile graced her face, disappearing quickly. She curled up to her
knees, using her tails as a backrest as she started into the fire. Meanwhile, Frater
stared at the sky with a smile.
“Tell me, Frater,” Amri started.
“Hm?” Frater turned to her.
A moment of silence passed. “If I am not meant to guide or care, then what
am I? Simply a tired kitsune?” she asked, her scars dimming further.
Frater hummed, turning back to the sky. “I… honestly don’t know.” He
sighed. “I don’t have every answer after all.” He paused for a moment. “You know
something interesting? I’m really bad at barrier magic. So, I know you have
enough power to break this barrier in an instant. Yet, you didn’t. Why?”
Silence rang again. Amri shifted, curling her tails around her this time. “I…
do not know.”
“Valid,” Frater said. He raised his arm, and finally, the pressure from before
completely evaporated. “There. That’s much better,” he said, stretching a bit.
Amri didn’t move an inch, staring as if trying to track where the sparks
spitting out from the fire went. Frater let the silence linger.
“Can you tell me… what I should do?” she finally asked, her voice the
lowest it has been in two centuries.
Frater thought for a moment. “I can’t just tell you to become good again. I
can’t tell you to completely stop pillaging either. I know it’s not as easy or simple.
All I can tell you is… live. Consider, and live.”
Amri’s ears quirked up. “Consider… what exactly?”
“Now that’s up to you, isn’t it? What do you want to consider?”
Amri didn’t reply. But her grey fur was starting to recede a little, the white
flickering out. She looked at her hands, now fully white with those long-forgotten
red markings. Frater finally stood up and took the pot off the fire. He poured the
stew into two bowls and handed one to her. Amri stared at it for a moment before
finally accepting it, uncurling her tails from around her. She took a spoonful and
chewed slowly.
“Hm.” Frater’s eyes narrowed. “Something’s missing…”
“Salt,” Amri then said. “A little bit more salt.”
“Ah, you’re right!” Frater groaned. “I don’t know why, but I always get that
wrong. It’s like a serious curse!”
A moment of silence passed. Amri finally smiled, then chuckled, then
finally… laughed.
“I’m serious!” Frater said, smiling. He laughed too.
They calmed down a minute later and ate the stew quietly, setting their
bowls down. They sat there quietly for a moment, looking out to the horizon
beyond the cliff. Amri’s tail swayed gently behind her, the grey fur receding a bit
farther. Frater finally stood up and walked toward the cliff. Amri’s eyes widened,
as if sensing his departure. She quickly stood up too.
“Wait!” she called. It was instinctive this time.
He stopped, glancing over his shoulder. “Yeah?”
Amri found herself at a loss for words, trying to think quickly. She rested a
hand on her chest. “Earlier, you mentioned you wanted to talk so you could
understand me,” she said, her now blue eyes locking onto his. “Did you?”
“Maybe,” he replied, offering a gentle shrug.
“That’s a vague answer.”
“It’s meant to be. The only one who can truly understand you is… you.”
Another breeze blew. Frater turned to the view, taking a deep breath,
smiling. Amri hesitated for a moment, then took a step forward.
“Well,” he sighed softly. “It’s about time I leave for now.”
“Wait.” This time her hand reached out as she took another step closer.
He turned fully to face her. “Hm?”
A single tear broke free, slowly rolling down and wetting the fur on her
cheek. She reached out further, but stopped just short of touching, as if doing so
might do something she might not be able to handle anymore.
“Are you… real?” she whispered, her eyes boring into him as if trying to
decipher the answer.
Frater gave a small, wry smile. “Elaborate.”
“Don’t… act coy,” she snapped softly, a spark of her old fury reigniting,
before softening instantly. “I remember that night. I remember well, you dying in
my arms all those years ago. Speared through the chest. The very night everything
shattered.”
“I was protecting your hoard,” he said.
“I know what you were protecting!” She exhaled, her breath ragged, closing
her eyes for a fraction of a second, trying to anchor herself. “I buried you with my
own two hands. So I am asking once more. Are you… actually here?”
Frater stared at her for a moment, then met her eyes. “I could be. I could not
be. This could all be in your head, but why must it mean it’s not real? Your feelings
are real after all. So, I’ll leave that up to you to consider.”
Amri remained silent for a moment. Then, a soft, traitorous laugh bubbled
up in her throat. For the first time in two hundred years, a genuine smile graced her
face. A maternal smile.
“You’re weird, you know that?” she asked, finally touching his cheek.
Frater chuckled warmly, leaning into the touch. “Is that a bad thing?”
Amri closed her eyes and exhaled. “No, it had never been.”
But when she opened her eyes again, he was gone. She was alone, standing
at the edge, her hand holding nothing but air. Another tear rolled down her face.
“Farewell,” she muttered, sniffling.
She turned. The field, the fire, the cabin, the covered-up hole were still there.
Yet, the man who did them wasn’t. She looked at her hands. They were dirty. Her
fur still had more grey than white, more purple scars than red markings, but it was
a change. She walked around and wondered for a moment, touching everything. It
felt real, yet so surreal. She turned to the fields and noticed a single wheat stalk
swinging in the air, surrounded by weeds. Gently, she stepped forward and cut
them out, piling the dirt closer to the wheat. To her, this wasn’t just a plant. It was a
way forward.
excerpt: The Fox Lady
